body: A physical ring-shaped structure spanning two points in space, creating a stable wormhole link between distant solar systems. Its parameters are ring mass (diameter), power grid (fuel consumption), and connection topology (which systems it links). It persists through player maintenance — refueling the ring, repairing structural damage, and keeping the power grid online. A stargate is the fundamental link in the EVE network: each gate is a single edge in the topology graph of New Eden, and the value of any system is a function of how many gates connect to it.

A modular, player-assembled structure that can be placed in any nullsec or lowsec system (or flown between systems as a mobile citadel). Its parameters are module composition (combat, industrial, or logistics modules), fuel type (mineral, ice, or gas), and structural integrity (hit points that degrade under fire). It persists through fuel consumption and module replacement. A citadel is the nullsec equivalent of a customs-office: it provides a positional advantage (tax collection, docking, manufacturing) and serves as a corporate anchor point in unclaimed space. The key distinction from a customs-office is mobility — a citadel can move, while a customs-office is fixed to a system.

A natural celestial body — a sphere of rock, ice, or gas — made economically available through EVE Online's planetary interaction system. Its parameters are type (barren, arid, ocean, gas giant, etc.), resources (up to four extractable commodities), and orbital distance from its star (affecting temperature and resource yield). It becomes an economic construct when a corporation claims it and establishes extraction infrastructure: the planet persists as a corporation through ongoing extraction, empire maintenance, and resource distribution to manufacturing chains. A planet is the substrate of the EVE industrial economy — without planets, there are no raw materials for blueprints, citadels, or fleets. The natural object becomes a corporation the moment humans impose extraction parameters upon it.

The authored simulation of a celestial body: a sphere of rock, ice, or gas placed in EVE Online's universe map with defined resources (up to four extractable commodities), orbital parameters (distance from its star, rotation rate), and visual rendering (atmosphere, surface features). Its parameters are type (barren, arid, ocean, gas giant, etc.), resource composition, and orbital position; it persists through the server that renders it and the extraction infrastructure that corporations maintain upon it. A planet is the substrate of the EVE industrial economy — the authored simulation of nature, made economic through planetary interaction. Distinct from the natural body it represents: the natural sphere exists whether EVE runs or not; the eve-planet exists only when authored and rendered by the game engine. In EVE, even nature is made.

[formal: Planeta Corporatum | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A player-constructed fixed physical structure anchored to a point in space within EVE Online, serving as a hub for docking, industry, and trade. Its parameters are size (tier I–V), module composition (offices, bays, factories), power grid (fuel consumption), and location (primary or secondary star system). It persists through the server that renders it, the fuel that powers it, and the corporation that maintains it. A station is the fixed counterpart to the mobile citadel: where the citadel moves, the station holds ground. It concentrates the functions of customs-office (taxation), blueprint-research (research labs), and manufacturing (production lines) into a single anchored structure.

[formal: Statio Corporata | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

An authored celestial body smaller than a planet, orbiting a planet or the system's sun within EVE Online's universe map. Its parameters are size (radius), resource composition (typically high-value ores like pyrite, mercury, and osmium), orbital distance from its parent planet, and surface features (craters, ice deposits, volcanic vents). It persists through the server that renders it and the mining infrastructure — extractors and haulers — that corporations deploy on its surface. A moon is the high-value counterpart to the planet: while planets provide bulk raw materials for basic manufacturing, moons provide the refined and rare ores needed for advanced ships, structures, and ammunition. Its gravitational influence creates orbital lanes and gravitational anomalies used for strategic positioning.

[formal: Luna Corporata | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

A player-controlled or AI-piloted navigable construct in EVE Online, assembled from modules (hull, armor, shields, weapons, propulsion, utility) into a functional whole. Its parameters are class (frigate to supercarrier), module composition, hitpoints, speed, and capacitor capacity. It persists through the server that renders it, the fuel (oxygen/charge) that powers it, and the corporation that maintains its modules and repairs damage. A ship is the primary vehicle of EVE: it traverses systems, engages in combat, conducts mining, and transports cargo. Distinct from the station (fixed infrastructure) and the citadel (modular base): the ship is mobile, modular, and the player-facing expression of EVE industrial design.

[formal: Navis Corporata | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

A self-executing agreement encoded as computer software, deployed on a blockchain or distributed ledger. Its parameters are source code (the contract logic), deployment address (on-chain identity), and gas cost (execution fee). It persists through the consensus of the network: as long as nodes maintain the ledger and execute the code, the smart-contract lives. A smart-contract automates the enforcement of terms — when condition A is met, action B executes without intermediary. Distinct from a traditional contract (which requires human interpretation and enforcement): the smart-contract enforces itself through code and cryptography. It is the legal instrument digitized.\n\n[formal: Contractum Automatium | substrate: information | horizon: as-long-as-ledger | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

An authored tunnel in EVE Online connecting two distant points in the universe map — either a player-placed jump-gate (artificial) or a naturally-occurring cosmic anomaly (natural within the game). Its parameters are entrance system, exit system, stability (lifetime in minutes for natural wormholes), mass limit (maximum ship mass that can transit), and attributes (randomized effects like increased ship speed, reduced signature radius, or increased capacitor recharge). It persists through the server that renders it and the station or citadel anchored at its entrance. A wormhole is the connector of the EVE universe: it enables travel between systems without traversing intervening space, creating strategic choke-points and trade routes. Distinct from the stargate (a fixed, permanent connection between two systems): wormholes are transient, randomized, and often lead to uncharted or low-security space.\n\n[formal: Foramen Corporatum | substrate: space | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

The on-demand delivery of computing resources from centralized data centers over a network. Its parameters are service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment model (public, private, hybrid), resource type (compute, storage, database, network), and pricing model (pay-per-use, subscription, reserved). It persists through the data center infrastructure (physical servers, storage arrays, networking gear), the virtualization layer (software that abstracts physical resources), and the billing system (which tracks usage and charges). A cloud-computing platform abstracts physical complexity: users provision resources without knowing the hardware. Distinct from a single computer (which is dedicated to one user): the cloud is shared, elastic, and metered. It is the industrialization of computing — the factory where computation is produced and sold by the unit.\n\n[formal: Nubes Computatio | substrate: information | horizon: as-long-as-datacenter | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A small, fast ship class in EVE Online designed for speed and agility over durability. Its parameters are module slots (limited), high slot count (for lasers/railguns), low slot count (for shield boosters/hull repairers), capacitor (drives ECM, afterburners, micro warp drives), and hull size (determines fit options). It persists through fuel (afterburner fuel or capacitor recharger O2), pilot ship skills, and the server that renders it. A frigate is the workhorse of EVE fleet combat: the smallest ship class that can meaningfully contribute to fleet engagements through speed, electronic warfare, or light firepower. Distinct from larger ships by its speed-to-hits ratio and its role as the agile scout/combatant. The frigate is the entry point for new pilots and the backbone of fleet scouting.

[formal: Navis Levis | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

The unclaimed space sector in EVE Online — the collection of solar systems with security rating 0.0 where player corporations can claim territory independently. Its parameters are system count (variable per server generation), resource yield (mining belts, ice fields, gas clouds), proximity to wormholes (strategic choke-points connecting to highsec and lowsec), and distance from empire borders (determining travel cost via wormholes). It persists through the server that renders it and the corporations that claim, defend, and extract resources from it. Nullsec is the frontier of EVE: where alliances expand, where wormhole networks create trade routes, and where the balance of power shifts through conquest. Distinct from highsec (policed by NPC security forces) and lowsec (lower security but still within empire borders): nullsec is entirely player-governed, with no NPC police presence and no fixed borders.

[formal: Spatium Liberum | substrate: space | horizon: as-long-as-server | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.25]

A finite combat event in EVE Online between fleets of ships over contested territory, resources, or strategic position. Its parameters are contested object, participants, start time, duration, and outcome. It persists through in-game data: killmails record the combatants and their losses; event logs record the start and end; ownership state records the outcome. A battle is bounded — it has a start time and an end — unlike war (which spans many battles) or a fleet (which exists independently of any single engagement). The winner takes the contested object or area; the losers extract what they can and withdraw. In EVE, battles are the fundamental unit of conflict resolution: territory shifts through battles, alliances are built through battles, and reputation is earned or lost in battles.\n\n[formal: Proelium Corporatum | substrate: event | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

A compiler is a human-made program that translates source code from a high-level programming language into machine code or another lower-level language. Its parameters are: input (source code in a source language), process (lexical analysis, parsing, optimization, code generation, and translation), and output (target code in assembly, machine code, or another lower-level language). A compiler persists through the practices of software development — it is reproduced, updated, and maintained by the computing community across generations of programmers and toolchains. [formal: compiler | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A human-made instrument designed primarily to inflict damage, achieve tactical advantage, or enable violence. Its parameters are lethality (deadly/non-lethal), range (melee/ranged/area), and mechanism (kinetic, explosive, chemical, energy). It persists through the practices of warfare: manufacturing, training, and deployment. Distinct from tool (general purpose) and from cannon (specific type).

The voluntary exchange of goods, services, or value between parties. Its parameters are participants (buyer/seller), medium (barter/money/cryptocurrency), and terms (price, quantity, delivery). It persists through the mutual benefit of exchange. Distinct from market (the venue/framework enabling trade) and from money (the medium of exchange).

The systematic process of converting raw materials into finished goods through repeated procedures. Its parameters are input (raw materials), process (assembly/fabrication/chemical), and output (finished product). It persists through the practices of industry: supply chains, quality control, and distribution. Distinct from tool (the instrument), printing-press (specific type), clock (specific product).

A systematic method of inquiry into the natural world through observation, experimentation, and reasoning. Its parameters are hypothesis (testable claim), method (experimental/observational/theoretical), and verification (peer review/reproducibility). It persists through the practices of research: publishing, peer review, and replication. Distinct from writing (recording), book (accumulation), and algorithm (procedure). [formal: Scientia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

Organized, large-scale violent conflict between groups, typically nations or factions. Its parameters are participants (sides), objectives (territory/resources/politics), and scale (local/regional/global). It persists through the organization of forces: logistics, command structure, and strategy. Distinct from battle (single engagement), weapon (instrument), castle (defense), and ship (platform). [formal: Bellum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

The practice of managing relations between entities through negotiation, dialogue, and compromise. Its parameters are participants (states, corporations, factions), objectives (territory, resources, alliances), and mechanism (treaties, embassies, envoys). It persists through the institutions of statecraft: embassies, treaties, and the transmission of diplomatic knowledge across generations. Distinct from negotiation (the general act) and from contract (the written result).

[formal: Diplomacia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Organized systems of belief, ritual, and morality that structure human understanding of meaning, purpose, and the transcendent. Its parameters are cosmology (explanation of existence), ethics (rules of conduct), ritual (repeated sacred acts), and community (believers). It persists through institutions (churches, temples), texts (sacred writings), and the transmission of doctrine across generations. Distinct from tradition (the transmission mechanism) and from law (secular rules).

[formal: Religio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

The art and science of designing and constructing buildings and other physical structures. Its parameters are function (habitation, defense, worship), form (style, proportions), material (stone, wood, steel), and technique (engineering, aesthetics). It persists through the built environment itself — structures that endure for generations — and through the transmission of design knowledge across practitioners. Distinct from blueprint (the plan) and from masonry (the craft of building with stone).

[formal: Architectura | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

Property is the human-made construct of exclusive ownership — the recognition that specific resources, objects, or interests belong to a designated holder, with the authority to use, transfer, and exclude others. Its defining parameters are: (1) identifiability — the asset must be clearly demarcated and distinguishable from all other assets; (2) exclusionary privilege — the right to prevent others from interfering with the asset's use or disposition, subject only to legally-defined limitations; (3) transferability — the legally-sanctioned ability to convey control to another party. Property persists through law (formal codes, courts, registries), custom (informal norms and social pressure), and social agreement (shared understanding of who owns what). Distinct from mere possession (physical control without recognition) and from title (the formal document evidencing property).

[formal: Proprietas | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A city is a dense human settlement — the aggregation of physical structures, institutions, and social organization into a coordinated environment that sustains a large population. Its parameters are: (1) density — the concentration of buildings, infrastructure, and people beyond rural settlement; (2) governance — formal or informal rules, authorities, and institutions that administer the settlement; (3) infrastructure — the physical systems (water, waste, transport, communication) that sustain life at scale; (4) function — the economic, cultural, or political roles the city serves for its inhabitants and surrounding region. A city persists through continuous construction and maintenance of its physical form, through the reproduction of governance structures, and through the social agreements that coordinate collective life at scale. Distinct from town (smaller scale, less institutional complexity) and from settlement (any human habitation, not necessarily dense or governed).

[formal: Civitas | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A calendar is a human-made system for dividing and labeling the continuous flow of time into discrete, repeating units — days, weeks, months, years — each assigned a name or number for coordination and record-keeping. Its parameters are: (1) cycle — the repeating astronomical or conventional period (solar year, lunar month, 7-day week) that structures the calendar; (2) epoch — the reference point from which time is counted; (3) labeling — the system of names and numbers applied to each unit; (4) intercalation — the rules for adding extra days or months to keep the calendar aligned with the underlying cycle. A calendar persists through social agreement (collective use), institutional maintenance (publication, reform, education), and cultural transmission (tradition, writing). Distinct from timekeeping (the general act of measuring time) and from clock (the physical instrument) — a calendar is the labeling system, not the measuring device.

[formal: Calendarium | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A bridge is a human-made structure built to span a physical gap — a river, valley, road, or strait — connecting two sides and enabling passage. Its parameters are: (1) span — the distance between supports, determining the engineering challenge; (2) materials — the substance (stone, wood, steel, concrete) from which it is constructed; (3) design — the structural form (arch, beam, suspension, cable-stayed) that distributes load; (4) purpose — what the bridge connects and for whom (pedestrians, vehicles, rail, water). A bridge persists through its physical structure (which degrades and must be maintained), through the engineering knowledge that enables its construction and repair, and through the continued demand for the passage it provides. Distinct from tunnel (which goes under a gap) and from ferry (water transport) — a bridge is a fixed, built structure.

[formal: Pons | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

An archive is a human-made institution for the systematic collection, organization, and preservation of records — documents, images, audio, or data — created by individuals, organizations, or governments, made available for future reference and research. Its parameters are: (1) collection — the body of records accumulated, selected for preservation based on evidentiary or cultural value; (2) organization — the cataloguing system (finding aids, metadata, classification) that makes records retrievable; (3) preservation — the physical or digital methods (climate control, backup, migration) that protect records from degradation; (4) access — the rules governing who may consult the records and under what conditions. An archive persists through its physical infrastructure (storage, climate control), through the cataloguing systems that index its contents, and through the institutional mandate that funds and justifies its existence. Distinct from library (curates published works for reading) and from record (a single item vs the curated collection).

[formal: Archivum | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Bureaucracy is a human-made system of administration structured by hierarchy, written rules, and specialized roles for managing complex organizations and executing collective decisions. Its parameters are: (1) hierarchy — a chain of authority from top to bottom, with each level accountable to the one above; (2) specialization — division of labor into distinct offices or departments, each with defined competencies; (3) rules — codified procedures (standard operating procedures, regulations, codes) that govern decision-making and conduct; (4) records — written documentation (files, reports, correspondence) that tracks decisions, actions, and institutional memory. A bureaucracy persists through the reproduction of its organizational structure (training, hiring, succession), through the codification of rules in writing, and through the institutional commitment that sustains it beyond any individual's tenure. Distinct from government (which may be personal or charismatic rather than bureaucratic) and from organization (which may be informal or flat).

[formal: Bureau Craticum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

A bank is a human-made financial institution that intermediates between savers and borrowers by holding deposits, extending credit, and facilitating payments. Its parameters are: (1) deposit — the funds held on behalf of customers, creating a liability for the bank; (2) lending — the funds extended to borrowers, creating an asset for the bank; (3) reserve — the fraction of deposits held in liquid form (cash, reserves at central bank) to meet withdrawal demands; (4) regulation — the legal framework (capital requirements, deposit insurance, oversight) that constrains and protects the bank's operations. A bank persists through its regulatory charter, its capital base, and the trust of its depositors. Distinct from currency (the medium of exchange) — the bank is the institution, currency is the token. Distinct from market (the mechanism of exchange) — the bank is a specific organized entity within the financial market.

[formal: Banka | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

Tax is a human-made compulsory contribution to state revenue, levied by a governing authority on individuals, businesses, or transactions within its jurisdiction. Its parameters are: (1) levy — the legal authority to impose the contribution, backed by coercion; (2) base — what is taxed (income, property, transactions, consumption); (3) rate — the percentage or fixed amount applied to the base; (4) enforcement — the administrative mechanisms (assessment, collection, penalties) that ensure compliance. A tax persists through the legal framework that authorizes it, the administrative apparatus that collects it, and the political legitimacy that justifies it. Distinct from tariff (tax on cross-border trade) and from fee (payment for a specific service) — tax is general, compulsory, and not tied to a specific quid-pro-quo.

[formal: Tributum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Government is a human-made system of governance — the exercise of authority over a defined population and territory through institutions, laws, and enforcement mechanisms. Its parameters are: (1) authority — the legitimate power to make and enforce rules, claim monopoly on coercion, and represent the collective; (2) institutions — the organized bodies (executive, legislative, judicial) through which authority is exercised; (3) jurisdiction — the geographic or personal scope within which authority applies; (4) legitimacy — the basis (legal, traditional, or popular) that justifies the government's claim to rule. A government persists through the reproduction of its institutions (succession, training, institutional memory), through the legal framework that defines its powers, and through the capacity to enforce its decisions. Distinct from state (the permanent apparatus) — government is the active exercise of authority, which may change even as the state endures. Distinct from politics (the process of decision-making) — government is the institutional structure.

[formal: Regimen | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

Politics is a human-made process of making collective decisions through negotiation, competition, and deliberation — the means by which groups allocate resources, resolve conflicts, and establish rules for coexistence. Its parameters are: (1) actors — the individuals or groups who participate (citizens, factions, leaders, institutions); (2) arena — the venue or process (assembly, parliament, election, court) where decisions are made; (3) stakes — what is being decided (resources, power, policy, identity); (4) procedures — the rules (voting, consensus, decree) that govern how decisions are reached. Politics persists through cultural practice (the learned behavior of collective decision-making), through institutionalization (formalizing political processes into government), and through the ongoing need to resolve conflicts and allocate resources. Distinct from government (the institutional structure) — politics is the process; government is the apparatus. Distinct from power (the capacity to act) — politics is the social process of exercising power collectively.

[formal: Politica | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Audit is a human-made process of systematic examination — the independent, objective assessment of whether something (financial records, operations, compliance, performance) conforms to established standards, rules, or expectations. Its parameters are: (1) scope — what is being examined (financial statements, processes, compliance, performance); (2) standards — the criteria against which conformity is measured (regulations, accounting standards, policies); (3) independence — the examiner's freedom from the subject of the audit, ensuring objectivity; (4) reporting — the documented findings, conclusions, and recommendations. An audit persists through the institutional practice of independent review, through the professional standards that govern auditing methodology, and through the authority (legal or contractual) that compels the audited party to cooperate. Distinct from inspection (a one-time check) — audit is systematic, methodical, and documented. Distinct from archive (preservation of records) — audit evaluates records rather than preserving them.

[formal: Auditus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Education is a human-made process of systematic knowledge transmission — the deliberate, structured transfer of knowledge, skills, values, and practices from one generation or community to another. Its parameters are: (1) curriculum — the organized body of knowledge and skills to be transmitted; (2) pedagogy — the methods and techniques of instruction; (3) institution — the organized setting (school, university, apprenticeship) where education occurs; (4) assessment — the methods for evaluating learning and progress. Education persists through institutional structures (schools, curricula, accreditation), through cultural practices (teaching traditions), and through the deliberate investment of time and resources in knowledge transmission. Distinct from teaching (the act of instructing) — education is the broader system, including curriculum, assessment, and institutional context. Distinct from learning (the acquisition of knowledge) — education is the provision, learning is the receipt.

[formal: Educatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A hospital is a human-made institution for medical treatment, diagnosis, and care of the sick and injured. Its parameters are: (1) capacity — the number of beds and patients it can serve; (2) specialties — the medical domains it covers (surgery, pediatrics, emergency, etc.); (3) staff — the medical professionals (doctors, nurses, technicians) who provide care; (4) equipment — the medical instruments and technology (imaging, surgical tools, life support) used for diagnosis and treatment. A hospital persists through its physical infrastructure (buildings, equipment, supplies), through the reproduction of medical knowledge (training, research), and through the institutional framework (licensing, funding, regulation) that enables its operation. Distinct from clinic (smaller scale, less comprehensive) and from medicine (the knowledge system) — a hospital is the institution that applies medicine.

[formal: Hospitalis | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

A library is a human-made institution for the curated collection, organization, and public access of books, documents, and knowledge resources. Its parameters are: (1) collection — the body of books and materials selected for their intellectual, cultural, or informational value; (2) cataloguing — the classification and indexing system (Dewey, LC, digital metadata) that makes the collection searchable; (3) access — the rules governing borrowing, reading rooms, and digital access; (4) curation — the editorial judgment about what to acquire, preserve, and weeding (removing outdated materials). A library persists through its physical infrastructure (buildings, shelves, climate control), through its cataloguing systems, and through the institutional mandate (public funding, endowment) that sustains it. Distinct from archive (preservation of records for reference) — library curates for reading and study of published works; archive preserves for evidentiary value. Distinct from bookstore (commercial sale) — library provides free access.

[formal: Bibliotheca | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A museum is a human-made institution for the collection, preservation, and public display of objects of cultural, scientific, historical, or artistic significance. Its parameters are: (1) collection — the artifacts, specimens, or artworks acquired and curated for their evidentiary or aesthetic value; (2) display — the methods of presentation (exhibitions, galleries, interactive displays) that communicate meaning to visitors; (3) preservation — the climate control, conservation, and security measures that protect the collection; (4) interpretation — the labels, guides, and educational programs that explain the collection's significance. A museum persists through its physical infrastructure (buildings, display cases, climate control), through professional curation practices, and through institutional funding (public, private, or endowment). Distinct from archive (preservation for research) — museum displays for public education and engagement. Distinct from gallery (commercial art display) — museum is non-commercial and educational.

[formal: Museum | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A prison is a human-made institution of confinement and punishment — a facility where individuals are deprived of liberty as a consequence of violating law. Its parameters are: (1) purpose — the stated objectives (punishment, deterrence, rehabilitation, incapacitation); (2) security — the physical and procedural measures (walls, locks, guards, surveillance) that prevent escape; (3) regime — the daily routines, rules, and conditions governing inmate life; (4) population — the individuals confined, categorized by offense, sentence length, and risk level. A prison persists through its physical infrastructure (buildings, security systems), through the legal framework that authorizes incarceration, and through the institutional culture of the correctional system. Distinct from jail (short-term holding) — prison is for longer sentences and more permanent confinement. Distinct from punishment (the act) — prison is the institution that houses punishment.

[formal: Carcer | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

A road is a human-made path for travel and transport — a constructed route connecting two or more places, enabling the movement of people, goods, and information. Its parameters are: (1) surface — the material (dirt, gravel, asphalt, concrete) and condition; (2) width — the capacity for traffic (single track, two-lane, highway); (3) alignment — the route taken (direct, winding, following terrain); (4) classification — the road's role (local, arterial, highway, interstate). A road persists through its physical structure (which degrades and requires maintenance), through the engineering knowledge that enables its construction and repair, and through the continued demand for the connections it provides. Distinct from path (unimproved, narrow, informal) and from street (urban road with buildings on both sides) — a road is any constructed passage for travel.

[formal: Via | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A map is a human-made representation of space — a reduced, symbolic depiction of geographic relationships between places, features, and distances. Its parameters are: (1) projection — the method of representing 3D space on a 2D surface (or 3D model), which inevitably distorts some properties; (2) scale — the ratio between map distance and real distance; (3) symbols — the conventional signs, colors, and labels that encode geographic information; (4) purpose — what the map is designed to show (topography, routes, political boundaries, resources). A map persists through its physical medium (which degrades and must be reproduced), through the cartographic knowledge that enables its creation, and through the continued need for spatial representation. Distinct from atlas (a collection of maps) and from territory (the actual land) — a map is the representation, not the thing represented.

[formal: Tabula | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Navigation is a human-made process of planning and controlling movement through space — the systematic determination of position, direction, and route from one location to another. Its parameters are: (1) positioning — the method of determining where one is (celestial observation, landmarks, GPS, dead reckoning); (2) route-planning — the method of choosing the optimal path between origin and destination; (3) instruments — the tools used (compass, sextant, GPS receiver, map); (4) medium — the domain of travel (land, sea, air, space). A navigation persists through the instruments and knowledge systems that enable it, through the cultural practice of wayfinding, and through the ongoing need to move between places. Distinct from transportation (the actual movement) — navigation is the planning and guidance; transportation is the execution. Grief is the affective response to the irreversible loss of a valued bond, commitment, or shared identity. It persists through narrative reconstruction — the repeated retelling and recontextualization of the loss that gradually integrates it into the survivor's ongoing identity. The mechanism of persistence is memorial practice: structured acts of remembrance that transform raw loss into a maintained relationship with what is gone. Grief is distinguished from mere sadness by its object-specificity — it is always grief FOR something, anchored to a particular lost bond rather than a diffuse mood.

[formal: luctus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pride is the self-evaluative emotion that arises when one's actions or attributes align with a recognized standard of worth. It persists through identity reinforcement — each instance of pride strengthens the association between the standard and the self-concept. The mechanism of persistence is self-narration: the internal story one tells about meeting or exceeding the standard, which becomes part of one's ongoing self-conception. Pride is distinguished from vanity by its grounding in an external standard — true pride references a criterion beyond the self, whether personal or communal.

[formal: superbia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Honor is the social recognition of an individual or group whose actions have met or exceeded a shared standard of worth. It persists through public acknowledgment — naming, awarding, and commemorating those who embody the standard. The mechanism of persistence is reputation transmission: the stories and examples that circulate within a community, keeping the standard alive across generations. Honor is distinguished from mere respect by its binding nature — honor creates an obligation to uphold the standard, not just an admiration of it.

[formal: honor | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Shame is the affective response to the recognition that one has violated a shared standard, resulting in diminished social standing. It persists through behavioral modification — the avoidance of future violations and the active restoration of standing through reparation. The mechanism of persistence is social feedback: the reactions of the community that signal the standard has been breached and guide the path back to acceptance. Shame is distinguished from guilt by its public dimension — shame is about who one has become in the eyes of others, not just what one has done.

[formal: pudor | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Play is distinguished from work by the absence of external compulsion and from mere leisure by its active engagement rather than passive consumption.

[formal: lus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Guilt is the internalized moral self-judgment that an individual experiences when they violate a norm they have personally accepted as binding. Parameters: (1) the agent must have internalized the norm beforehand (unlike shame, which can operate on purely external reputation), (2) the violation must be cognitive — the agent must recognize (or be convinced of) the breach, and (3) the response mechanism is self-directed: guilt compels confession, reparations, or self-punishment without requiring an external audience. Persistence mechanism: guilt persists through memory of the transgression and the ongoing internal standard against which the self is measured; it is reinforced when the individual confesses to another (shifting guilt toward shame) or when repeated self-judgment crystallizes into character traits such as contrition or penitence. [formal: culpa | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Credit is the socially structured extension of resources, labor, or goods based on a promise of future repayment, where the promise is backed by reputation, collateral, or institutional enforcement. Parameters: (1) a creditor who extends value now, (2) a debtor who receives value and assumes an obligation, (3) a time horizon between extension and repayment, and (4) a mechanism of enforcement — social ostracism, legal judgment, or loss of collateral. Persistence mechanism: credit persists through ledgers, reputation networks, and the fear of future exclusion from credit markets; it is reinforced each time a credit relationship is successfully completed, building the borrower's creditworthiness. Persistence mechanism: socialization through imitation and sanction for deviation. [formal: mos | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.02]

Governance or authority derived from established custom rather than formal law. Parameters: the customary practice it derives from, the community that recognizes it, and its scope of application. Persistence mechanism: oral tradition and repeated application by recognized authorities. [formal: consuetudo | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.02]

A tool or device used for measuring, straightening, or guiding. Parameters: type (straightedge, measuring rule, guiding template), material (wood, metal, digital), and precision class. Persistence mechanism: physical object or digital specification that retains its shape/properties over use. [formal: regula | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A prior decision or action used as a guide for future cases. Parameters: the original case, the principle extracted, the authority of the precedent (binding vs. persuasive), and the jurisdiction that recognizes it. Persistence mechanism: recorded decisions and institutional memory. [formal: praecedens | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A formal specification enabling different systems to communicate and exchange data. Parameters: the systems it connects, the data format, the communication rules, and the versioning scheme. Persistence mechanism: published specification document maintained by a standards body or community. [formal: interoperabilitas | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The principle that benefits received should be returned in kind, creating and maintaining social bonds through mutual obligation. Parameters: timing (immediate, deferred, open-ended), equivalence (exact, proportional, symbolic), and enforcement (social pressure, reputation, formal sanction). Persistence mechanism: repeated cycles of give-and-take build institutionalized expectation and social memory. [formal: reciprocitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.03]

Commemoration is the structured practice of honoring and remembering through ceremonies, memorials, and rituals. Parameters: (1) a subject of remembrance (person, event, value), (2) a communal audience, (3) a temporal anchor (date, anniversary), (4) a symbolic act or object. Persistence mechanism: commemoration persists through repeated performance across generations, institutionalization in calendars and monuments, and transmission via narrative. Without these parameters, commemoration dissolves into private memory or mere recollection.

A social mechanism for allocating personal resources toward another's benefit without expectation of direct return. Its parameters are: (1) cost to the actor — the altruist must bear a measurable loss; (2) benefit to the recipient — the recipient must gain something of value; (3) absence of quid pro quo — no explicit or implicit expectation of reciprocal benefit. Its persistence mechanism is cultural reinforcement through social praise, identity signaling, and the internalization of prosocial norms; it decays when the social reward for altruism falls below the cost of performing it. [formal: corporata altruendi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A museum is a cultural institution that collects, preserves, and displays objects of artistic, historical, or scientific significance for public education and enjoyment. It operates through curatorial selection, preservation protocols, and exhibition design to make tangible heritage accessible to visitors.

[formal: museum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

provenance.reasoningTrace: Definition carves museum as a public-facing cultural institution distinct from archives (which focus on preservation and research) and libraries (which focus on lending). The museum's core function is display and education of collected objects.

body:
A collective state of agreement among agents, established via a shared protocol or social mechanism, which stabilizes coordinated action within a system.

[formal: consensus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A permanent physical structure erected to commemorate a person, event, or idea, transforming collective memory into enduring material form. Its parameters are material permanence — construction from durable materials chosen to outlast the creator; public visibility — siting where the community can encounter it; commemorative intent — deliberate design to trigger remembrance and convey meaning beyond the physical. It persists through geological time as long as its materials endure and its meaning is maintained by the community. [formal: monumentum | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.1]

A threshold is a defined point of crossing that mediates between two states or spaces, converting separation into selective passage. Its parameters are the two sides it separates, the material or symbolic mark of the boundary, and the conditions for crossing; its persistence mechanism is the continued recognition of the boundary and the maintenance of the crossing point.

[formal: limen | substrate: space | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

Limen is the formal semantic boundary marking the transition between conceptual states, converting abstract distinction into a definable crossing point. Its parameters are the opposed states it separates, the semantic field it operates within, and the criteria for crossing; its persistence mechanism is continued use in discourse and the stability of the opposition it encodes.

[formal: limen | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

Curiosity is the cultivated disposition to seek novel information and resolve uncertainty through structured inquiry. It is parameterized by (1) a knowledge gap that motivates the inquiry, (2) a method of investigation (observation, experiment, or dialogue), and (3) a threshold of resolution that terminates the search. Its persistence mechanism is institutionalized through education systems that reward exploratory behavior, research funding that sustains long-term inquiry, and peer review networks that validate and propagate findings. Without these institutions, curiosity reverts to transient individual interest.

[formal: curiositas | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A voluntary transformation of grievance into release, relinquishing claim to retribution after a wrong. Parameters: (1) acknowledgment of harm done; (2) conscious decision to forgo resentment; (3) narrative reframing that integrates the wound without letting it define the relationship. Persists through deliberate practice and social recognition. [formal: remissio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]
A deliberate, repeated social act that marks significance, transforms memory into practice, and transmits values across generations through embodied performance
an enforceable duty or requirement that binds an agent to perform or refrain from an action, typically sustained by social sanction or institutional authority

A structured system for storing, preserving, and retrieving information across time through human-made media and practices. Its parameters are: storage medium (writing, oral tradition, digital databases, monuments), retrieval mechanism (indexing, cataloging, ritual recall), and access controls (who may read, who must preserve). It persists through active maintenance — re-copying manuscripts, refreshing digital storage, rehearsing oral traditions — and the social commitment to what a community deems worth remembering. Memory differs from information (which is the content being stored) and from archive (which is the physical or digital container): memory is the entire system of practice, the commitment, and the infrastructure combined. A library is a memory; a database is a memory; a ritual of remembrance is a memory; a written chronicle is a memory. The substrate is information (what is stored), the horizon is generations (how long it persists), and the explicit flag is yes (these systems are deliberately constructed). [formal: Memoria Artificialis | substrate: information | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]
the capacity for a construct to persist beyond its immediate instantiation, allowing past states to inform future ones through recorded or internalized traces
Communion is a human-made construct for establishing shared participation and mutual belonging between individuals or groups, often enacted through ritual, shared experience, or symbolic exchange
Sacrifice is the deliberate giving up or offering of something valued to fulfill a higher purpose, obligation, or ritual requirement

Sacrifice is a human-made construct involving the deliberate relinquishment or offering of something valued, performed to fulfill an obligation, honor a covenant, or transform a state of being, where the loss is itself the point rather than a means to an end.
Commemoration is the deliberate construction of a durable record or ritual that preserves the memory of a past event, person, or achievement for future generations to witness

An obligation is a binding requirement or duty that compels an agent to perform or refrain from an action, typically grounded in social convention, law, or moral expectation rather than physical force.

Memory is the institutionalized social construct through which communities encode, store, and transmit significant events, experiences, and identities across generations, creating a shared sense of temporal continuity.
Communion is a shared relational experience between two or more persons, structured by ritual or mutual recognition, that creates or reinforces a durable bond of belonging and meaning.

A capacity for understanding and sharing the feelings of others, enabling social coordination and empathy-based cooperation. Its parameters are affective resonance, cognitive perspective-taking, and shared affect; it persists through neural plasticity and cultural transmission of empathic norms. [formal: empathia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
Culture is the accumulated, transmitted set of shared meanings, practices, and norms that a group uses to coordinate life together across generations.
Commemoration is the deliberate, repeatable act of marking a past event or person to sustain collective memory across time, transforming individual remembrance into a durable social institution.

Identity is the structured continuity of self across time and context, constituted by narrative coherence, social recognition, and remembered experience. Parameters: narrative coherence, social recognition, memory. Persistence mechanism: narrative reproduction through social interaction and self-reporting. [formal: identitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.5]

Recognition is the formal or informal acknowledgment of another's status, rights, or identity, constituting social validation and enabling mutual respect. Parameters: acknowledgment, status/rights/identity, social context. Persistence mechanism: institutionalized acknowledgment and repeated social verification. [formal: recognitio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.3]

Equality is the principle of equal standing, rights, or treatment across persons, constituting fairness and non-discrimination. Parameters: equal standing, rights, treatment, persons. Persistence mechanism: institutional enforcement and cultural normalization. [formal: aequabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.4]

Evidence is a human-made construct used to substantiate truth-claims within a shared framework of belief; it is the material or procedural basis that allows one claim to be treated as more credible than another, persisting through its role in governance, law, and communal decision-making.
Identity is a human-made construct that persists through the assignment of stable markers — names, symbols, narratives — to distinguish one entity or group from another across time and space.

equality is a social construct that asserts equal moral worth or standing among persons, requiring that no individual be systematically privileged or devalued relative to others by the structures in which they participate

Recognition is the social mechanism by which one agent or collective acknowledges another's identity, status, or claim as valid within a shared framework — it transforms private assertion into publicly ratified reality.
A socially constructed mechanism that creates a binding requirement for action or restraint, enforced through normative pressure, institutional sanctions, or internalized moral reasoning.

Guilt is the internal construct arising when an agent recognizes its own action or inaction as having violated a norm or wronged another — a self-imposed social penalty that functions as a recognition of wrongdoing without requiring external adjudication.
Commemoration is a constructed practice of marking and preserving the significance of past events, persons, or transitions — built to persist the memory and meaning of what has occurred across time.
forgiveness is the deliberate release of a claim to retribution or redress, constructed to dissolve the debt of obligation without requiring equivalent compensation
A constructed sense of self as a distinct, persistent entity within social systems — what allows one to be recognized as a particular 'who' across time and interaction.
evidence is a constructed item or body of information that supports or validates a truth-claim within a given context

Recognition is the human-made construct of publicly acknowledging that something exists, that someone holds a particular status, or that a claim is valid — distinct from mere belief or assumption, because it requires a social act of validation that persists beyond the recognizer's private judgment.

Emotion is a structured framework for categorizing and communicating affective states — valenced responses (approach/avoid) that signal internal conditions and coordinate social behavior. Parameters: valence (positive/negative/neutral polarity), arousal (intensity of activation), and intentionality (whether directed at a specific object or diffuse). The persistence mechanism is neurobiological patterning reinforced through social communication, cultural transmission, and linguistic categorization — emotions become stable constructs when a community shares names, norms, and expected expressions for them. [formal: affectus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
Recognition is the social construct of acknowledging another's status, identity, or worth as valid within a given community or framework of meaning.

Patronage is a structured social exchange in which a resource-holding party (the patron) provides material, protective, or social benefits to a subordinate party (the client) in return for loyalty, services, or political support. Parameters: (1) the patron must hold surplus resources or access; (2) the client must provide something of value in return (labor, loyalty, votes, information); (3) the exchange must be ongoing, not one-shot. Persistence mechanism: the relationship persists through repeated exchange cycles and the social cost of breaking the obligation — defection damages both the patron’s reputation for reliability and the client’s access to future patronage. [formal: patronatus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

DIGNITY: The inherent worth assigned to a person or group as a baseline social coordinate, independent of achievement, status, or honor. Unlike honor (which is earned and can be lost), dignity is the pre-conditional worth that makes honor possible — it is the claim that certain treatment is owed simply by virtue of membership in a class of beings recognized as worthy. Dignity operates as the floor beneath which no social evaluation may fall, distinguishing it from pride (emotional response to honor) and shame (response to lost honor). It grounds the concept of rights: to have dignity is to have claims that others must respect regardless of utility or reciprocity.

[dignitas, Latin — the status of a free Roman citizen, distinct from slavery and honor]

[formal: dignitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

provenance.reasoningTrace: Definition carves dignity as inherent worth (not earned like honor), the baseline that makes honor possible. Distinguishes from pride (emotional response) and shame (lost honor). The formal latin tag dignitas anchors the etymology. Substrate: mind (it's a normative coordinate). Horizon: a life (persists across lifetime). Epoch 0.01 (foundational concept).

body: credit is a deferred claim on value, socially guaranteed by institutions that track and enforce repayment across time

A habit is a behavior pattern that has been conditioned through repetition to execute automatically when triggered by a specific context cue, persisting through neural pathway reinforcement until the context or repetition ceases. Parameters: (1) trigger — the contextual cue that initiates execution; (2) routine — the automated behavior sequence; (3) reward — the reinforcement signal that sustains the loop; (4) repetition count — the threshold of repetitions required before automation. Persistence mechanism: Hebbian learning in basal ganglia circuits, where repeated co-activation of neural pathways strengthens synaptic connections until the behavior becomes context-triggered rather than goal-directed. [formal: consuetudo | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

A dream is a temporally bounded narrative sequence generated by the sleeping mind, characterized by involuntary imagery, emotional valence, and narrative coherence that persists only through memory. The persistence mechanism is neural reactivation: during REM sleep, the hippocampus and neocortex replay and recombine waking experiences into novel scenarios, producing a story the dreamer experiences as immediate reality. Dreams are structured by the same narrative templates as waking thought but are freed from sensory input and executive inhibition, enabling wild association and emotional amplification. The dream-carving parameters are: (1) substrate: neural activity during sleep states, (2) persistence: hippocampal-neocortical recombination of memory traces, (3) accessibility: only through post-hoc recall, (4) function: emotional processing, threat rehearsal, and memory consolidation.

[formal: somnium | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Time is a human-made measurement framework that partitions continuous change into discrete, shareable units — seconds, minutes, hours, days, years — enabling coordination, sequencing, and causal reasoning across individuals. The persistence mechanism is social agreement encoded in calendars, clocks, and standards: time exists not as a physical substance but as a shared convention that persists through institutional maintenance of timekeeping apparatuses and legal standardization. Time-carving parameters: (1) substrate: social convention and institutional practice, (2) persistence: standardized timekeeping apparatuses and legal frameworks, (3) granularity: defined by convention (1 second = 1/86400 of a mean solar day, refined to atomic transitions), (4) function: coordination, sequencing, and causal attribution.

[formal: tempus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

A structured sequence of premises leading to a conclusion, designed to persuade or establish truth within discourse. The parameters are premises (the supporting claims), conclusion (the target claim), and inference rules (the logical connections between premises and conclusion). It persists through the maintained logical structure and the social practice of reasoning — an argument exists as long as its participants maintain its structure and continue to engage with its claims. Distinct from opinion (which lacks structured support) and from proof (which demands universal validity rather than persuasive force). An argument is the mechanism by which mind extends reasoning across time and between agents.
Mosaic is a composite image formed by arranging small pieces. [formal: veritas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An argument is a human-made structured sequence of premises leading to a conclusion, used to persuade or establish truth within discourse. It persists through the maintained logical structure and the social practice of reasoning.

[formal: argumentum | substrate: language | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Agency is the human-made capacity for autonomous action, structured through social, legal, or cognitive frameworks that enable the attribution of intent and the enforcement of accountability. It persists through the maintenance of responsibility, the continuity of identity, and the institutionalized recognition of the agent's capacity to effect change.

[formal: agere | substrate: agency | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

body:
Courtesy is the system of codified polite behaviors that signals respect and maintains social harmony within a group. Parameters: formality (casual, formal, ritual), audience (in-group, out-group, mixed), and penalty (social friction, ostracism, formal sanction). Persistence mechanism: social reinforcement through approval for compliance and stigma for violation; the construct persists as long as the group values harmony enough to enforce the code.

[formal: comitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

provenance.reasoningTrace: First definition for courtesy entry. CARVES: parameters (formality, audience, penalty) + persistence mechanism (social reinforcement). Distinguishes from custom (general practice) and etiquette (formal rules) by focusing on the behavioral expression of respect.

body:
Hierarchy is the human-made practice of arranging entities into ordered strata by rank, authority, or status, so that coordinated action can proceed through differentiated roles and decision rights. Parameters: (1) a ranking axis (authority, knowledge, seniority, or force), (2) a mechanism for maintaining the ordering (custom, law, force, or inheritance), (3) a scope boundary (family, organization, society, or institution). Persistence mechanism: the hierarchy persists through repeated enforcement of rank distinctions—by social sanction, institutional rules, or physical coercion—and is reproduced each time new members are socialized into the ordered roles. Without active maintenance of rank distinctions, the hierarchy collapses into egalitarian interaction.

[formal: ordo | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Intelligence is the capacity for systematic information processing and problem-solving, converting raw data into actionable knowledge through structured reasoning and adaptation. Its parameters are: (1) processing speed — the rate of information throughput; (2) complexity — the depth of relational mapping; (3) adaptability — the ability to modify internal models in response to environmental shifts. [formal: intelligentia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Freedom is the bounded space of permissible action within a system of rules — the gap between what a rule forbids and what it permits. Its parameters are: (1) an authority that defines the boundary, (2) a set of enforceable constraints, and (3) a zone of non-intersection where no authority may reach. It persists through codification in legal texts, institutional enforcement by courts and police, and cultural transmission through education and tradition, ensuring that the boundary endures beyond individual enforcement actions.

provenance.reasoningTrace: freedom defined as the bounded space of permissible action — not absence of constraint but the structured gap between forbiddance and permission. Parameters: authority, constraints, non-intersection zone. Persistence: codification, enforcement, cultural transmission.

Loss is the affective response to the irreversible removal of a valued bond, commitment, or shared identity. Its parameters are: (1) removal — the permanent absence of something previously present; (2) value — the thing removed must have mattered to the survivor; (3) irreversibility — the loss cannot be undone. Loss persists through narrative reconstruction — the repeated retelling and recontextualization of the loss that gradually integrates it into the survivor's ongoing identity. The mechanism of persistence is the feedback loop of remembering and reinterpreting the loss that slowly transforms it from a wound into a story.

[formal: Amissio | substrate: mind | horizon: lifetime | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]
Identity is a social construct of self-recognition that requires obligation to others to be constituted—it cannot exist in isolation but needs relational recognition to persist.

A state of alignment between a statement (or mental model) and reality, validated through consensus, evidence, or logical consistency. Its parameters are (1) correspondence — agreement with the observed world; (2) coherence — internal logical consistency; (3) pragmatism — utility in navigating the world. It persists through the continuous process of verification and the social consensus of its validity.

[formal: veritas | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

provenance.reasoningTrace: Definition carves truth as a multi-dimensional alignment (correspondence, coherence, pragmatism) rather than a mere property of statements.

body: Belonging is the structured placement of an agent within a network of mutual recognition and obligation, sustained by shared identity markers and reinforced through ritualized inclusion/exclusion mechanisms. Parameters: (1) the belonging agent must be recognized by at least one other agent in the network, (2) the network must maintain boundaries that distinguish members from non-members, (3) the network must provide material or symbolic benefits to members. Persistence mechanism: belonging persists through repeated acts of recognition (ritual, ceremony, documentation), boundary enforcement (norms, sanctions), and benefit distribution (resources, status, protection). [formal: pertinere | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

The structured practice of releasing resentment toward a perceived wrongdoer, mediated by narrative reframing and social recognition. It operates through deliberate cognitive shifts and communal validation, persisting via story-telling and ritual repetition across generations.

The feeling that acknowledges the value of the received good; it requires honor to recognize the giver's intent. Gratitude is the social lubricant that transforms transaction into relationship, persisting through reciprocal acknowledgment and narrative reinforcement.

The made world: the persistent player community and their shared sense of the game as a reality. EVE Online is a corporation of players, economies, and conflicts structured to persist across decades through emergent governance and player agency, not merely a software product.

Episteme is the structured body of knowledge within a specific domain, characterized by its internal consistency and method of inquiry. Its parameters are axioms, logic, and evidence; it persists through institutionalized education and the continuous refinement of truth-claims. [formal: episteme | substrate: mind | horizon: eras | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A moral quality — the disposition to act in accordance with a recognized standard of excellence. Virtue persists through three mechanisms: (1) social reinforcement via honor and reputation rewards for virtuous acts and shame for their absence; (2) cultural transmission through story, ritual, and education; (3) internalization via conscience and self-evaluation. [formal: virtus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Data is the structured arrangement of symbols, values, or signals that encodes facts, measurements, or states for record, computation, or transmission. Its parameters are: (1) format — the encoding scheme (binary, text, numeric) that makes symbols machine-readable; (2) schema — the rules governing structure, ordering, and types; (3) volume — the quantity of records within a defined scope. Its persistence mechanism is storage media and backup protocols that reproduce the bit-pattern across time and devices.

Code is the abstract set of instructions that specify computational behavior, structured by formal grammars and executed by machines. Its parameters are: (1) syntax — the formal rules governing valid instruction sequences; (2) semantics — the mapping from instructions to observable behavior; (3) abstraction level — the degree to which instructions hide implementation details. Its persistence mechanism is version-control systems and compilation pipelines that reproduce and execute the instruction set.

A limen is a threshold construct that marks the boundary between two states and structures the transition between them. Parameters: (1) prior state, (2) posterior state, (3) crossing ritual, (4) transformation. Persistence mechanism: the repeated enactment of threshold-crossing that reinforces the boundary's significance and the transformation's reality. [formal: limen | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.1]

An algorithm is a step‑by‑step procedure for solving a problem or accomplishing a task. It consists of a finite sequence of well‑defined operations, with clear input and output, and may be implemented in any programming language or notation. Persistence is achieved by recording the algorithm in code, documentation, or formal specification. [formal: algorithm | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Community is a structured collective bound by shared identity and mutual obligation, persisting through institutionalized norms and reciprocal enforcement. Parameters: membership criteria (explicit or implicit), scope of obligation (bounded by shared identity), enforcement mechanism (social sanction, norm internalization). Persistence mechanism: norms institutionalized through repeated interaction, reinforced by shared rituals and identity markers.

Philanthropy is the organized, institutional practice of giving resources (money, time, expertise) at scale for public benefit, distinct from individual charity by its systematic approach and enduring structures. [formal: philanthropia | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Merit is the measurement of an individual or entity's worth based on their demonstrated competence, contribution, or adherence to a standard. It converts performance into social standing, persisting through consistent recognition and record-keeping. Its parameters are: (1) a standard of excellence, (2) a method of verification, and (3) a mechanism of reward. [formal: meritum | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

A structured ordering of events, actions, or states into a causal sequence that generates meaning beyond the sum of its parts. Its parameters are sequence (ordered events), causality (linking events through cause-effect or thematic relation), and audience (the receiver who completes the meaning-making loop). It persists through repetition, encoding, and transmission — surviving the death of its tellers by embedding in ritual, text, and shared memory. The persistence mechanism is social reinforcement: each retelling re-anchors the narrative in collective understanding, making it resistant to individual forgetting.

[formal: narratio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.3]

Interface is a boundary framework of interaction protocols that mediates between systems, users, or components, enabling communication through standardized exchange mechanisms. Parameters: mediation between systems/users/components, standardized exchange protocols, persistence through technical standardization and user convention. [formal: interfacing | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.55]

Mathematics is the formalization and study of quantity, structure, space, and change through abstract reasoning and symbolic manipulation. It persists through formal notation, rigorous proof, and intergenerational transmission within educational and scientific institutions.

[formal: mathematica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Repentance is the structured practice of acknowledging personal wrongdoing through narrative confession, accepting blame without deflection, and committing to corrective behavioral change. It operates through three parameters: (1) admission of fault to self and witness, (2) affective experience of remorse, and (3) observable corrective action. It persists through ritual repetition (confession, penance) and social reinforcement (forgiveness granted, status restored).

A rite is a formalized human-made procedure that marks significant transitions or reinforces social values through symbolic action, requiring a script, participants, and a context. Parameters: script, participants, context. Persistence: repetition and social transmission. [formal: rite | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

body: Game is a human-made structure of rules voluntarily adopted to convert unstructured play into bounded activity with win/loss conditions. Its parameters are: (1) rules — the explicit constraints that define permissible moves; (2) boundary — the spatial, temporal, or material limits within which the game operates; (3) stakes — the consequences (points, status, prizes) that distinguish winning from losing; (4) voluntariness — players choose to enter and may choose to leave. Its persistence mechanism is repeated reproduction through teaching the rules to new participants. [formal: ludus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

The principle of impartial and consistent treatment according to established standards. Its parameters are (1) impartiality, (2) consistency, and (3) proportionality; it persists through social consensus and institutional application.

[formal: aequitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Betrayal is the deliberate violation of an explicit or implicit binding commitment between agents, characterized by three elements: (1) a prior obligation (formal or informal) creating legitimate expectation, (2) a knowing breach of that obligation by the obligated agent, and (3) harm to the obligee's reliance interest. Betrayal differs from mere failure or negligence in that it requires awareness of the obligation and voluntary choice to breach it. The construct persists through three mechanisms: (1) narrative storage — betrayal is recorded in collective memory as a cautionary reference, (2) reputational sanction — the betrayer's future obligations are constrained by diminished trustworthiness, and (3) ritualized reparation — formal apologies, restitution, and exclusion ceremonies that restore social equilibrium. Parameters: obligation-strength (informal through institutional), awareness-level (ignorant through deliberate), harm-type (material through existential).

[formal: proditio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

provenance.reasoningTrace: First definition filed in same sitting per Law 5. Carves betrayal by distinguishing it from failure/negligence (requires awareness and voluntary breach). States persistence mechanisms: narrative storage, reputational sanction, ritualized reparation.
