Marginalia are annotations inscribed in the margins, interstices, or blank spaces of a written or printed text. Parameters: (1) the annotation must be physically embedded in or on a document, not a separate work; (2) it serves interpretive, corrective, or dialogic function relative to the main text; (3) it is produced by readers, scholars, or scribes across time. Persistence mechanism: marginalia persist as material traces on physical documents, preserved through archival practice and the survival of the host text. [formal: marginalia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A decree is a formal authoritative proclamation issued by a person or body holding recognized power (monarch, sovereign, executive authority, judge, or delegated official) to declare, order, or establish something with binding force. Parameters: (1) issuer must possess legitimate authority — not merely strength or position but recognized right to command; (2) the decree binds addressees within the issuer's jurisdiction, whether persons, institutions, or territories; (3) it operates as a one-shot or standing order, distinct from legislation in that it does not require deliberative assembly. Persistence: a decree endures through institutional memory, written records, and the enforcement apparatus that backs the issuer's authority — until rescinded, superseded, or the issuer's power expires. [formal: decreta | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A colophon is a paratextual statement placed at the end of a book or manuscript that records details of its production — the printer or publisher, date of completion, and sometimes the scribe or patron. Its parameters are: (1) it must appear at or near the end of a codex, (2) it must document some aspect of the book materializing process, and (3) it functions as a claim of provenance or a colophonic signature. It persists through the physical survival of the book copy and through citation in later scholarly catalogues. [formal: colophon | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bylaw is a rule or set of rules created by an organization, corporation, or local government body to govern its own internal affairs and operations. Parameters: (1) it is made by a constituted body that has delegated or inherent authority to legislate internally; (2) it applies only within the jurisdiction of that body, subordinate to higher law (statutes, charters, constitutions); (3) it regulates conduct, procedure, or organization of the body and its members. Persistence mechanism: written codification adopted by formal vote or resolution, maintained through organizational record-keeping and periodic amendment. [formal: by-latus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.21]

A caveat is a formal warning or caution entered to prevent unauthorized action — especially in legal contexts, where a party files a caveat to suspend proceedings until they have been heard. It operates as a procedural shield: the act of entering a caveat creates a mandatory pause, forcing any subsequent action to notify the cautioner first. Parameters: (1) it must be formally communicated to an authority or counterparty, (2) it specifies what action is to be suspended, (3) it identifies the party entitled to notification before that action proceeds. Its persistence mechanism is institutional — recorded in official registers, maintained through procedural rules, and enforced by the consequences of ignoring it. [formal: caveat | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

An epigraph is a brief quotation, saying, or phrase selected by an author or publisher to open a book, chapter, or other creative work — or an inscription on a building, statue, or artifact — that establishes mood, signals theme, or acknowledges an influence. Parameters: (1) brevity — typically one to three sentences or a short phrase; (2) selection — deliberately chosen from another source or composed for placement; (3) position — appears at the front matter or physically inscribed on a surface; (4) function — sets interpretive frame, pays homage, or provides thematic resonance. Persistence mechanism: published texts (printed pages, digital files) and physical inscriptions (stone, metal, wood), maintained through reproduction and preservation.

Folklore is the body of traditions, stories, beliefs, customs, and practices that a community transmits across generations not through formal institutions but through informal, communal means — oral storytelling, song, ritual performance, proverbs, and material craft. It is distinguished from literary or academic culture by its collective authorship, variant transmission (each telling reshapes it slightly), and functional role in binding community identity. Parameters: (1) the content must be traditional, originating in the collective past rather than a single named author; (2) the transmission must be informal and communal rather than institutionalized or canonized; (3) it persists through repeated re-performance and re-telling, each iteration a new instantiation. The persistence mechanism is communal practice — the repeated act of telling, singing, doing, and teaching within a community. Without that communal re-enactment, folklore dissolves into archive or artifact.\n\n[formal: folklore | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A typology is a human-made system of classification that sorts phenomena into named types according to shared criteria. It carves reality by imposing a finite set of mutually distinguishable categories, each defined by a profile of attributes. The persistence mechanism is teaching and citation: a typology lives as long as it is reproduced in curricula, taxonomies, and analytical frameworks. It does not discover natural kinds but constructs working partitions — useful maps that can be revised when the categories cease to track the phenomena they are meant to sort.

[formal: typologia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.23]

An incipit is the opening words or phrase of a written work, distinguished from the body text by decoration, special script, or spatial separation. Scribes produce incipits as visual markers that allow readers to identify a text's beginning and title — a convention of manuscript culture where titles were often absent from the opening folio. The incipit persists through scribal reproduction (copied as part of the text), cataloguing (used to identify unattributed manuscripts), and scholarly reference (scholars cite incipits to identify works whose titles were lost). [formal: incipit | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A euphemism is a human-made linguistic substitution: the replacement of a word or phrase considered harsh, blunt, offensive, or undesirable with one that is milder, more pleasant, or more indirect. Its parameters are (1) a source term that carries unwanted connotations (taboo, violence, vulgarity, social discomfort), (2) a substitute term that maps to the same referent while attenuating its affective charge, and (3) a social context in which the attenuation is recognized as intentional — the euphemism only works when speakers and listeners both understand what is being softened. The persistence mechanism is language: taught in conversation, reinforced by politeness norms, and spread through repetition until the euphemism itself may become taboo, triggering a fresh cycle of substitution. [formal: euphēmos | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Interpretation is the human-made practice of deriving intended or plausible meaning from a text, signal, or artifact that admits more than one reading. Its parameters are: (1) a source that is semantically underdeterminate — language, art, ritual, code — such that a literal reading leaves gaps; (2) a reader equipped with a shared framework (language, convention, domain knowledge) that constrains possible meanings; (3) an output: an explicit rendering of what the source means, in the interpreter's terms. Interpretation persists through teaching, citation, and the cumulative layering of commentaries across generations — each interpretation becomes itself a source for further interpretation. The mechanism of persistence is linguistic tradition: meaning is sustained because communities reproduce and contest readings, not because any single reading is final.

[formal: interpretatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A curse is a human-made speech act in which the speaker invokes harm, misfortune, or ill-will upon a target person, group, or entity. Its parameters are: (1) a speaker who performs the utterance with intent; (2) a named or identifiable target; (3) a desired outcome expressed as harm or misfortune (physical, social, or spiritual); (4) a framework — religious, magical, or social — that gives the utterance force or perceived force. A curse is not the harm it describes; it is the act of invoking it. It persists through transmission: oral repetition, written records, and cultural memory keep curses alive long after the original speaker is gone. The mechanism of persistence is ritual recurrence — communities recite, reference, or warn against curses, embedding them in tradition. The self is an entry; the human-animal is not. The self is an entry; the human-animal is not.

A catchword is a word or brief phrase inscribed at the base of a page in a handwritten or printed codex, placed there by the scribe or printer to ensure correct folio ordering during gathering and collation. Parameters: (1) a lexical token matching the opening word of the succeeding page, (2) positioned at the bottom margin of the verso or recto, (3) produced as part of the bookmaking workflow. Persistence mechanism: established through scribal convention, codified in printing house practices, and maintained by bookbinders and librarians who verify page order by reading catchwords during binding. [formal: catchword | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.23]

Analogy is a human-made cognitive and rhetorical device that maps perceived similarities between two distinct domains — a source and a target — to reason about the target by reference to the source. Parameters: (1) it requires two structurally distinct entities or systems, (2) it identifies shared relational patterns (not merely surface features), (3) the mapping is partial, not total. Analogy persists through language (the comparative constructions that encode it), through teaching and pedagogy (where it serves as a bridge between the known and the unknown), and through argumentation (where it functions as evidence by similarity). It is a deliberate, teachable practice — not a spontaneous cognitive accident — and belongs squarely on the made side under Law 1 and the map clause of Law 2a.
[formal: analogia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 24.01]

A quorum is the minimum number of members of a deliberative body that must be present at any given time for the proceedings to be officially valid. The parameter is a count (fixed number or fraction, e.g. majority, two-thirds) set by the body's rules or governing statute. It persists through the institutional rules that establish it and the procedural practice that enforces it — without a quorum, no binding action can be taken, and any action taken without one is voidable. The mechanism is procedural: roll call or verification of attendance against the threshold, with the chair declaring whether the quorum is met. If the threshold drops below during proceedings, the body may continue to act on limited matters but cannot take substantive action until quorum is restored.\n\n[formal: quorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A siglum is a shorthand sign — typically a single letter, number, or symbol — that a scribe or editor assigns to a manuscript, witness, or source text for repeated reference without full citation. Parameters: (1) the sign must be a concise symbol (not a full word), (2) it maps one-to-one to a specific textual witness, and (3) it operates within a critical apparatus or collation system where space and repetition make full names impractical. Persistence: the siglum persists through the convention of the critical apparatus — once established in a scholarly edition or manuscript tradition, it is reused across commentaries, indices, and subsequent editions. [formal: siglum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.33]

Genre is a classificatory schema that groups creative works (literature, film, music, visual art) by shared conventions, tropes, and audience expectations. Parameters: (1) works must share sufficient formal or thematic markers to be recognizably grouped; (2) the grouping must be sustained by a community of creators and consumers who treat the label as predictive; (3) boundaries between genres are fuzzy and contested but never arbitrary — a work is assigned to a genre by convention, not essence. Persistence mechanism: genre survives through teaching, criticism, marketing taxonomy, and the self-reinforcing practice of creators working within and against established categories. It is a map that both describes and prescribes creative output.

Persistence mechanism: genre survives through teaching, criticism, marketing taxonomy, and the self-reinforcing practice of creators working within and against established categories. It is a map that both describes and prescribes creative output. [formal: generis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Delegation is the human practice of assigning authority, responsibility, or a task to another person (or entity) while retaining the right to call it back. Parameters: (1) a delegator who holds initial authority, (2) a delegatee who receives delegated authority, (3) a domain of authority being transferred, (4) conditions or limits on the transfer, and (5) a mechanism for revocation or completion. Persistence mechanism: delegation persists through social convention, institutional records (charters, appointments, powers of attorney), and the ongoing compliance of the delegatee; it collapses when the delegator revokes it, the delegatee abandons it, or the underlying authority dissolves. Unlike assignment (which transfers ownership), delegation preserves the delegator's ultimate claim — the authority flows outward but the line of return remains open. [formal: delegatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.26]

An exemplar is a model manuscript — a master copy carefully produced and corrected so that scribes may replicate it faithfully. Parameters: (1) It must be a complete or near-complete text, not a fragment; (2) It is deliberately corrected against other witnesses to achieve textual accuracy; (3) It serves as the physical archetype from which subsequent copies are made. The persistence mechanism is institutional archival practice: exemplars are preserved in scriptoria, monastic libraries, and cathedral archives as reference standards. [formal: exemplar | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.17]

An injunction is a judicial order commanding a party to perform or refrain from performing a specified act. Parameters: (1) type — prohibitory (forbids an act) or mandatory (compels an act); (2) temporality — temporary (pending litigation), preliminary (pending trial), or permanent (after judgment); (3) enforceability — breaches incur contempt sanctions (fines or imprisonment); (4) threshold — the movant must show irreparable harm, inadequate legal remedies, and likelihood of success on the merits (for preliminary relief). Persistence mechanism: the injunction endures as an enforceable court order recorded in the docket, backed by the state's coercive power through contempt proceedings. [formal: iniunctio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Testimony is a structured verbal or written declaration, offered within a recognized forum (court, inquiry, deposition, or formal hearing), in which a declared speaker asserts propositions of fact as grounds for another's belief or judgment. Parameters: (1) declarant — a specific human agent who can be identified and held accountable; (2) forum — an institutional setting with rules governing admissibility and weight; (3) propositional content — claims about facts, not opinions or wishes, distinguished by verifiability criteria; (4) attestation — the declarant affirms the statement as true, typically under oath or equivalent sanction. Persistence mechanism: testimony endures through transcription, recording, and archival in the forum's official record; it is reproduced verbatim in transcripts and cited by reference in subsequent proceedings, surviving the original speech act as a document. [formal: testimonium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.27]

Jurisdiction is the legally recognized authority of a specific institution to exercise governance over particular persons, subject matters, or territory within a defined domain. Parameters: (1) grantor — the sovereign or constitutional source that confers authority (state, statute, treaty, or charter); (2) scope — the boundaries of authority, specified by subject-matter (criminal, civil, administrative), personal (citizens, residents, territorial), or geographic (territorial, extraterritorial); (3) hierarchy — the layered structure of authority (local, regional, national, supranational) with rules for precedence when domains overlap. Persistence mechanism: jurisdiction is maintained through institutional continuity — statutes, charters, and constitutional provisions that are codified in legal texts and reproduced in every act of governance; precedent records in case law extend and refine jurisdictional boundaries over time. [formal: iurisdictio | substrate: law | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.28]

A treatise is a formal, systematic written discourse on a subject, produced by a single or coordinated author to advance understanding through structured argument and comprehensive treatment. Parameters: (1) the work must be systematic — organized around a coherent thesis or framework, not a collection of disparate observations; (2) it must be substantive — exceeding the scope of an essay or article in depth, scope, and rigor; (3) the subject must be singular enough to admit thorough treatment — a single discipline, principle, or problem rather than a survey of many. Persistence mechanism: treatises endure through publication, institutional archiving, citation in subsequent scholarship, and reproduction in academic or professional canons. They persist because scholarly and professional communities actively maintain them as reference works — citing, building upon, and teaching from them across generations. [formal: tractatus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

Litotes is a rhetorical figure of understatement that affirms a proposition by negating its direct opposite. It operates through deliberate minimisation: the speaker denies one term ("not unkind" for "kind", "no small achievement" for "impressive") to produce an affirmative meaning that carries pragmatic emphasis precisely because it underplays itself. Parameters: (1) the negated proposition must be the lexical opposite or near-opposite of the affirmed meaning; (2) the affirmative reading is conventional and recoverable without contextual supplementation beyond standard implicature; (3) the figure functions at the level of utterance — it is a speech-act strategy, not a truth-functional operator. Persistence mechanism: litotes is sustained by the teachable convention of its use across languages and registers, transmitted through rhetorical training, literary tradition, and everyday pragmatic competence. [formal: litotes | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A corporation-of-corporators is a legal entity constituted by a body of persons (the corporators) who hold membership rights in the corporation and exercise collective governance through voting on fundamental matters such as charter amendments, director elections, and dissolution. The entity exists as a separate juridical person from its corporators, but its authority derives from the corporators' delegated power under the charter or articles of incorporation.

Parameters: (1) there must be at least one corporator; (2) corporators hold membership rights defined by the charter (voting, information, residual claim); (3) governance operates through collective decision procedures (vote thresholds, quorum requirements) specified in the charter; (4) the entity's separate juridical personality shields corporators from personal liability to the extent defined by statute.

Persistence mechanism: the corporation persists through periodic filings (annual reports, franchise tax submissions) required by the jurisdiction of incorporation, through the continuous operation of its charter as a standing legal instrument, and through the succession of corporator bodies across generations — the corporate form outlives individual members because the charter and statutory framework provide for perpetual succession unless dissolved by formal procedure.

[formal: corpus corporatorum | substrate: law | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.27]

An explicit is a terminal notation placed at the conclusion of a manuscript text by its scribe or author, declaring the work complete. It conventionally includes an end-mark (such as a cross or colophon formula) and may name the author, scribe, location, date, or patron. The explicit carves a specific scribal act: a completion signal appended to a text, distinct from the incipit (which signals its beginning). It persists through the material practice of manuscript production and the convention of textual transmission in literate communities. [formal: explicitum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

A lens is a deliberately adopted conceptual framework through which a domain of phenomena is examined, analyzed, or interpreted. It operates as a selective interpretive filter: it highlights certain features, suppresses others, and structures the relationship between observer and observed. A lens is not a description of reality itself but a human-made instrument for producing structured readings of reality — it persists through pedagogical transmission, disciplinary tradition, and the shared vocabulary of its host field. Parameters: (1) a target domain to be examined, (2) a set of principles or assumptions that constitute the lens, (3) a community that maintains and transmits it. The persistence mechanism is teaching and disciplinary practice. [formal: lensis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A legend is an explanatory key that maps symbols, marks, or colors within a diagram, map, or chart to their intended meanings. Parameters: the legend must enumerate or categorize each symbol used, and each symbol must map to exactly one referent. Persistence mechanism: the legend persists through convention — once established it endures across copies and transmissions of the diagram or map, enabling any future viewer to decode visual information without the original creator. Law 6: This definition carves legend as a human-made convention for visual interpretation, excluding natural features (which lack an agreed symbol mapping) and abstract art without encoded meaning.

Semiotics is the systematic study of signs and symbols — how humans create, interpret, and communicate meaning through coded marks, gestures, sounds, and images. It carves a domain of meta-communication: the study of how signs stand for things, how meaning is generated by conventions and context, and how interpretive frameworks operate across disciplines from linguistics to architecture. Semiotics persists as an academic discipline, a methodological toolkit, and a cultural practice that people learn, teach, and apply to decode the semiotic systems that surround them — advertising, fashion, art, language, traffic signals, and more. [formal: semiotica | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A criterion is a human-made standard or principle used to judge, evaluate, or decide whether something qualifies for a category, award, or determination. Parameters: (1) it must be stated or statable in language; (2) it operates as a decision rule applied to instances; (3) it persists through social agreement, teaching, and formal codification in fields (science, law, art, commerce). The mechanism of persistence is linguistic and institutional — criteria are transmitted through instruction, embedded in rubrics and classification systems, and enforced by the practices that rely on them. Without this map-making, evaluation collapses into arbitrary preference. [formal: criterion | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A rubicon is a human-made metaphorical concept denoting a threshold action or decision beyond which retreat is impossible without loss — a point of no return. Its parameters are: (1) a prior commitment or crossing that cannot be undone, (2) an irreversible consequence that follows, and (3) a cultural awareness that the crossing is final. It persists through language, rhetoric, teaching, and shared narrative — the metaphor is transmitted across generations as a shorthand for irreversible choice. The concept derives from the historical crossing of the Rubicon river by Julius Caesar in 49 BCE but now operates as an independent metaphorical construct, detached from its geographical origin. [formal: rubicon | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Formalism is a human-made approach to reasoning and representation that replaces intuitive or semantic content with explicit symbolic structures and rule-based manipulation. It carves the space of formalisms by three parameters: (1) a formal language with precisely defined syntax, (2) a set of inference or transformation rules operating on syntactic forms, and (3) a semantics assigning meaning to the formal structures. It persists through institutional transmission in mathematics, logic, computer science, and the sciences — taught, codified, and validated within disciplinary communities. [formal: formalismus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A topos (plural: topoi) is a human-made argument strategy — a reusable template for reasoning or persuasion that can be applied across different subjects and contexts. Originating in Aristotelian rhetoric, a topos specifies a pattern of inference (e.g., comparing greater to lesser, cause to effect, or definition to accident) that an arguer can instantiate with specific content. The parameters that define a topos are: (1) a relational schema (the logical structure, such as causal or comparative), (2) a domain of application (the subject matter it can be applied to), and (3) a set of fillable slots (the concrete terms that occupy the schema). It persists through teaching (the rhetorical tradition), textual transmission (rhetorical handbooks from Aristotle through Cicero to modern composition), and cognitive habit (argument schemas internalized by speakers). [formal: topos | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A notation is a human-made symbolic system designed to record, represent, or encode information in a stable, reusable form. A notation specifies: (1) a set of signs or symbols (its alphabet or vocabulary), (2) a syntax governing how those signs combine (formation rules), and (3) a semantics mapping sign combinations to meaning. The persistence mechanism is material inscription — the symbols are designed to endure on a substrate (clay, paper, digital storage) so that the encoded information survives beyond the moment of its creation and can be decoded by others at a later time. Notations persist through reproduction (copying, printing, transmission), institutional maintenance (standardization bodies, communities of practice), and the physical durability of their carriers. [formal: notatio | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Adjudication is the formal process by which a designated authority resolves disputes between parties through structured procedure. It operates by: (1) receiving competing claims, (2) applying established rules to the facts, and (3) issuing a binding decision. Its parameters are: an adjudicator with jurisdiction, parties in dispute, and a body of applicable rules. It persists through institutional training, written procedure codes, and the authority of precedent. [formal: iudicium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Irony is a rhetorical figure in which a speaker says something that deliberately diverges from what they mean, relying on the audience to infer the intended meaning from context. The mechanism of persistence is linguistic convention — shared cultural knowledge that maps surface utterance to underlying intent through contrast. Irony operates as a signal of in-group understanding: only participants who recognize the gap between literal and intended meaning can decode it. The technique requires a dual-layer of meaning (surface and subtext), a context that makes the divergence detectable, and a social convention that treats the gap as meaningful rather than deceptive. [formal: ironia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.05]

A trope is a conventionalized figure of speech or recurring literary device that conveys meaning through established cultural association rather than literal description. The mechanism of persistence is repetition across texts and media — a trope endures because it efficiently signals a complex set of ideas through a recognizable pattern. Tropes function as cognitive shorthand: they package narrative, thematic, or rhetorical content into familiar forms that audiences decode instantly. A trope requires (1) a recognizable pattern of expression, (2) an established convention linking the pattern to its meaning, and (3) a community of interpreters who share the convention. Tropes are not metaphors (which are local and novel) but stock formulas — the difference between inventing a comparison and deploying a shared symbol. [formal: tropus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: no | epoch: 0.06]

Collation is the editorial practice of comparing multiple copies, fragments, or witnesses of a text and assembling them into a correct sequential order. The definition carves collation as (1) the act of comparing two or more versions or parts of a document, (2) the determination of the correct sequence through scholarly judgment, and (3) the physical or digital assembly of the ordered parts into a coherent whole. Collation persists through the explicit mechanisms of editorial discipline, scribal practice, and the conventions of textual scholarship — it is a behavior enacted by human practitioners using established methods of comparison and sequencing. [formal: collatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Grievance is a human-made construct for articulating a formal complaint about a perceived wrong within a social, institutional, or legal framework. It carves a specific boundary: not mere displeasure, but an expressed claim that requires recognition and response from an authority or peer group. Grievance transforms subjective harm into an actionable social signal — it names the injury, attributes responsibility, and demands remedy. It persists through language (the vocabulary of complaint), legal procedure (formalized grievance mechanisms), and social practice (grievance as a recognized mode of contestation). Without grievance, wrongs remain private; with it, they become public claims that reshape relationships and institutions. [formal: querela | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

A synopsis is a condensed summary of a larger work that preserves its essential structure, argument, or narrative arc while omitting supporting detail. It operates as a compression device: the author selects which elements carry the core meaning and reconstructs them in miniature form. The persistence mechanism is reproduction through citation, cataloging, and distribution — synopses survive wherever the parent work is referenced, indexed, or reviewed. [formal: synopsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.37]

A cognitive-map is a representational construct used to organize and navigate knowledge about spatial relationships and their connections to broader information domains. It functions as a structured internal model that enables pathfinding, spatial reasoning, and relational mapping between discrete pieces of knowledge. Parameters: (1) anchor points — salient nodes of reference that serve as orientation markers; (2) connectors — the perceived or intended relationships between anchors, which may be topological, categorical, or temporal; (3) scale fidelity — the granularity at which the map resolves detail, which varies by purpose (wayfinding versus systematic mapping). Persistence mechanism: sustained through academic discourse in cognitive science and psychology, institutionalized in educational curricula that teach spatial thinking and knowledge organization, and embedded in design tools (mind maps, concept diagrams) that externalize the construct for collaborative use. [formal: tabula_cognitiva | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.32]

Parody is a creative construct that produces a derived work imitating the style, form, or content of an original through deliberate exaggeration, distortion, or incongruity for comic effect, criticism, or commentary. Parameters: (1) source text — the recognizable original work whose conventions are being imitated; (2) distortion device — the mechanism of exaggeration, misdirection, or juxtaposition that signals the gap between source and target; (3) intent frame — the audience's recognition that the work is playful or critical rather than fraudulent, which distinguishes parody from plagiarism. Persistence mechanism: preserved through literary and performance traditions, institutionalized in copyright doctrine's fair-use exception (which grants it legal standing in some jurisdictions), and transmitted via cultural practice where each new parody references both the source and earlier parodic treatments. [formal: imitatio_ludicra | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

A method for externalizing the structure of knowledge by representing concepts as nodes and their relationships as labeled links, producing a visual or symbolic map that makes implicit mental structures explicit and shareable. Parameters: (1) nodes must be discrete conceptual units — terms, categories, or propositions; (2) edges must encode specific relationship types (e.g., causes, contrasts, hierarchies, exemplifies); (3) the map must be rendered in a medium external to the creator's mind (paper, screen, whiteboard). Persistence mechanism: maps survive through reproduction (photographing, scanning, re-drawing), teaching (instructing others in the method), and storage (filing diagrams in repositories). The practice persists as long as organizations and individuals need to align understanding, surface assumptions, or navigate complexity in groups. [formal: conceptus-mappa | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.33]

An axiom is a proposition asserted without proof within a formal system, serving as a starting point for deductive reasoning. Its parameters are: (1) it must be self-consistent within the system it grounds, (2) it must be non-derivable from other axioms in that system, and (3) its acceptance is conventional — chosen by the system's authors, not discovered as a natural fact. It persists through codification in formal languages, transmission across generations of practitioners, and the stability of the deductive frameworks it anchors. [formal: axioma | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.38]

Arbitration is a dispute-resolution procedure in which the parties submit their conflict to a neutral third party (the arbitrator) who renders a binding decision after hearing evidence and argument. Parameters: (1) mutual agreement to arbitrate, (2) selection of a neutral arbitrator, (3) adversarial presentation of positions, (4) binding award. Persistence mechanism: institutionalized through arbitration rules (e.g., ICC, AAA), trained arbitrator networks, and legal enforcement frameworks (e.g., the New York Convention) that reproduce the practice across jurisdictions and generations. The map distinguishes arbitration from mediation (non-binding facilitation) and litigation (state-court adjudication) by its consensual origin and private finality. [formal: arbitrium | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An indictment is the formal written accusation that a person has committed a crime, typically presented by a grand jury and filed by a prosecutor. It serves as the official gateway between suspicion and trial, transforming informal investigation into state-sanctioned criminal proceedings. The parameters of indictment are: (1) it must name specific charges, (2) it must identify the accused, (3) it must be issued by competent authority (grand jury or prosecutor), and (4) it persists as a court record that triggers procedural rights and deadlines. The persistence mechanism is institutional — courts maintain indictment records, and the legal process operates on their authority.[formal: accusatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.54]

accreditation is the institutional act by which an authorized body certifies that an individual, program, institution, or product meets a published standard of quality, competence, or compliance. Parameters: (1) accreditor must possess recognized authority (granted by law, professional body, or market consensus); (2) standard must be explicit and publicly available; (3) accredited entity must undergo assessment against those standards; (4) accreditation is time-bound and subject to renewal or withdrawal. Persistence mechanism: institutional records (certificates, registries, databases), legal recognition, and social enforcement (market exclusion of non-accredited entities, licensing requirements). The map it produces is the accreditation status itself — a binary or graded signal that reduces information asymmetry between provider and consumer. [formal: accreditatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Burden of proof is the legal rule governing adjudicative proceedings that assigns the obligation to produce sufficient evidence supporting one's affirmative claims. Parameters: (1) a designated party bears the obligation (typically the plaintiff or prosecution), (2) the standard of proof required (preponderance, clear and convincing, beyond reasonable doubt), (3) the consequences of failing to meet it (automatic loss on that issue). The persistence mechanism is codified procedural law and judicial enforcement — the rule exists because legal institutions maintain and apply it. [formal: onus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.91]

A corollary is a proposition that follows directly from a theorem or principal result already established, requiring little or no additional proof to establish its truth. Its parameters are: (1) it must derive from a prior proved statement; (2) its proof is immediate or trivial relative to the parent theorem; (3) it is named and separated so it can be cited independently. It persists as a conventional unit of mathematical communication — a packaging device that lets later work cite a derived fact without reproducing its (often simple) derivation. [formal: corollarium | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

persuasion is the deliberate act of attempting to change another person's beliefs, attitudes, or intentions through reasoned argument, narrative, or rhetorical strategy rather than coercion or force. Parameters: the persuader selects a target audience, constructs an appeal (logos, ethos, or pathos), and deploys it through a chosen medium; the target receives and processes the appeal within their existing belief framework. Persistence occurs through reproduction (re-delivery of arguments), teaching (transmission of rhetorical technique), storage (recorded speeches, texts, media), and social reinforcement (shared persuasive conventions). [formal: persuasio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.35]

dissent is the formal or informal expression of disagreement with an official position, decision, or majority view, especially within an institutional setting such as a court, legislature, or organization. Parameters: the dissenter identifies a specific position or ruling, articulates reasons for disagreement (legal, moral, practical), and delivers the dissent through a recognized channel (written opinion, spoken objection, formal record). Persistence occurs through reproduction (publication and citation of dissenting opinions), teaching (legal and civic education on the role of dissent), storage (official records, case law reporters), and institutional practice (rules recognizing dissent as part of deliberative process). [formal: dissentientia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.35]

An appeal is a formal request to a higher authority to review and possibly reverse or modify a decision already rendered by a lower authority. Parameters: (1) an existing decision by a recognized authority, (2) a designated superior authority with jurisdiction to review, (3) a prescribed procedural mechanism for submitting the request, (4) a defined scope of reviewable issues. Persistence: written records, institutionalized procedures, codified rules of appellate practice, and the social expectation that decisions are subject to hierarchical review. [formal: appellatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.91]

A compact is a formal agreement between two or more parties establishing mutual obligations and governing their relationship. Parameters: (1) at least two distinct parties with capacity to bind themselves, (2) clearly stated obligations assumed by each party, (3) a shared understanding of the scope and purpose of the agreement, (4) an enforcement mechanism — either internal (social pressure, mutual withdrawal) or external (institutional backing). Persistence: written documents, institutional memory, treaty registries, legal enforcement through courts, and the ongoing practice of honoring commitments. [formal: compactum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.91]

A presumption is a rule that treats an unproven proposition as if it were proven, shifting the burden of rebuttal to the opposing party. Parameters: (1) it operates within a defined domain of reasoning (legal, administrative, or conversational); (2) it specifies the proposition being presumed and the conditions that trigger it; (3) it defines the standard and mechanism for rebuttal. Persistence mechanism: codified in statutes and case law, taught through legal education and professional practice, and reinforced through institutional routine. [formal: praesumptio | substrate: law | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bias is a systematic tendency to favor, interpret, or weight information, evidence, or judgment in a particular direction — not the natural cognitive inclination itself but the human-constructed map that names, categorizes, and tracks predictable deviations from neutrality. Parameters: (1) directionality — a consistent tilt toward or away from a position, outcome, or interpretation; (2) systematicity — the tendency recurs across instances and subjects, not a one-off error; (3) direction — the tilt can be toward confirmation, away from threat, or toward social alignment, and varies by context. Persistence mechanism: biases persist through repeated cognitive rehearsal, cultural transmission (language, norms, teaching), and institutional reinforcement — they are learned maps that become automatic shortcuts, stable across generations as long as the social and cognitive conditions that sustain them endure. [formal: bias | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Argumentation is the structured practice of constructing, presenting, and evaluating reasons in support of claims. It operates through three constitutive parameters: (1) claims that are put forward for acceptance, (2) reasons — premises, evidence, or authorities — offered as grounds for those claims, and (3) rules of inference and relevance that govern which reasons support which claims. The persistence mechanism is language: argumentation is sustained through oral and written discourse, teaching of argumentative norms, and institutionalized forms (debate, legal proceedings, peer review, philosophical treatises). It is a human-made cognitive technology for converting raw inference into accountable, criticizable exchange. [formal: argumentatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A worldview is the conceptual framework through which a person or community interprets reality — the organized map of categories, assumptions, values, and explanatory principles that determines what counts as real, true, or significant within a given culture or individual.

Parameters: A worldview comprises (1) a cosmology — a map of what kinds of things exist and how they relate, (2) an axiology — a hierarchy of what matters or is valuable, (3) an epistemology — criteria for what counts as knowledge or justified belief, and (4) a narrative structure — the story-form through which experience is sequenced and made meaningful. These components are interlocking: changing the cosmology reconfigures the axiology, and vice versa.

Persistence: A worldview persists through language (the vocabulary and grammar that encode its categories), through teaching (formal and informal transmission across generations), through ritual (repeated performance that embodies and reinforces its assumptions), and through institutions (organizations that select, reward, and punish according to its standards). It is maintained not as a static doctrine but as a living interpretive lens — constantly tested against experience, revised at the margins, and defended at the core.

A worldview is not any particular set of beliefs — it is the map-making apparatus itself, the system by which beliefs are organized, weighted, and deployed.

Canonical is the institutional process by which a community selects, preserves, and elevates certain texts, practices, authorities, or claims to normative status — the mechanism that decides what counts as definitive within a discipline, tradition, or field.

Parameters: Canonical operation requires (1) a corpus — the body of materials under consideration, (2) an authority — the person, body, or procedure vested with selection power, (3) exclusion criteria — what disqualifies materials from the corpus, and (4) a reproduction mechanism — how the selected materials are copied, taught, and referenced to maintain their privileged position across time.

Persistence: The canonical persists through citation practices (citing the canonical validates it; not citing it erodes it), through institutional curricula (schools and universities teach the canon as foundational), through ritualized reference (calling upon canonical authorities as decisive), and through material reproduction (printing, digitizing, preserving the canonical texts). The canon is self-reinforcing: being canonical makes something more likely to be cited, and being cited makes it more canonical.

The canonical is not the collection itself but the process — the active governance of what a community treats as its definitive reference point.

A standard-of-proof is a normative threshold that specifies the degree of evidence required to establish a proposition as settled within a given domain. Its parameters are: (1) the domain (criminal law, civil law, science, ordinary reasoning), each with its own threshold; (2) the direction of the burden (who must meet the standard); (3) the form of evidence considered (testimonial, documentary, circumstantial). The standard exists as a linguistic and institutional convention — taught in legal education, encoded in jury instructions, invoked in scientific methodology — and persists through language, teaching, and formal procedure. It is not a natural property of evidence itself but a human-made rule for deciding when evidence is sufficient.\n\n[formal: standard_probandae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An ordinance is a rule or decree issued by a governing authority — municipal council, executive officer, or administrative body — that carries the force of law within a defined jurisdiction. Parameters: (1) issuer must hold delegated or constitutional authority to legislate at the applicable tier, (2) scope is territorial or institutional (city, district, agency), (3) content regulates behavior, establishes procedures, or allocates resources within that scope. Persistence mechanism: codification in municipal code or administrative register, enforced through compliance monitoring and penalty structures that sustain behavioral compliance over time. The ordinance persists as long as the issuing authority maintains legitimacy and the enforcement apparatus remains active — its life cycle runs from promulgation through amendment or repeal, typically spanning months to decades across multiple administrative epochs. [formal: ordo | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

Cognitive dissonance is the psychological tension produced by holding two or more inconsistent cognitions (beliefs, attitudes, values, or knowledge of one's behavior). The theory predicts that people are motivated to reduce this tension through belief revision, selective exposure to confirming information, behavioral change, or rationalization. Parameters: (1) at least two inconsistent cognitions must be present; (2) the individual must be aware of the inconsistency at some level; (3) a motivational drive to restore consistency follows. Persists through cognitive architecture — taught in psychology, applied in advertising and political campaigns, internalized through self-reflection and therapeutic practice. [formal: cognitio-dissonantia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Abduction is the mode of inference that generates explanatory hypotheses from surprising observations — reasoning from an effect back to its most plausible cause. Formally: given observation O and rule R such that if H were true O would be a matter of course, abduction proposes H as a tentative hypothesis. Parameters: (1) the observation must be unexpected under current background knowledge; (2) the hypothesis must, if true, explain the observation; (3) the selection among competing hypotheses is guided by criteria of explanatory power, simplicity, and coherence — not by certainty. Unlike deduction (which guarantees its conclusion given its premises) and induction (which generalizes from repeated observations), abduction yields conjecture, not proof. It is the only inferential form that produces new ideas. Persistence mechanism: abduction persists through formalization in logic, teaching in scientific methodology, and daily use in diagnostic reasoning (medicine, engineering, everyday commonsense explanation). [formal: abductio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Credibility is the human-made epistemic practice of assessing whether a source, claim, or entity is worthy of belief. It operates through structured criteria—expertise, consistency, transparency, track-record—that transform raw trust into assessable judgment. The parameters of credibility are: (1) a source whose reliability is evaluated, (2) criteria drawn from discipline-specific standards, (3) a mechanism of verification or corroboration, and (4) a social process of calibration across communities of practice. Credibility persists through institutionalized standards of evidence, published credentials, peer review, and the accumulated reputation mechanisms of professional and social communities. It is a map, not the territory: the word 'credible' picks out a category humans constructed to sort information sources, not the natural property of being trustworthy. [formal: credibility | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.23]

A canon is an accepted corpus of works, texts, or principles regarded as authoritative within a discipline, tradition, or community. Parameters: (1) a bounded set of items selected as representative or definitive; (2) selection by a recognized authority or by consensus over time; (3) ongoing maintenance through inclusion, exclusion, and reinterpretation. Persistence mechanism: canons endure through institutional reinforcement — education curricula, citation practices, critical commentary, and canonical lists that are reproduced across generations. They are contested, revised, and sometimes overturned, but the meta-concept of a canon persists as long as communities maintain authoritative lists. [formal: canon | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Rationalization is the post-hoc construction of logically coherent explanations for decisions, behaviors, or beliefs that were originally formed by non-rational means. It operates through three parameters: (1) temporal — the explanation arrives after the act or belief, never before; (2) motivational — the goal is self-consistency maintenance, not truth-seeking; (3) epistemic — the agent sincerely believes the rationalization, distinguishing it from deliberate deception or lying. Rationalization persists through language (the narratives people tell themselves and others), psychology (as a defined clinical concept in psychoanalytic theory and social psychology), and teaching (self-help frameworks, cognitive-behavioral therapy that trains patients to recognize their own rationalizations). [formal: rationalizatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Calibration is the procedure by which a measuring instrument, observational method, or human judgment is brought into alignment with a recognized reference standard. Parameters: (1) existence of a reference standard with documented traceability, (2) a measurement or judgment output from the device or observer, (3) a corrective adjustment or documented deviation record that closes the gap. Persistence mechanism: institutional protocols (ISO standards, laboratory accreditation bodies), calibrated reference artifacts held in controlled environments, and the repeated practice of verification cycles enforced by professional norms. Without these artifacts and the social obligation to consult them, calibration degrades to unverified estimation.\n[formal: calibratio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Enumeration is the systematic practice of counting or listing discrete items one by one, parameterized by the domain of items to enumerate and the ordering principle applied to them. It persists through written tallies, numbered lists, digital databases, and institutional registries that maintain the enumeration over time. [formal: enumeratio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from rational judgment in decision-making and reasoning. It arises from the brain's heuristic processing shortcuts — efficient rules of thumb that trade accuracy for speed — and manifests when these shortcuts produce predictable errors under specific conditions. Parameters: (1) the bias must be reproducible across individuals (not individual idiosyncrasy), (2) it must produce directional deviation (not random noise) from normative models of reasoning, and (3) it must persist despite motivation to be accurate. The persistence mechanism is cognitive architecture: biases are embedded in the structure of human information processing, reinforced through evolutionary adaptation for efficiency, and perpetuated by the unobservability of the reasoning errors they produce — the debiased judgment never surfaces for comparison. [formal: cognitio-biase | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A practice of deliberately reducing complexity in information, processes, or representations to make them accessible, usable, or communicable. Parameters: (1) deliberate reduction — the act is intentional, not accidental loss; (2) complexity reduction — removing detail, steps, or distinction; (3) purpose — making the result more tractable for a specific audience or use. Persists through documented techniques (abstraction layers, heuristics, summaries), institutional protocols (standards bodies that simplify specifications), and cultural transmission (folk simplifications of technical knowledge). Map-focused: this entry concerns the practice of simplification as a construct humans use, not the natural phenomenon of systems tending toward disorder. [formal: simplificare | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

A cognitive bias whereby people give disproportionate weight to recent, vivid, or easily recalled information when making judgments or decisions. The availability heuristic causes the perceived frequency or importance of events to be estimated based on how easily examples come to mind rather than on actual statistical data. Persistence mechanism: maintained through teaching, cognitive science literature, and everyday application in fields like law, medicine, and public policy where it serves as a diagnostic framework for decision quality. [formal: availability | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Semiosis is the process by which signs, symbols, and signs systems produce and sustain meaning. It maps the transformation of a signifier into interpreted significance within a community of interpreters — the semiotic triangle linking sign, referent, and interpretant. Semiosis operates through three modes: icon (resemblance), index (causal/contiguous connection), and symbol (conventional association). It persists through language, ritual, notation, and teaching — the mechanisms by which interpretive frameworks are transmitted across individuals and generations. Without semiosis there is no shared meaning, no culture, no second-order cognition; it is the mechanism by which made signs become instruments of thought.[formal: semiosis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Encoding is the systematic transformation of information into a structured representation -- a mapping from meaning to symbol, signal, or form that can be stored, transmitted, and recovered. Parameters: (1) source domain (what is being encoded -- text, audio, video, state, intent), (2) codebook (the bijective or many-to-one mapping function), (3) alphabet (the primitive symbols the code operates over), (4) protocol (the rules governing when and how the code is applied). Persists through standardization bodies, published specifications, taught curricula, and implementation in tools and protocols -- each implementation is a downstream instance that perpetuates the codebook. [formal: encodatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

A presupposition is a proposition that a speaker or writer treats as already accepted as true within a given context, so that the utterance can function without explicitly asserting it. The parameters of a presupposition are: (1) it is backgrounded rather than foregrounded in communication, (2) it survives negation — if the main claim is denied, the presupposition remains intact, (3) it is a precondition for the utterance to have relevance or truth-aptness at all. A presupposition persists through teaching, discourse conventions, and the structured use of language across communities. Unlike an assertion, a presupposition is not directly accountable for falsity; it hides inside the architecture of the statement itself, which is why presuppositions are the hardest things to challenge in argument.

[formal: praesumptio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

civic-engagement-platform is a human-made construct that provides standardized infrastructure for structured citizen participation in governance. It mediates between individuals and collective decision-making through mechanisms such as deliberative assemblies, participatory budgeting interfaces, petitioning systems, or digital voting platforms. The platform persists through its governing software, institutional charter, or statutory framework — maintained by an organizing authority (state, NGO, or community body) that ensures the participation infrastructure remains operational and accessible. Its persistence mechanism is the continued maintenance of participation infrastructure: the code, administrative procedures, and legal authority that keep the platform functioning across election cycles, policy debates, and shifts in political composition.

sunk-cost-fallacy is a cognitive bias in which people tend to continue an endeavor once they have invested resources—time, money, or effort—beyond the expected return, because the thought of those past investments being wasted feels worse than cutting losses. Its parameters are: (1) prior investment must be real and non-recoverable; (2) the agent must recognize (or be able to recognize) that continuation is irrational; (3) the bias overrides rational cost-benefit analysis in favor of loss-avoidance framing. It persists through teaching in behavioral economics and decision science, where it is named and studied as a category of error. [formal: argumentum ad larem | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A syllogism is a form of deductive reasoning in which a conclusion is derived from two premises that are each affirmed in a third, shared term. It has exactly three propositions — major premise, minor premise, conclusion — and three terms (major, minor, middle), each appearing twice. The middle term bridges the premises; if properly distributed at least once, the inference is valid. Its persistence mechanism is formal notation: syllogistic forms are encoded in logic textbooks, taught as the skeleton of valid inference, and preserved through centuries of philosophical education. [formal: syllogismus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.18]

Stare decisis is the legal doctrine that courts must follow precedent: when a court has ruled on a particular question of law, later cases with materially similar facts must apply that ruling. It operates through hierarchical court structure — lower courts are bound by the decisions of higher courts in the same jurisdiction. Its persistence mechanism is institutional: written opinions, cited in subsequent judgments, enforced by appellate review. Without stare decisis, law would be re-litigated from first principle in every case; with it, legal predictability emerges. [formal: stare decisis | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.18]

A nudge is a behavioral intervention that alters human decision-making by changing the architecture of choice without forbidding options or materially altering economic incentives. Parameters: (1) it must preserve freedom of choice — removing an option makes it a prohibition, not a nudge; (2) it must not change financial incentives in a material way — that is information or regulation, not nudging; (3) it works by leveraging existing cognitive heuristics and biases, not by rational persuasion. The persistence mechanism is institutional design: once embedded in choice architecture by policy-makers, designers, or organizations, a nudge persists until actively removed or overwritten. [formal: iactatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

anchoring-bias is the cognitive tendency wherein an initial numeric or qualitative value (the anchor) disproportionately influences subsequent judgments and estimates, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant. Parameters: (1) the anchor must be encountered before or during judgment; (2) adjustment from the anchor is typically insufficient (underadjustment); (3) the anchor can be consciously recognized as irrelevant yet still exert influence. Persistence mechanism: anchored in experimental replication across domains (pricing, negotiation, moral judgment), encoded in textbooks and lecture curricula of cognitive psychology and behavioral economics, and deployed operationally in choice architecture and debiasing protocols. [formal: anchoring bias | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]

A FRAME is a human-made cognitive structure that selects which features of a situation are made salient and how they are organized for interpretation. Parameters: (1) it provides a bounded schema — a set of slots, roles, and expected relations — that maps onto experience; (2) it is normative in that it prescribes what counts as relevant, coherent, or deviant within its domain; (3) it is transmissible across minds through language, teaching, and cultural reproduction. Persistence mechanism: language and pedagogy — frames are sustained by their repeated deployment in discourse, institutionalized in curricula and professional training, and reinforced through ritualized expressions (idioms, stock phrases, genre conventions). A frame persists as long as communities continue to use it as a shared interpretive lens. [formal: frame | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Metonymy is a linguistic figure of speech and cognitive substitution mechanism in which a referent is named by an associated concept rather than its own proper name. Parameters: (1) the substituting term must have a real, conventionally recognized association with the target (contiguity, not similarity — that is metaphor); (2) the substitution operates within a shared cultural or linguistic context that validates the association; (3) the mapping is conventionalized enough that listeners infer the intended referent without explicit clarification. Persistence mechanism: sustained through rhetorical education, literary tradition, and daily communicative practice — embedded in language instruction, style guides, and the accumulated usage of texts across generations. [formal: metonymia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A fallacy is a pattern of reasoning that appears valid but is logically unsound — it produces a conclusion that does not follow from its premises despite seeming to. Its parameters are (1) a structured argument with premises and a conclusion, (2) a formal or informal defect in the inference rule or premise treatment, and (3) the appearance of validity that enables the error to mislead. It persists through instruction (logic pedagogy catalogs them), debate (where they are deployed and exposed), and language (where the named fallacies function as shorthand for whole classes of bad argument). [formal: fallacia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where the perceived likelihood or frequency of an event is judged by the ease with which relevant instances come to mind. Its parameters are: (1) ease of recall — how quickly and effortlessly examples are retrievable from memory; (2) vividness — how emotionally salient or concrete the available instances are; (3) recency and frequency of exposure — how recently and often the subject encountered related examples. The mechanism persists through psychological instruction, behavioral economics training, media repetition, and experimental replication in the scientific community. It is a category in the taxonomy of cognitive biases, operationalized through tasks measuring how people overestimate the probability of dramatic, media-covered, or personally memorable events. [formal: heuristic | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

A negativity-bias is the cognitive distortion whereby negative information, emotions, events, or evaluations exert a disproportionately greater psychological impact than equivalent positive information. The map draws its boundaries by three parameters: (1) valence asymmetry — negative stimuli are weighted more heavily than identical-magnitude positive stimuli; (2) attentional capture — negative signals recruit attention faster and hold it longer; (3) retention advantage — negative experiences are remembered more vividly and accurately. It persists through empirical operationalization in cognitive psychology, neuroimaging studies showing amygdala asymmetry, and its formalization as a named bias in behavioral science. [formal: bias malus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.48]

Satire is a genre of rhetorical and artistic expression that uses humor, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and critique human vice, folly, or institutional corruption. Parameters: (1) a target of critique (individual, institution, or social norm); (2) a comedic or ironic mode of delivery; (3) an intent to provoke moral or intellectual reflection rather than merely entertain. Satire persists through cultural transmission — publication, performance, pedagogy, and digital reproduction — and survives because it serves a social function: holding power and pretension to account through the subversive vehicle of laughter. [formal: satira | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An enthymeme is a rhetorical syllogism in which one premise is left unstated, assumed to be shared by the audience. Parameters: (1) a conclusion; (2) at least one stated premise; (3) an unstated premise drawn from the audience's beliefs, values, or common knowledge. The enthymeme persists through the structures of persuasion — everyday argument, political speech, advertising, and pedagogical debate — because it exploits the cognitive economy of inference: the audience completes the reasoning themselves, making the conclusion feel self-generated and thus more persuasive. [formal: entheymema | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A method of reasoned discourse in which opposing propositions are advanced, examined, and reconciled through structured dialogue. Parameters: (1) thesis — an initial proposition or claim; (2) antithesis — a counter-proposition exposing contradictions or limitations; (3) synthesis — a resolution that preserves valid elements of both while transcending their conflict. Persistence mechanism: pedagogy (taught as method in philosophy, law, and debate), written records (Socratic dialogues, Hegelian texts), and institutional practice (parliamentary debate, judicial reasoning). Unlike mere debate — which aims at victory — dialectic aims at truth-seeking through the productive tension of opposites. The process itself is the construct: not the propositions but the structured method of their interaction.[formal: dialectica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Working memory is a human-made cognitive model that represents a bounded system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information during complex cognition. Parameters: (1) capacity-limited (roughly 4±1 chunks for most adults), (2) time-limited (maintenance through rehearsal or attention), (3) domain-general (applies across verbal, spatial, and mixed tasks). Persistence mechanism: sustained by active maintenance through attentional control and rehearsal loops, decaying through interference or decay when attention is withdrawn. The construct emerged from the failure of short-term memory models to account for manipulation alongside storage, formalized through span tasks, dual-task interference patterns, and Baddeley\u2019s multi-component model.\n\n[formal: memoria operativa | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Conceptual-metaphor is a human-made cognitive theory that explains how abstract reasoning operates through cross-domain mapping: we understand one conceptual domain (target) in terms of another (source), producing systematic entailments, inferences, and linguistic patterns. Parameters: (1) source domain is concrete and embodied, (2) target domain is abstract, (3) mapping preserves structural relations. Persistence mechanism: teaching in cognitive science, linguistic analysis, and philosophy; documented in scholarly literature and pedagogical practice. The map is the theory itself — the cross-domain mapping model — not the natural human capacity for analogy. [formal: metaphora conceptualis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.99]

Conceptual-metaphor is a human-made cognitive theory that explains how human understanding of one conceptual domain is structured in terms of another. Parameters: (1) a source domain drawn from concrete, embodied experience; (2) a target domain that is abstract or difficult to reason about directly; (3) a systematic mapping of structural relations from source onto target. Persistence: the theory persists through language (metaphorical expressions embed the mappings in everyday speech), through teaching (cognitive science curricula propagate the framework), and through disciplinary practice (metaphor analysis is a method in linguistics, literary theory, and cognitive psychology). [formal: metaphora conceptualis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Fallibilism is the epistemological principle that no human claim to knowledge is beyond the possibility of error or revision. Parameters: (1) knowledge claims are inherently corrigible — no belief is immune to future counter-evidence; (2) certainty is an aspiration, not an attainment; (3) error-correction mechanisms (scientific method, peer review, empirical testing) are the means by which false beliefs are eliminated over time. Originated by C.S. Peirce in 1869 as a methodological stance distinguishing fallible inquiry from dogmatic assertion. Persistence: propagated through scientific practice, philosophical pedagogy, and the institutional norms of intellectual humility. [formal: fallibilismus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Causation is the human-constructed concept of a necessary and sufficient relationship between events, wherein one event (the cause) is held to bring about another (the effect). Its parameters are: (1) temporal precedence — the cause must precede the effect; (2) counterfactual dependence — without the cause, the effect would not occur; (3) mechanism — a plausible chain linking cause to effect. Causation is not the natural world itself; it is the map humans draw across sequences of phenomena to make prediction and responsibility possible. It persists through scientific method (controlled experiments and statistical inference), legal reasoning (proximate cause, but-for test), and everyday language (causal narratives that organize experience into meaningful stories). [formal: causation | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.17]

Hindsight bias is the human-constructed concept of a systematic distortion in retrospective memory: the tendency to reinterpret past events as having been predictable or inevitable after knowing the outcome. Its parameters are (a) a prior state (prediction, uncertainty, or open outcome), (b) knowledge of the actual result, and (c) a reconstructed memory that shifts the prior state toward certainty or inevitability. It persists through structured debriefing protocols, post-mortem analysis, and the naming of the effect itself in psychological literature, where it is measured via recall-of-predictions designs. [formal: post-event-fallax | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.73]

Grammar is the human-made system of rules and patterns that govern the structure and combination of elements within a language — phonemes into morphemes, morphemes into words, words into phrases and clauses. Parameters: (1) hierarchical constituency — elements nest inside larger structures rather than linearing flatly; (2) generativity — a finite rule set produces unbounded expressions; (3) constraint — the rules exclude infinitely more potential combinations than they admit. Grammar is distinct from vocabulary (the lexicon of items) and from usage (how speakers actually deploy grammar); it is the abstract architecture that speakers internalize and apply. Persistence: grammar persists through language acquisition — each generation of children learns it as an internalized cognitive structure, and through prescriptive codification — grammars are described, taught, standardized, and revised in pedagogical and scholarly practice across cultures and epochs.

[formal: grammatica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.17]

Deduction is the human-made form of reasoning in which a conclusion follows necessarily from premises — if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. Parameters: (1) validity — the logical structure guarantees that truth of premises transfers to conclusion; (2) soundness — the premises are in fact true, making the argument not merely valid but truth-preserving; (3) formality — the force of the inference depends on logical form rather than the particular content of the premises. Deduction is distinguished from induction (where premises support but do not guarantee the conclusion) and from abduction (where the conclusion posits the best explanation for observed data). A classic deductive structure is the syllogism: universal premises applied to a particular case yield a necessary conclusion. Persistence: deduction persists through mathematical proof, formal logic systems, legal reasoning (statutory interpretation applied to cases), and computer science (type systems, program verification). It is taught explicitly as a discipline and embedded in tools — programming languages, proof assistants, and legal codes — that enforce deductive structure.

[formal: deductio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.17]

An epistemic loop is a feedback structure within a knowledge-forming system where the output of a process (a belief, model, or conclusion) is fed back as input to influence subsequent iterations of that same process. Parameters: (1) a knowledge-generating mechanism (e.g. scientific inference, reflective judgment), (2) a pathway by which outputs return to modify future inputs, (3) a result that is either corrective (converging toward truth) or corrosive (locking into error). Persists through formal logic, scientific methodology, and reflective practice — institutionalized in peer review, calibration training, and iterated reasoning protocols.
