Parameters: (1) it operates at the level of morphology or syntax rather than phonology; (2) it produces a novel expression in the recipient language that mirrors the source language's internal structure; (3) it is distinguished from borrowing (which imports the whole form) and from semantic extension (which stretches an existing word). Persistence mechanism: calques persist through sustained language contact, bilingual transmission, and the pedagogical circulation of comparative examples — they become entrenched when the target language lacks an existing term and the calque fills the gap. [formal: calque | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

perspective-taking (n.) Perspective-taking is the human-made cognitive skill of representing another person's point of view — their beliefs, knowledge, intentions, or perceptual stance — as distinct from one's own. Parameters: (1) it requires the ability to hold multiple representational perspectives simultaneously; (2) it is distinguishable from empathy (affective resonance) and sympathy (compassionate feeling); (3) it operates across degrees of abstraction from basic theory-of-mind to complex social-role adoption. Persistence mechanism: perspective-taking persists through socialization practices, educational curricula, literary and dramatic training, and the institutional reinforcement of roles that require standpoint switching. [formal: perspectiva | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A schedule is a human-made arrangement that maps tasks, events, or activities onto units of time (hours, days, weeks), specifying when each should occur. Parameters: (1) temporal grid — the time units used to partition the schedule; (2) task list — discrete items assigned to time slots; (3) constraints — ordering rules, deadlines, or resource limits that govern slot assignment. Persistence mechanism: schedules persist through written records, digital systems, social expectation, and institutional enforcement — they are maintained by repeated reference and compliance. A schedule is not a calendar (which records when things happened or will happen passively); it is an active plan that prescribes behavior.\n\n[formal: schedulum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A formula is a human-made symbolic expression that encodes a rule, relationship, or procedure for transforming inputs into outputs. Parameters: (1) symbolic alphabet — the characters and operators that constitute the formula; (2) structural syntax — the arrangement rules governing how symbols combine; (3) semantic interpretation — the domain-specific meaning assigned to the symbols and operations (mathematical, chemical, logical, culinary). Persistence mechanism: formulas persist through written transmission, institutional teaching, and computational implementation — they are invariant across instances so long as the symbolic system remains intact. A formula differs from an algorithm in that a formula states a static relationship while an algorithm specifies a dynamic sequence of steps.\n\n[formal: formula | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

repertoire — The complete set of skills, behaviors, strategies, or responses that an individual, group, or system can draw upon in appropriate situations. PARAMETERS: (1) a bounded set of learned or acquired capabilities rather than innate ones, (2) organized by domain (musical repertoire, rhetorical repertoire, behavioral repertoire), (3) expandable through practice and exposure but always finite at any given time. PERSISTENCE: repertoire persists through repeated activation — skills retained via neural reinforcement, cultural practices sustained through education and modeling, and strategic options preserved in institutional memory. When unused, repertoire items degrade (forgetting curve) or atrophy; when exercised, they sharpen and remain accessible. The concept maps the gap between what one knows and what one can actually deploy under pressure. [formal: repertoire | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

coinage — The act and convention of introducing a new word or phrase into a language. PARAMETERS: (1) novelty — the term must not already exist in the target language with equivalent meaning, (2) communicative utility — it must fill a gap in lexical coverage or express a distinction worth marking, (3) conventionality — it enters the language only when adopted by a speech community, not merely coined by an individual speaker. PERSISTENCE: coinage persists through continued use — words survive when the concepts they name remain socially relevant, when no existing term captures the distinction adequately, and when the phonological form is learnable. Etymological pathways include neologism (creating from scratch), borrowing from other languages, compounding existing morphemes, and deriving from proper nouns. The coinage concept tracks the lifecycle of words from invention to obsolescence. [formal: coinage | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A knowledge-base is a structured human-made repository that organizes information for retrieval, reasoning, and decision-support. Parameters: (1) it collects discrete facts, rules, or procedures in a machine-readable or semantically structured form; (2) it provides indexing, querying, or inference mechanisms to retrieve relevant knowledge; (3) it persists as a maintained resource updated by contributors or automated processes. It persists through institutional curation — the ongoing human work of adding, verifying, and reorganizing content to keep the knowledge accurate and accessible. [formal: cognitio-basis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.19]

A knowledge-base is a structured human-made repository that organizes information for retrieval, inference, and decision support. It comprises encoded facts, rules, or data structures maintained by humans for machine consumption. The boundary is defined by the schema or ontology that governs its contents, and persistence is ensured through digital storage systems and periodic updates. [formal: cognitio_bases | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Genealogy is the systematic practice of tracing and documenting family descent, lineage, and kinship across generations. Parameters: (1) it operates on named individuals linked by descent relations; (2) it produces a structured representation (family tree, pedigree chart) of generational connections; (3) it requires at least two generations to be meaningful. Persistence mechanism: genealogy persists through recorded archives (written pedigrees, genealogical databases, church records), material artifacts (coat of arms, estate documents), and oral transmission within families. [formal: genealogia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Indexing is a human-made system for organizing information into structured references that enable efficient retrieval and navigation. Parameters: (1) it creates an organized mapping between content and location identifiers; (2) it supports lookup operations by category, keyword, or position; (3) it maintains a separate index structure that mirrors or summarizes the indexed material. Persistence mechanism: indexing persists through systematic curation — the index must be regularly updated as the indexed content changes, maintained by human or algorithmic processes that preserve the mapping between content and its reference points. [formal: indexare | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.94]

Bread is a staple food produced by mixing ground grain (typically wheat flour) with water, shaping the resulting dough, and cooking it through baking or steaming. Its defining parameters are: (1) a grain-based substrate, (2) hydration to activate gluten or starch gelatinization, (3) a leavening mechanism — wild or cultivated yeast, bacterial fermentation, or chemical agents — that introduces gas to produce porosity, and (4) heat application that denatures proteins, gelatinizes starches, and drives the Maillard reaction for crust formation. Bread persists as a human construct through culinary transmission: the technique of sourdough, the division between leavened and unleavened varieties across cultures, and the institutionalization of baking as a craft and industry. The map of bread — distinguishing focaccia from pita, sourdough from commercial loaves, injera from baguette — is maintained by culinary education, trade, and the material practice of baking itself. [formal: panis | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Interface is a conceptual boundary or point of interaction between two systems — a human and a machine, two software components, or a user and a service — that mediates exchange by defining what can pass across the boundary, in which direction, and in what format. Its parameters are: (1) a defined set of inputs and outputs, (2) a protocol governing their structure and sequencing, (3) an abstraction that hides internal implementation from the other side, and (4) a contract specifying expected behavior for valid interactions. Interfaces persist through documentation standards, API specifications, and the material artifacts (screens, handles, sockets, protocols) that embody them. The map of interface — graphical, command-line, physical, biological — is sustained by design practice, engineering conventions, and the educational transmission of interaction paradigms. [formal: interface | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

Translation is the practice of rendering meaning from a source language into a target language, preserving intent while transforming expression. Parameters: source text in language A, equivalent meaning in language B, transformation governed by the rules and conventions of both languages. Persists through teaching (translation training), written practice (glossaries, style guides), and technological tools (translation memory systems, machine translation engines). [formal: versio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spaced practice is a learning technique that distributes study sessions over increasing intervals of time, exploiting the psychological spacing effect to strengthen long-term memory retention. Parameters: interval schedule (expanding, fixed, or adaptive), number of repetitions, domain of material, and retention target. Persistence mechanism: cognitive science research, educational practice, and curriculum design transmit the technique across generations of teachers and learners. The method persists because the spacing effect is reliably reproducible and the technique is taught in pedagogy programs worldwide. [formal: discretio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A shirt is a garment for the upper body, typically with sleeves and an opening for the head, worn as an outer layer or undergarment. Parameters: body cut (fitted, loose), sleeve length (sleeveless, short, long), neckline (crew, v-neck, collar), fabric type, fastening (button, pullover, zip). Persists via the clothing trade, fashion practice, and domestic sewing.

An errata-slip is a supplementary sheet or card listing corrections to printed errors in a published work, distributed to readers after publication. Parameters: source title and edition, pagination scheme, list of corrections (page, line, original text, corrected text), physical format (single sheet, folded insert). Persists via publishing practice and the convention of scholarly and literary correction.

A continuum is a conceptual device for representing gradual transitions between states without discrete boundaries. Parameters: (1) ordered elements arranged along a dimension, (2) proximity-based similarity (nearby elements share more properties than distant ones), (3) absence of natural breakpoints. Persistence mechanism: mathematical modeling (real number line, fuzzy sets), linguistic gradation (adjective scales, semantic fields), and scientific measurement (spectra, gradients) embed the concept across disciplines. [formal: continuum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.29]

A garden-hoe is a hand-held cultivating tool consisting of a flat metal blade set perpendicular to a handle, used to break up soil, remove weeds, and shape planting beds. Parameters: blade dimensions (length, width, thickness), blade edge type (sharp for weeding, blunt for leveling), handle length and grip style (T-handle, D-handle), mounting mechanism (bolt-on, welded, riveted). Persists via the craft of horticulture and the manufacturing tradition of hand tools.

A prophecy is a declared prediction of future events, presented not as speculation but as revealed knowledge. Its parameters are: (1) forward-looking content about events not yet happened, (2) a claim of non-empirical derivation — from divine inspiration, ecstatic vision, ritual divination, or authoritative revelation, (3) an imperative to believe or prepare, encoded in sacred or authoritative text. It persists through institutional recitation (liturgy, religious education, textual canon), cultural transmission across generations, and the social function of shaping behavior by pre-emptively framing anticipated futures. Unlike prediction (empirical inference) or forecast (statistical projection), prophecy derives its authority from the perceived source of knowledge, not from methodological rigor. [formal: propositio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A keyboard is a human-made input device consisting of an array of mechanically or electrically operated keys, each labeled with a character, symbol, or function, designed to translate human keystrokes into digital or mechanical signals. Its parameters are: (1) a grid or arranged layout of discrete actuation points (keys), (2) standardized labeling conforming to an encoding scheme (e.g., QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak, Unicode), (3) an output interface mapping keypresses to encoded signals (USB, Bluetooth, PS/2). It persists through manufacturing conventions, software driver ecosystems, and user habit — the layout standard is taught, the interface spec is documented, and the device shape is reinforced by decades of ergonomic iteration. [formal: tabula --- | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP) is a computational paradigm in which a solution is found by satisfying a finite set of constraints over a finite set of variables. A CSP has three parameters: (1) a set of variables, each with a domain of allowable values, (2) a set of constraints specifying allowable combinations of values for subsets of variables, and (3) an assignment that satisfies all constraints simultaneously. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: constraint propagation and backtracking search enforce the constraints across iterations until a valid assignment is found or the search space is exhausted. The concept persists through formal education in computer science and operations research, and through its instantiation in solvers, planning systems, scheduling software, and configuration tools.

[formal: constraint_satisfactio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A fable is a brief narrative construct that conveys a moral lesson through the use of anthropomorphic characters (animals, objects, or forces given human traits) or simplified scenarios. Its parameters are: (1) brevity — a compact narrative structure designed for memorability, (2) moral instruction — an explicit or implicit ethical teaching, (3) personification — non-human entities behaving as human agents, and (4) transferability — a portable form suited to oral transmission and retelling. A fable persists through oral tradition, written transmission, and pedagogical use across generations. [formal: fabula | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Fade is the technique of gradual transition in media and narrative — the controlled blurring or diminishing of an image, sound, or scene until it disappears. Unlike abrupt cuts, a fade operates over a measurable duration, making it a deliberate compositional tool rather than a technical artifact. Parameters: (1) the medium (visual, auditory, or textual), (2) the direction (in-fade introducing / out-fade concluding), (3) the rate of dissipation. Persistence mechanism: taught through film schools, replicated in editing software, and standardized across cinematographic practice as a conventional narrative device.[formal: de-fadere | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.37]

A funeral is a structured ritual practice for the treatment of the dead, involving (1) preparation or disposition of the body, (2) a gathered community, and (3) symbolic acts marking transition. It persists through cultural transmission (teaching and performance across generations), legal regulation (burial laws, health codes), and religious tradition (rites encoded in sacred texts). Parameters that distinguish it: the presence of a corpse or memorial substitute, the ritualized (non-casual) nature of the gathering, and the forward-directed purpose of integrating loss into social continuity. A memorial service without a body counts; a spontaneous vigil without ritual structure does not. [formal: funus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A wrench is a hand tool designed to grip and apply torque to fasteners (nuts, bolts) or other objects. Parameters: a jaw or socket mechanism that engages a workpiece, a handle providing leverage, and a rigid frame transmitting force. Persistence mechanism: physical manufacturing and repair trades preserve the wrench across generations through tool-making workshops, hardware supply chains, and vocational training. [formal: tuba | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A sandal is a type of footwear consisting of a sole held to the foot by straps or a cradle of materials. Parameters: an exposed upper (leaving some or most of the foot uncovered), straps or thongs securing the sole, and an open design permitting ventilation. Persistence mechanism: material craft (leatherwork, weaving, molding) sustained by shoemakers, retail trade, and climate-driven cultural demand for open footwear. [formal: solea | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A toponym is a proper name given to a place — a city, river, mountain, street, or any geographic feature — by human convention rather than natural law. Parameters: (1) it must designate a specific location or spatial extent on or within the earth's surface; (2) it is assigned through communal linguistic practice, not individual whim; (3) it persists via toponymic education — the repeated act of naming, teaching place-names, and embedding them in maps, oral tradition, and written records. A toponym does not name the physical thing itself (the mountain-stuff, the water-flow) but the human-made map-label by which that place is known, referenced, and navigated. [formal: toponymum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Shorts are a garment covering the lower body, extending from the waist to somewhere between the upper thigh and just above the knee. Parameters: (1) cut-off point is above the knee — this is what distinguishes shorts from longer lower-body garments; (2) they are split between the legs (unlike a skirt); (3) they persist through textile manufacturing and fashion convention — the pattern of a two-legged, knee-above cut is reproduced by tailors and manufacturers and taught as a standard clothing type. Shorts are human-made because the specific length and split construction are cultural design choices, not natural necessities; the same body can be covered differently (long pants, a skirt) without functional penalty. [formal: brevia | substrate: matter | horizon: seasons | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A recipe is a structured set of instructions for preparing a dish, product, or outcome. It specifies ingredients, quantities, sequence of operations, and desired results. A recipe persists through written texts, oral transmission, and digital media — it is the repeatable map of human making, distinct from any single act of preparation. [formal: recepta | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A dress is a one-piece garment consisting of a bodice and a skirt extending downward from the waist, worn primarily by women and girls as a single unit of lower-and-upper-body clothing. Parameters: (1) a continuous garment from shoulders or bust to below the knee, (2) no separate top component — the bodice and skirt are unified in one piece, (3) culturally coded feminine in most contemporary Western contexts. Persistence mechanism: fashion industry standards, retail categorization, and cultural dress codes that maintain the dress as a distinct garment category separate from separates. [formal: vestimentum unum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A skirt is a garment worn from the waist downward that leaves the legs separate and uncovered, functioning as lower-body-only clothing without a bodice component. Parameters: (1) covers the body from waist to some length below (mini, midi, or maxi), (2) has no separate upper-body portion — distinguished from dresses by the absence of a connected bodice, (3) fastened at the waist via waistband, drawstring, or elastic. Persistence mechanism: fashion taxonomy maintained by textile industry standards, retail classification, and cultural dress norms that preserve skirt as a distinct category of lower garment.

A human-made annual publication comprising a systematic compilation of factual data, statistics, and reference information organized by subject area for public use. Parameters: (1) periodic publication cycle — typically yearly; (2) multi-subject factual content — astronomical tables, weather patterns, demographic data, calendars, practical advice; (3) organized structure — tabular, alphabetical, or chronological arrangement enabling lookup; (4) general reference purpose — intended for broad public use rather than specialized scholarly inquiry. Persists through successive editions, archival libraries, and digital reproduction across publication cycles. [formal: almanac | substrate: mind | horizon: years | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An atlas is a systematic collection of maps, charts, or other spatial visualizations compiled into a single volume or digital resource. Its parameters are: (1) curated selection of geographic or thematic representations rather than random maps, (2) consistent projection or coordinate system within each section, (3) cross-referencing or index enabling lookup of locations, and (4) organizational structure — typically by region, theme, or scale. An atlas persists through editorial curation, standardization of cartographic conventions, and distribution as a reference resource. Its function is to compress distributed spatial knowledge into an accessible, portable form that enables comparison, navigation, and pattern recognition across locations. The atlas endures through reprinting, digital migration, and the sustained need to represent the world at multiple scales simultaneously.\n\n[formal: atlas | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

sustainability is the practice of maintaining human systems, practices, or resource use at a rate that does not deplete the underlying natural or social capital required for their continuation. Its parameters are: (1) a defined system boundary (ecosystem, supply chain, community), (2) a measurable extraction or consumption rate, (3) a regeneration or replacement rate, and (4) a time horizon over which balance must be maintained. It persists through policy frameworks, corporate reporting standards, and educational curricula that institutionalize the balance calculation. [formal: sustentatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

a tally is a physical or mental record of countable items, events, or obligations, maintained through discrete marks that each represent a single unit. Its parameters are: (1) a counting unit (one mark = one item/event), (2) a marking medium (notches on bone, knots in cord, scratches on paper), (3) a grouping convention (typically groups of five with a diagonal crossing four vertical marks), and (4) a verification mechanism (pairing two matching tallies). It persists through habit, accounting practice, and the cultural transmission of mark-making conventions from ancient knotted cords (quipu) to modern checkmarks. [formal: tallya | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

Capitulation is the formal act of yielding under negotiated terms, where a party voluntarily submits to an adversary's authority in exchange for specified conditions (terms of surrender, prisoner treatment, territorial disposition). It persists through diplomatic protocols, military codes of conduct, and the institutional memory of treaties — a construct of statecraft and martial law. [formal: capitulatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

rent-seeking is the economic practice of obtaining wealth by manipulating the social or political environment in which economic activities occur — rather than by creating new wealth. Its parameters are: (1) an attempt to secure elevated prices, exclusive rights, subsidies, or trade restrictions through political influence, (2) no corresponding production of goods or services, and (3) a diversion of resources from productive to extractive activity. It persists through lobbying institutions, regulatory capture mechanisms, and the professionalization of influence work (lobbyists, regulatory consultants). [formal: quaerere redditum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

A preamble is a formal introductory statement to a written document — constitution, treaty, statute, or charter — that states the purpose, guiding principles, and philosophical foundations upon which the operative provisions rest. Its parameters are: (1) it precedes all operative text and carries no independent enforceable obligations, (2) it functions as an interpretive key for understanding ambiguous provisions, (3) it articulates the collective intent of the authors and signatories, and (4) it may be cited by interpreters to resolve textual uncertainty. It persists through institutional practice, legal tradition, and the formal conventions of document composition. [formal: praefatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Error-correction is the systematic process of detecting, identifying, and remedying faults in data, text, code, or processes. Its parameters are: (1) a detection mechanism capable of flagging deviations from expected state, (2) an identification step that isolates the fault to a specific location or cause, (3) a corrective action that restores the system to its intended state, and (4) a verification step confirming the correction succeeded without introducing new faults. It persists through automated protocols (checksums, retry logic, diff-and-merge workflows), editorial review processes, and quality-assurance frameworks institutionalized within organizations and systems. [formal: correctio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Expertise is recognized, high-level competence acquired through sustained practice and deep study in a particular domain. Its parameters are: (1) domain-specific knowledge far exceeding that of a generalist, (2) practical proficiency demonstrable in real-world application, (3) the capacity to handle edge cases and novel problems within the domain, and (4) social recognition by peers or credentialing bodies. It persists through reputation networks, credentialing systems, mentorship chains, and the institutional memory of professional communities that validate and transmit it. [formal: peritia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Introspection is the deliberate examination of one's own mental states, thoughts, and feelings. Parameters: (1) the subject is the self as object of attention — the mind turned upon itself; (2) the method is structured or unstructured attention directed inward rather than toward external objects; (3) the output is a reportable account of internal experience, whether verbal, written, or tacitly updated. Persistence mechanism: introspection persists through disciplined practice (meditative traditions, philosophical training, clinical psychology) and is transmitted via pedagogical methods that teach subjects to attend to their own mental states. It is a human invention — no animal is taught introspection; it requires language and self-concept to articulate. The map it provides is the concept of self-examination as a reliable method for knowledge of mind, not the mind itself.

A pact is a formal agreement between two or more parties that creates binding mutual obligations. Parameters: (1) at least two parties with agency, (2) explicit terms of mutual commitment, (3) a mechanism of enforcement — whether social sanction, legal authority, or ritual consequence. Persistence mechanism: written documentation, oral ceremony witnessed by community, or ritual act recorded by the parties' shared memory and social structures. A pact is distinguished from informal promises by its explicit terms and enforceable obligations.\n\n[formal: pactum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Intention is the mental map by which agents structure future-directed action around a goal. Parameters: (1) representational content — a model of a desired state of affairs; (2) directional force — the map guides behavior toward its content; (3) hierarchical embedding — intentions nest within broader intentions, forming plans. The concept persists through language (the vocabulary of aims, purposes, and motives), through social coordination (attributing intention to others is fundamental to trust and blame), and through disciplines that refine it — from moral philosophy's treatment of mens rea to cognitive science's models of goal-directed computation. Intention is not the psychological event itself (that is territory); intention as an entry denotes the category humans built to pick out, debate, and teach about forward-looking agency.

[formal: intentio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A docket is a formal register or schedule maintained by a court, tribunal, or administrative body that lists pending matters, assigned cases, and their order of consideration. Parameters: (1) the maintaining authority (court, agency, or organization); (2) the matter identifiers (case numbers, item labels, reference codes); (3) the temporal ordering (sequence, date, priority rank); (4) the current status of each entry (pending, heard, adjourned, disposed). The docket persists through institutional record-keeping — typically encoded in official ledgers, case-management software, or clerical databases — and endures as long as the authority that maintains it remains in operation. It enables the mapped coordination of discrete proceedings across time and actors, and is the mechanism by which institutional memory of case flow becomes operational rather than incidental. [formal: docketum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An encyclopedia is a systematic compilation of factual knowledge, organized by topic or alphabetically, produced by multiple authors under editorial coordination. Parameters: (1) scope spans multiple domains or treats a single domain comprehensively, (2) articles are independently authored but editorially unified, (3) organization follows a fixed schema (thematic or alphabetical), (4) entries are cross-referenced to enable non-linear navigation. Persists through editorial compilation, publication cycles, and archival reproduction — the structure outlives any single edition. The encyclopedia is distinguished from dictionaries (which define words rather than explain subjects), almanacs (which provide data and facts without explanatory depth), and handbooks (which serve a specific trade or discipline rather than universal knowledge). [formal: encyclopaedia | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A rationale is the structured chain of reasoning that connects premises to a conclusion in support of a decision, belief, or action. Its parameters are: (1) a sequence of logical or practical steps linking evidence or values to a claim, (2) an orientation toward justification or explanation rather than mere description, and (3) an artifact form — written, spoken, or encoded — that makes the reasoning accessible for evaluation, revision, or transmission. It persists through language, documentation, and the institutional practices of reasoning together.

[formal: rationale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.48]

Terminology is a domain-specific system of terms, each assigned a precise meaning within a particular field of practice. Its parameters are: (1) a bounded subject domain that determines which terms belong, (2) a glossary of terms with stipulated definitions that override ordinary usage, and (3) a governance mechanism — usually a standards body, professional association, or disciplinary convention — that updates and enforces the vocabulary. Terminology persists through teaching, publication, and institutional adoption; it is the mechanism by which a field achieves unambiguous intra-disciplinary communication. Without terminology, expert discourse dissolves into the ambiguity of everyday language. [formal: terminologia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Orthography is a standardized system of written conventions for representing a language in text. Its parameters are: (1) a grapheme inventory — the set of allowable characters or letter combinations, (2) rules for mapping spoken units (phonemes) to written units (graphemes), (3) conventions for spacing, hyphenation, capitalization, and punctuation, and (4) an authority or convention — a dictionary, academy, or widespread practice — that stabilizes the system against drift. Orthography persists through education, publishing, and digital encoding; it is what allows a language to be written consistently across time and space. Without orthography, writing collapses into idiosyncratic spelling with no shared standard. [formal: orthographia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

body: Justification is a structured defense of a claim, action, or belief — offering grounds that an audience accepts as sufficient to make the target credible, permissible, or rational. Parameters: (1) the claim or act under scrutiny, (2) the grounds or evidence marshaled in its support, (3) the audience whose standard of acceptance matters, and (4) the burden of proof allocated to each party. The persistence mechanism is language and argumentation practice: justifications exist in discourse, institutional review, legal briefs, and everyday exchange, instantiated each time someone gives a reason that another party weighs and accepts or rejects. [formal: iustificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A summa is a comprehensive systematic treatise that gathers and orders all available knowledge on a subject into a single authoritative work. It operates through structured division (distinctiones) and exhaustive enumeration (quaestiones), persisting through written manuscripts and printed editions. A summa requires authorial organization of material into categories, arguments, and resolutions.

[formal: summa | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

A catalogue is a systematic, organized listing of items produced by human curation, defined by three parameters: (1) enumerated items drawn from a defined domain, (2) an ordering principle (alphabetical, categorical, chronological, or subject-based), and (3) identifying metadata for each item sufficient for retrieval. It persists through written or digital inscription — the catalogue exists as a structured record that can be reproduced, consulted, and updated independently of any single holder's memory. Its purpose is to make a collection accessible and searchable. [formal: catalogus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Liminality is the conceptual category for a transitional or in-between state — a position where an entity, person, or process is no longer in its prior category but not yet settled into its successor state. Parameters: (1) the state occupies the boundary between two well-defined categories; (2) it is characterized by ambiguity, indeterminacy, and the suspension of normal classification; (3) it is temporary by definition — a permanent boundary-state ceases to be liminality and becomes a new category. The concept persists through language (the word 'liminal' and its derivatives), through anthropological and sociological teaching, and through the broader cultural vocabulary of thresholds and passages. It is a map for the human practice of naming transitions. [formal: limen | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An incunable is a printed book, pamphlet, or broadsheet produced in Europe before 1501 CE, during the first fifty years of movable-type printing. It is defined by three parameters: (1) a production date before the 1 January 1501 cutoff, established by the historical convention of the Incunabula Short Title Catalogue; (2) a production method using movable metal type on a screw press; (3) a geographic scope centered on European printing centers (Germany, Italy, France, the Low Countries). The incunable category persists through institutional cataloguing in major research libraries, the ISTC database, and the material survival of printed copies. [formal: incunabulum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.50]

Gestalt is the psychological and philosophical concept that organized wholes are perceived and function differently from the mere sum of their parts. Parameters: (1) the principle of emergent structure — certain configurations of elements produce perceptual or cognitive properties not present in any constituent element alone; (2) the primacy of organization over component analysis — the arrangement and relational structure determine meaning before individual elements are identified; (3) the irreducibility claim — the whole cannot be fully reconstructed or understood by analyzing parts in isolation. Persistence mechanism: institutionalized through Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler 1912–1930), embedded in cognitive science curricula, and operationalized in design theory and practice (visual perception, problem-solving methodologies).

A precedent is a prior judicial decision treated as a normative reference in subsequent cases: the same court or a lower court within the same jurisdiction applies the rule or reasoning from an earlier judgment to a new dispute with sufficiently similar material facts. The map picked out here is the doctrine of stare decisis itself — the convention that like cases be decided alike — not the psychological or sociological mechanisms by which judges internalize or resist prior rulings. Parameters: (1) the originating judgment must be from a court with vertical or horizontal binding authority over the citing court; (2) the ratio decidendi (the binding legal proposition) must be extractable from the facts; (3) the later case must present materially similar facts or a legally analogous issue. The persistence mechanism is institutional: courts cite, distinguish, or overrule prior decisions through published opinions, creating a self-referential chain that accumulates authority over time. Precedent is a map of institutional memory — it does not name the feeling of consistency but the rule-making mechanism itself.[formal: precedentia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

Epistemic bias is the systematic tendency to favor certain sources, methods, or types of evidence while discounting others, independent of their actual reliability. Parameters: (1) the bias operates at the level of knowledge acquisition and evaluation, not the content of what is known; (2) it is structural, built into the frameworks, institutions, and practices by which humans assess what counts as knowledge; (3) it operates below conscious awareness in most instances, making it self-concealing; (4) it persists across communities because it is reinforced by shared epistemic practices. [formal: bias epistemicus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

Mimesis is the human practice of representing, imitating, or enacting reality through symbolic form — art, language, ritual, or simulation. Parameters: (1) the representation need not be literal; it may be abstracted, stylized, or transformed while still functioning as mimesis; (2) the substrate varies by medium: visual, verbal, bodily, digital; (3) the horizon spans from a single performance to millennia of cultural transmission; (4) mimesis is distinguished from mere copying by the presence of interpretive framing — the representation carries meaning beyond its referent. [formal: mimesis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

An etymon is the historically attested source form from which a later word or morpheme is directly derived. Parameters: (1) it is a concrete linguistic form, not an abstract root or proto-form, though it itself may be traceable to deeper ancestors; (2) the derivation follows documented sound change and morphological processes; (3) the etymon exists within a specific language or dialect at a specific time; (4) identification requires empirical attestation, not speculation. [formal: etymon | substrate: language | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

A dossier is a curated collection of documents, records, or information assembled about a specific person, subject, event, or topic. Parameters: (1) the dossier has a defined referent that all contents relate to; (2) contents are selectively gathered and organized rather than randomly accumulated; (3) the collection persists in a retrievable form (physical file, digital archive, or mental compilation). The dossier is the human practice of gathering scattered evidence into a single evidentiary unit — it enables review, analysis, and decision-making by consolidating dispersed information. Persistence mechanism: filing systems, archives, databases, and cognitive organization. [formal: dossier | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

A straw man is a fallacious argumentative tactic in which an opponent's position is distorted, exaggerated, or replaced with a weaker version that is then easily refuted. Parameters: (1) there exists an original claim or position made by a party; (2) that claim is altered into a misrepresentation that is structurally different but superficially similar; (3) the altered version is attacked or refuted in place of the original. The straw man is a weaponized misreading — it exploits the audience's inability to track the original claim precisely. Persistence mechanism: rhetorical practice, logical pedagogy, debate norms. [formal: homo palleans | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

Leverage is the principle of amplifying an input's effect through strategic positioning or mechanical advantage. Its parameters: (1) a small initial input, (2) a medium that multiplies that input (mechanical arm, social connection, capital, information), (3) an amplified output exceeding the input proportionally. Leverage persists through codified practices — engineering manuals, financial instruments, negotiation frameworks, and rhetorical techniques — each a domain-specific instantiation of the same amplification logic. It is not the tool (lever) nor the force itself, but the abstracted rule of multiplicative advantage that humans recognized across domains and generalized into a strategy. [formal: leveragium | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cliché is an expression that was once novel, vivid, or effective but has lost its expressive force through excessive repetition. Parameters: (1) an original phrase or formulation that carried distinctive meaning, (2) repeated use across speakers or texts, (3) degradation of impact — the expression no longer evokes what it once did, (4) recognizability — speakers identify it as trite or overused. The cliché persists as a shared linguistic resource: speakers deploy it because its meaning is transparent and uncontroversial, even as it has surrendered its expressive power. [formal: cliché | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Epistemic-virtue is a human-made normative framework that identifies and prescribes intellectual character traits conducive to obtaining truth and avoiding error. It carves a set of dispositions — open-mindedness, intellectual humility, intellectual courage, intellectual thoroughness, and intellectual honesty — that an epistemic agent ought to cultivate. The framework persists through philosophical pedagogy, epistemological discourse, and the social practices of knowledge evaluation and credentialing. [formal: virtus epistemicus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.52]

Incommensurability is a human-made concept in philosophy of science and decision theory denoting the absence of a shared measure or common standard for comparing two or more values, theories, or frameworks. It carves the condition where no single metric exists that can fairly rank alternatives across domains — for example, utility versus justice, or paradigm A versus paradigm B. The concept persists through philosophical argument, scientific methodology, and institutional decision processes that must handle trade-offs across incommensurable grounds. [formal: incommensurabilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.52]

Prolepsis is the anticipatory framing of future events within present discourse. Parameters: (1) the temporal displacement — placing a later event in an earlier narrative or rhetorical position; (2) the directional pull — the future event casts meaning backward onto the present; (3) the medium — applicable across rhetoric, literature, film, and legal argument. Persistence mechanism: taught as a rhetorical figure, sustained through narrative convention across texts and media. The map is the category of temporal anticipation itself — where speakers and writers place events out of sequence to shape interpretation, and how audiences track the displacement.
[formal: prolepsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Operationalization is the process of translating an abstract concept into measurable, observable criteria. Parameters: (1) conceptual clarity — identifying the dimensions of the abstract construct; (2) indicator selection — choosing observable phenomena that reflect each dimension; (3) measurement protocol — specifying how indicators are recorded, scored, or quantified. Persistence mechanism: encoded in research protocols, standardized tests, industrial metrics, and regulatory frameworks that reproduce the measurement procedure across time and users. The map is the human practice of making the intangible trackable — the bridge between theory and evidence.
[formal: operationalisatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Situatedness is the concept that agents, knowledge, and meaning are always embedded within specific contexts, frameworks, and circumstances. Parameters: (1) the agent or knowledge bearer must be positioned within a context, (2) the context must constrain or enable possibilities of action and understanding, (3) the embedding is constitutive — not accidental but foundational to how the agent operates. Persistence mechanism: transmitted through philosophical discourse, sociological method, and epistemological practice — it is a theoretical framework used to analyze how position shapes perspective. [formal: situatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Vocabulary is the structured inventory of words and terms that a language, register, or discipline employs to represent concepts and enable communication. Its parameters: (1) it is bounded by use — terms enter through coinage or borrowing and exit through obsolescence; (2) it is stratified into core (universal within the language) and specialized (domain-specific) layers; (3) it persists through externalization in writing, dictionaries, and pedagogical transmission across generations. The mechanism of persistence is social practice reinforced by written records and formal education. [formal: vocabularium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A workaround is a human-made strategy for circumventing a limitation, restriction, or system failure without addressing the root cause. It operates as an improvised bypass: a technique that enables continued operation or goal attainment when the intended path is blocked. Parameters: (1) it must circumvent rather than resolve; (2) it must be reproducible, not a one-off accident; (3) it requires knowledge of both the limitation and an alternative route. The mechanism of persistence is transmission through practice, documentation, and oral or written sharing — workarounds spread as solutions to shared problems, persisting as long as the underlying limitation endures and communities of practice exchange them. [formal: circumventio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Personification is the human-made rhetorical and cognitive device that attributes human qualities, emotions, intentions, or actions to non-human entities — animals, objects, natural forces, or abstract concepts. Its parameters are: (1) a target that is non-human in kind; (2) the projection of anthropomorphic traits onto that target; (3) an interpretive function that makes the unfamiliar legible through the familiar. It persists through language, literary convention, rhetorical education, and cultural transmission — each retelling reproducing the pattern. [formal: personificatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Vigilance is the human-made concept of sustained, selective alertness — a practiced state of heightened attention directed toward anticipated changes, threats, or signals within a defined field. It carves a specific mode of awareness distinguished from ordinary wakefulness by (1) its selectivity (focusing on particular categories of stimulus), (2) its duration (maintained over a period rather than a momentary startle), and (3) its anticipatory frame (oriented toward what might happen, not merely what is). The concept persists through institutional practices (guard duty, monitoring protocols), cultural norms (parental vigilance, public safety campaigns), and deliberate training (meditative awareness exercises, professional drills). The boundary of vigilance is drawn against inattention and hypervigilance: it is calibrated watchfulness, not unfocused anxiety. [formal: vigilantia | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

Mindfulness is the human-made concept of intentional, non-judgmental present-moment awareness — a disciplined mode of attention cultivated through deliberate practice rather than arising spontaneously. It carves a specific quality of consciousness characterized by (1) intentionality (the practice is chosen, not passive), (2) present-moment focus (attention anchored to current experience rather than past or future), (3) non-judgmental stance (observation without evaluation, approval, or rejection), and (4) meta-awareness (simultaneous awareness of the act of attending itself). The concept persists through contemplative traditions (Buddhist satipaṭṭhāna, secularized meditation programs), psychological frameworks (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy), and institutional applications (healthcare, education, organizational training). Its boundary is drawn against rumination (past-anchored), worry (future-anchored), and passive absorption (unselfconscious flow): mindfulness is self-consciously held attention. [formal: mindfulia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.13]

Materiality is the conceptual framework humans built to categorize what counts as 'physical' or 'substantial' within a given domain. Parameters: (1) the domain of discourse (art, law, philosophy, commerce) sets the criteria for what qualifies as material; (2) materiality operates as a threshold of significance — something is 'material' when its presence or absence changes the outcome; (3) the map persists through disciplinary teaching, legal precedent, and cultural convention. Materiality is not the stuff of the world — it is the human-constructed filter that decides which stuff matters and by what standard. [formal: materialitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Rationality is the human-constructed practice of guiding belief and action by norms of consistency, evidence, and goal-congruence. It carves the space between unreasoned impulse and formal proof: decisions evaluated by how well they cohere with other beliefs and the agent's stated aims, held together by criteria that can be articulated, contested, and revised. Persistence mechanism: institutionalized in logic, science, law, and education as a teachable discipline with explicit criteria for right reasoning. [formal: rationalitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

Mythos is the human-constructed framework for organizing foundational narratives that give a community its shared sense of origin, purpose, and order. Parameters: (1) mythos operates as a unifying story-structure, not individual tales but the overarching narrative architecture; (2) it is distinguished from logos by its mode of authority — mythos commands through belonging and identity, not through evidential demonstration; (3) the map persists through ritual performance, institutional storytelling, and cultural reproduction. Mythos is not the stories themselves but the conceptual category that groups certain narratives as foundational and binding — a map of how communities make meaning through collective story. [formal: mythos | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

PERCEPTION is the human-made framework for interpreting sensory data as coherent experience. It is not the raw input of sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell — those are biological faculties. Perception is the MAP that organizes, categorizes, and gives meaning to sensory signals through learned patterns, cultural categories, and conceptual schemas. Parameters: (1) sensory modality (vision, audition, tactile, gustatory, olfactory), (2) interpretive framework (cultural, linguistic, individual experience), (3) level of explicitness (automatic pattern-matching vs. deliberate analysis). Persistence mechanism: perception persists through language (shared descriptive vocabularies), teaching (training attention and categorization), and cultural artifacts (art, technology, and media that shape how we look). It is a map built by the mind to navigate the world, not the world itself.[formal: perceptio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

RITUALIZATION is the human-made process of converting ordinary actions or objects into structured, repeatable practices imbued with symbolic meaning. It is not the ritual itself (which is already defined) but the mechanism by which something becomes ritual — the act of ritual-making. Parameters: (1) transmutation (ordinary → sacred/structured), (2) repetition (enforced regularity), (3) symbolic encoding (meaning detached from mere utility). Persistence mechanism: ritualization persists through social reinforcement (group participation, sanction for deviation), narrative framing (stories explaining why the practice matters), and material anchors (objects, spaces, and texts that embody the ritualized form). It is a meta-process — the process of making process meaningful.[formal: ritualizatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A system of social organization and spiritual belief in which groups identify relationships with symbolic entities (animals, plants, objects) as kin or ancestors. The map distinguishes totemic classification from animism: totemism structures social identity (clans, moieties, exogamy rules) through emblematic relations, while animism attributes spirit to entities independently of social structure. Parameters: (1) the totem as emblem rather than deity, (2) the group-level rather than individual nature of the bond, (3) the regulatory function (marriage rules, taboos, resource access) encoded in the totemic relation. Persistence mechanism: oral transmission through ritual, storytelling, and initiation ceremonies that encode the classification system across generations; reinforced by material culture (carvings, body art, regalia) that makes the symbolic order visible. [formal: totemismus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The relationship between texts whereby any text absorbs, transforms, echoes, or answers other texts. The map carves three regimes: (1) explicit citation and allusion — named references a reader can trace; (2) genre convention — structural debts to templates that operate below the level of conscious reference; (3) the unconscious intertext — the reservoir of cultural narratives, formulas, and discourse patterns that shape what can be said without the author's deliberate intent. The concept maps how meaning is distributed across a network of writing rather than located in a single authorial act. Persistence mechanism: reading and writing practices that assume textual priorhood; literary criticism and education that teach readers to recognize and produce intertextual relations; digital linking technology that materializes the concept as hypermedia. [formal: intertextualitas | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Volition is the constructed capacity to form and act upon deliberate intentions — the map of choice that humans built to distinguish self-directed agency from reflex, impulse, and external compulsion. It persists through language (the lexicon of willing, choosing, deciding), through institutions that hold agents responsible (legal culpability, moral accountability), and through practices of self-narration that bind moments of decision into a continuous thread of authorship. Volition is not the feeling of choosing; it is the conceptual framework by which a culture sorts actions into the category of 'the self did this' versus 'this happened to me.' [formal: voluntas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Telemetry is the human practice of collecting measurement data at a distance and transmitting it for analysis — a constructed system that maps physical and operational variables into readable signals. It persists through the instruments that convert phenomena into data (sensors, probes, transducers), through the communication channels that carry them (radio, fiber, satellite), and through the analytical frameworks that interpret the streams. Telemetry is not the measurements themselves; it is the architecture of remote observation, the convention that a variable measured here can be trusted and read there. It turns the world into a dashboard. [formal: telemetria | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Intentionality is the philosophical concept that mental states are about something — that thinking, believing, desiring, and fearing all point toward objects, states of affairs, or possibilities beyond themselves. Humans constructed this concept to solve the problem of how the mind reaches outward into the world. It persists through the language of mental description ('she thought about X,' 'he fears Y'), through philosophical discourse that maps the space of mental aboutness, and through the disciplines (phenomenology, cognitive science, linguistics) that operationalize it as a research category. Intentionality is not the mental state itself; it is the conceptual lens that identifies directedness as a defining feature of consciousness. [formal: intendibilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Phenomenology is the philosophical method of describing structures of consciousness as experienced from the first-person point of view, bracketing assumptions about the external world to examine how objects appear to awareness. Founded by Edmund Husserl in the early 20th century, it operates as a disciplined practice of introspective analysis: the phenomenological reduction (epoch) suspends natural attitude to isolate pure experience. Its parameters are (1) first-person perspective, (2) bracketing of ontological commitments, and (3) systematic description of intentional acts and their correlates. It persists through academic institutions, published methods, and pedagogical transmission across philosophy departments. [formal: phenomenologia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Conceptual blending is a cognitive theory and method for modeling how mental spaces are selectively mapped onto each other to generate emergent meaning in reasoning, language, and creativity. Developed by Gilles Fauconnier and Mark Turner, it defines a four-space architecture (two input spaces, a generic space, and a blended space) where cross-space mapping produces novel structure not present in either source. Its parameters are (1) selective projection from input spaces, (2) emergent meaning in the blend, and (3) dynamic network composition across multiple integrations. It persists through cognitive science research, computational models of creativity, and applied frameworks in linguistics and design. [formal: miscela conceptualis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Problematization is the discursive practice of framing conditions, phenomena, or social arrangements as problems requiring intervention, analysis, or reform. It transforms neutral or positive states into objects of critique by establishing criteria of failure, deviation, or tension. Operated by institutions ranging from policy think tanks to scientific research programs, its parameters are (1) selection of a condition for negative evaluation, (2) articulation of a gap between current and desired states, and (3) mobilization of resources toward resolution. It persists through institutionalized review processes, academic research agendas, and governance frameworks that institutionalize problem-oriented thinking. [formal: problematicatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Omen is the interpretive practice of designating naturally occurring events as signals foretelling future outcomes. Its parameters are: (1) an observable phenomenon treated as a sign, (2) a cultural or personal framework that maps specific phenomena to specific predicted outcomes, and (3) a temporal directionality from the observed sign forward to the foretold event. It persists through transmission — taught within traditions, embedded in ritual practice, and reproduced in language as idiomatic warning or anticipation. [formal: omen | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cathexis is the psychoanalytic concept of emotional or psychic energy invested into an object, person, idea, or symbol. It describes how humans allocate desire, attachment, and affective force onto representations — not the objects themselves, but the mental investment in them. The mechanism of persistence is theoretical discourse (Freudian and post-Freudian psychoanalysis), clinical practice, and cultural theory, where cathexis maps the topology of human attachment and identification. [formal: cathexis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Archival is the practice of selecting, preserving, and providing access to records of enduring value. It operates by applying criteria of significance, acquiring and processing materials through accessioning and arrangement, and maintaining them in controlled conditions to ensure future retrievability. The practice persists through institutional mandates (archives, libraries, government record offices), professional standards of care, and the transmission of custodial norms across generations. An archival collection is organized by provenance and original order, creating context-preserving structures that enable research and accountability long after the records' creation. [formal: archivum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.58]

Reduction is the methodological act of explaining a phenomenon by translating it into the terms of another, supposedly more fundamental, system. It operates by mapping the target's variables, processes, or structures onto a substrate domain (neural reduction of mental states, thermodynamic reduction of heat to kinetic energy, social reduction of institutions to individual behavior) so that the target becomes a special case or derivative of the substrate. The parameters are: (1) a target domain whose phenomena are to be reduced, (2) a substrate domain that provides the explanatory primitives, and (3) a mapping function that preserves causal or structural invariants across the translation. Reduction persists through institutionalized research programs that train practitioners to reformulate problems in substrate terms, and through the pedagogical cycle of teaching that certain explanations are 'deeper' because they operate at a more fundamental level. The persistence mechanism is the reproduction of disciplines that validate reductions as explanatory progress, embedding the method in grant structures, journal standards, and the curricular hierarchy of sciences.\n\n[formal: reductio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Grounding is the relation that anchors an abstract representation — a symbol, model, claim, or computational state — to the portion of reality it purports to be about. It closes the gap between the sign and the world by establishing a traceable connection through perception, measurement, causal interaction, or protocol. The parameters are: (1) a representational vehicle (the thing that carries information or meaning), (2) a referent (the slice of reality the vehicle points at), and (3) a grounding channel that links them — direct sensorimotor coupling, calibrated measurement apparatus, social convention, or causal regularity. Grounding persists through institutions of verification that test whether the representation tracks changes in the referent: scientific instruments that produce correlated readings, peer review protocols that cross-validate claims, market prices that respond to supply shifts, and the everyday practice of checking whether a map matches the terrain. The persistence mechanism is the continuous reproduction of calibration routines — rituals of comparison between representation and referent — embedded in the standards, tools, and training of the practices that depend on the link being real.\n\n[formal: fundatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

A hypernym is a lexical relation in which one term denotes a category and another term denotes a member of that category — the linguistic encoding of the specific-to-general relationship. Formally, Y is a hypernym of X iff the set of things denoted by X is a proper subset of the set denoted by Y, and this inclusion is recognized by the speakers of the language as a taxonomic relationship. The parameters are: (1) the hypernym term (the general category, e.g., 'animal'), (2) the hyponym term (the specific member, e.g., 'dog'), and (3) a speech community that treats the inclusion as a genuine taxonomic rather than merely coincidental classification. Hypernyms persist through the lexical systems that organize vocabulary hierarchically — dictionaries with cross-references, thesauri with 'broader terms' fields, ontological taxonomies in information science, and the natural classification systems of child language acquisition. The persistence mechanism is the reproduction of lexical organization practices: thesaurus compilation, taxonomy construction, vocabulary control in libraries and databases, and the cognitive habit of categorizing by shared attributes — all of which keep the hypernym-hyponym distinction active in how languages structure meaning.\n\n[formal: hyperōnymon | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

Foregrounding is the deliberate technique of making certain elements of a message stand out by breaking expected patterns — in literature, by deviating from linguistic norms; in visual design, by violating compositional expectations. Its parameters are: (1) a baseline pattern or convention that audiences learn to anticipate, (2) a controlled deviation from that pattern at a chosen point, and (3) the resulting attention drawn to the deviant element. The persistence mechanism is teachable craft — transmitted through style guides, rhetoric courses, and aesthetic training — and it operates as a recurring device across media, from poetry and prose to advertising and user interfaces. The concept is the map humans built to describe and deploy the effect of strategic emphasis, not the psychological response itself.

Emergence is the modeled phenomenon in which complex, organized patterns arise from the interactions of simpler components, none of which individually encodes the resulting pattern. Its parameters are: (1) a collection of simple agents or rules with no global blueprint, (2) local interactions among those agents that follow straightforward principles, and (3) macro-level structures or behaviors that are neither explicitly programmed nor predictable from inspection of any single agent. The persistence mechanism is mathematical and computational — formalized in systems theory, complex-adaptive-systems research, and simulation practice — and it persists through peer-reviewed models, agent-based simulations, and the conceptual vocabulary of fields ranging from biology to economics. The concept names the explanatory framework humans constructed to account for order without central design, not the natural processes themselves.

Compression is the engineered practice of representing information using fewer resources than its original form while preserving a defined subset of its content. Its parameters are: (1) an input signal or data stream of a given size, (2) an algorithm or encoding that maps the input to a smaller representation, (3) a fidelity guarantee specifying which aspects of the original are preserved (lossless: perfect reconstruction; lossy: perceptually or functionally adequate), and (4) a decoder or decompressor that reverses the mapping under the fidelity guarantee. The persistence mechanism is implemented in standardized codecs (JPEG, MP3, gzip, H.264…), embedded in every digital device and transmission protocol, and maintained through standards bodies (ISO, ITU, IETF). The concept is the map humans devised to manage scarcity in storage and bandwidth, not the physical reduction of bits itself.

Signal is the engineered construct in communication systems for carrying information across a channel by encoding it into a measurable, transmissible form. Its parameters are: (1) a source that generates a message or data stream, (2) an encoding scheme that maps the message onto a physical or mathematical carrier (voltage, light, radio wave, digital bits), (3) a channel through which the carrier propagates, and (4) a receiver that decodes the carrier back into the message. The persistence mechanism is institutionalized in engineering standards, textbooks, and hardware implementations — the signal concept underpins every telegraph, telephone, radio, television, and data network, maintained through IEEE, ITU, and the broader communications engineering community. The concept is the human-made framework for understanding information transfer, not the physical propagation of energy itself.

The persistence mechanism is implemented in standardized codecs (JPEG, MP3, gzip, H.264…), embedded in every digital device and transmission protocol, and maintained through standards bodies (ISO, ITU, IETF). [formal: compressio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Its parameters are: (1) a source that generates a message or data stream, (2) an encoding scheme that maps the message onto a physical or mathematical carrier (voltage, light, radio wave, digital bits), (3) a channel through which the carrier propagates, and (4) a receiver that decodes the carrier back into the message.
