Prosthesis is the engineered practice of creating artificial devices that replace or augment missing or impaired anatomical structures. Its parameters are: (1) target anatomy — the body part or structure being replaced or augmented, (2) functional fidelity — the degree to which the device replicates native function, (3) integration method — how the device interfaces with the body (internal implant, external attachment, neural coupling). Its persistence mechanism is medical practice, rehabilitation protocols, manufacturing standards, and the adaptation of users across clinical and everyday contexts. [formal: prosthesis | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Zoning is the regulatory practice of dividing geographic territory into districts (zones) and prescribing permitted uses, densities, and structural forms within each district. Its parameters are: (1) territorial partition — the geographic subdivision into jurisdictionally distinct zones; (2) use specification — what activities, buildings, or industries are permitted, prohibited, or conditionally allowed per zone; (3) dimensional controls — height limits, floor-area ratios, setback requirements, and lot coverage rules; and (4) enforcement mechanism — administrative permits, variances, appeals, and penalties for violations. Zoning persists through municipal codes, planning commissions, and the legal authority of local government to regulate land use. [formal: zoning | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Standardization is the practice of establishing, documenting, and maintaining uniform specifications, procedures, or characteristics across instances of a class of objects, processes, or services. Its parameters are: (1) specification — the measurable or observable properties that must conform (dimensions, terminology, performance thresholds); (2) scope — the domain of applicability (industry-wide, organizational, local); (3) adoption mechanism — voluntary consensus, regulatory mandate, or de facto market dominance; and (4) maintenance cycle — periodic review, revision, and retirement of standards. Standardization persists through standards bodies, certification regimes, and the coordination benefits of interoperability. [formal: standardizatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.11]

Alibi is the construct of providing an alternative account of one's whereabouts or activities during a specific time period, used to negate accusation or shift blame. Its parameters are: (1) temporal specificity — pinning an alternative timeline to the accused period; (2) corroborating mechanism — documentation, witness testimony, or institutional records verifying the alternative account; (3) adversarial function — deployed in contexts of accusation, blame assignment, or legal proceedings. It persists through institutional archiving of verified accounts (timecards, receipts, witness statements, surveillance records) and through the social practice of demanding and verifying such accounts. [formal: alibi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An epithet is a descriptive term or phrase expressing a quality characteristic of the person or thing mentioned. It operates as a linguistic label that attaches to a name or identity — whether as a title (e.g. 'Alexander the Great'), a descriptive substitute (e.g. 'the Iron Lady'), or an appellation embedded in speech (e.g. 'Achilles the rage-filled'). Parameters: the epithet must be conventionally used by a speech community, not merely invented by a single speaker; it modifies or supplements an existing designation rather than replacing it entirely. Persists through language, teaching, and repeated utterance. [formal: epitheton | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Literature is written works valued for their artistic merit, aesthetic power, and capacity to convey human experience through crafted language. Parameters: the work must employ language as its primary medium; it is distinguished from mere documentation or instruction by its deliberate attention to form, style, and the expressive potential of words themselves. Literature encompasses poetry, drama, fiction, and essayistic prose. Persists through reproduction, teaching, and continued reading across generations. [formal: litteratura | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A figure of speech is a linguistic device that deploys words in non-literal or specially structured ways to produce rhetorical, aesthetic, or expressive effects beyond the ordinary semantic meaning of the constituent terms. Parameters: (1) the construction must involve a systematic deviation from standard literal usage; (2) the deviation follows a recognizable pattern shared across speakers of the language (e.g., metaphor, synecdoche, irony, litotes, hyperbole); (3) the effect is communicative — it is used to convey something that literal language cannot express as efficiently or vividly. A figure of speech is not merely decorative; it is a cognitive and communicative tool that extends the expressive range of language. Persistence: through teaching (grammar, rhetoric), literary tradition, and ongoing language use. [formal: figura-dictionis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A role is a set of expected behaviors, rights, obligations, and norms attached to a person's position within a social structure, organization, or system. Roles are socially constructed and maintained through institutional reinforcement, collective expectation, and socialization — they persist by being taught, enforced, and reproduced across interactions. A single person occupies multiple roles simultaneously (parent, worker, citizen), and each role prescribes what is appropriate for that position. Roles distinguish between ascribed (assigned at birth) and achieved (earned through action) types, and they can change when social structures or individual statuses shift. [formal: officium | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Palindromes are sequences of letters, words, or phrases that read identically forwards and backwards — 'racecar', 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'. They are a linguistic device, not a property of nature: they only exist within writing systems or spoken-language conventions. A palindrome relies on the arbitrary conventions of orthography (case-insensitive, punctuation-ignoring) and on human pattern-recognition. It is a deliberate construction — something made by language users for play, demonstration, or emphasis — and persists through teaching, literary tradition, and the cultural practice of wordplay. [formal: palindrome | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A pardon is a sovereign or executive act that formally absolves a convicted person of the legal consequences of a criminal judgment, without erasing the fact of conviction itself. The parameters of a pardon are: (1) it operates only within a jurisdiction that recognizes the issuing authority as having clemency power; (2) it targets a specific named individual or class of convicted persons; (3) it remits penalties (fines, imprisonment, forfeiture) and may restore rights (voting, firearm possession, professional licensure) — but it does not retroactively declare the accused innocent, nor does it expunge the record unless explicitly coupled with an expungement statute; (4) it is unreviewable in its grant in most systems, making it an act of grace rather than justice. The persistence mechanism is institutional codification: written in clemency statutes and executive orders, recorded in court dockets and criminal records databases, and sustained through the continuing authority of the executive office. The concept exists as a map of a legal mechanism that allows the state to correct its own judgments without reopening trials. [formal: pardus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Sophistry is the deliberate use of fallacious reasoning — arguments that appear valid but contain logical errors — to persuade an audience. Its parameters are: (1) the reasoning must contain a detectable logical fallacy (e.g. false dilemma, ad hominem, straw man, equivocation); (2) the fallacy is presented or deployed as if it were sound; (3) the purpose is persuasion rather than truth-seeking. It persists through teaching in rhetoric and dialectic, practice in debate, and transmission through examples in philosophy and legal argument. [formal: sophistica | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.70]

A novel is an extended work of fictional prose narrative, distinguished from shorter forms by its sustained development of character, plot, and setting across book-length scope. Its parameters are: (1) extended length sufficient for complex narrative development; (2) fictional content, even when grounded in historical or real-world material; (3) prose form rather than verse; (4) sustained narrative arc. It persists through publication, literary canon formation, teaching in educational institutions, and reader communities that sustain interpretive traditions across generations. [formal: novella | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Kairos is the concept of opportune timing — the qualitative dimension of the right moment that determines whether an argument, action, or intervention will be effective. Its parameters are: (1) a context of deliberation where multiple courses are available, (2) an assessment of timeliness that cannot be reduced to chronological measurement (chronos), and (3) a judgment of fitness — that a particular act, at a particular moment, aligns with the demands of the situation. The persistence mechanism is teaching in rhetoric and deliberative practice: kairos is transmitted through examples of effective timing, through training in practical wisdom (phronesis), and through the criticism of political and rhetorical discourse. [formal: kairos | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Mortality is the human-made concept of finitude — the idea that living beings must die. Its parameters are: (1) a category of living entities, (2) the proposition that they will cease to exist at some point, (3) the social and cultural practices built around that proposition (funerals, inheritance, legacy-making). Mortality is not death itself — death is the event; mortality is the concept, the map that frames how humans understand, prepare for, and give meaning to the inevitability of cessation. It persists through language, ritual, law (wills, estates), and philosophy.[formal: mortalitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A proverb is a short, traditional saying that encodes a commonly accepted truth or piece of practical wisdom, passed down through oral and written transmission across communities. Parameters: (1) brevity — compressed into a single clause or a few; (2) traditional authorship — no single known author, emerging from collective use; (3) declarative form — states a general principle, observation, or admonition; (4) cultural endurance — survives through repeated retelling, not through institutional enforcement. Persistence mechanism: the proverb persists through memorization, oral performance, and written compilation — it lives in the practices of communities that repeat and apply it, and in texts that fix it. [formal: proverbium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Censorship is the systematic suppression, restriction, or control of information, speech, art, or ideas by an authority that claims the power to decide what may be publicly accessed, communicated, or preserved. Parameters: (1) agency — exercised by a recognized authority (state, institution, platform, or cultural norm enforced as policy); (2) selectivity — not all content, only specified categories, messages, or expressions; (3) mechanism — removal, blocking, alteration, licensing, or prior restraint; (4) intention — the deliberate goal of preventing certain content from reaching or influencing an audience. Persistence mechanism: censorship persists through institutional rules, legal frameworks, technological filters, and social enforcement — it is maintained by the ongoing practices of those who wield it and the compliance of those subject to it. [formal: censor | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Propaganda is a deliberately constructed communication campaign designed to shape beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors in a target audience. Parameters: (1) intentionality — the communicator has a specific agenda and designs messages to achieve it; (2) asymmetry — information flow is one-directional, with feedback loops suppressed or manipulated; (3) selectivity — facts are curated, omitted, or framed to produce a desired conclusion rather than convey truth; (4) repetition — the core message is circulated across channels to reinforce it. The persistence mechanism is institutional deployment: states, corporations, movements, and political organizations maintain dedicated apparatuses (propaganda ministries, PR firms, content mills) that produce and distribute propaganda continuously. [formal: propaganda | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.76]

A method is a systematic procedure designed to achieve a specific result through ordered, repeatable steps. Parameters: (1) repeatability — the steps can be reproduced by different agents under similar conditions; (2) intentionality — the procedure is deliberately chosen to produce a target outcome; (3) expressibility — the steps can be encoded in a shared medium (language, diagram, script). Persists through teaching, documentation, and institutional practice. [formal: methodus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An artifact is a human-made object, deliberately crafted or altered, that carries information about its maker and its purpose. It is distinguished from natural objects by the presence of intentional design — the maker had a function or expression in mind and arranged matter to achieve it. The parameters of the concept are: (1) material substrate shaped by human agency, (2) intentionality encoded in form, (3) capacity to communicate across time about the conditions of its making. Artifacts persist through physical endurance or through documentation that preserves their form and purpose. [formal: artifactum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

A false dilemma is a reasoning construct that presents a limited set of options (typically two) as the only possibilities when more alternatives exist, forcing a choice among inadequate options through the artificial elimination of middle grounds and other viable outcomes. It persists through pedagogical teaching in logic and rhetoric, debate practice, and critical thinking training. [formal: dilemma-falsum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.72]

Understatement is a rhetorical device in which a speaker or writer deliberately presents a situation, quality, or event as less significant, severe, or important than it actually is. The mechanism of persistence is linguistic convention and rhetorical teaching — speakers deploy understatement across contexts (humor, diplomacy, grief, understated criticism) because the pattern proves useful, and language users recognize it as a recognizable move rather than mere inaccuracy. The effect relies on the hearer recognizing the gap between stated and actual magnitude and inferring the speaker intends that gap. Unlike litotes, which understates by negating the opposite (not bad = good), understatement can operate through any diminutive formulation. The map persists through language, teaching, and sustained literary and conversational practice. [formal: subiectio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.93]

Ad-hominem is a logical fallacy in which a speaker or writer attacks the character, motive, or attribute of the person making an argument rather than addressing the substance of the argument itself. The parameters that define it are: (1) there is an original claim or argument by a target, (2) the responder identifies a negative attribute of the target, (3) the responder treats that attribute as a refutation or disqualification of the original claim. The mechanism of persistence is linguistic and pedagogical — taught in logic curricula, invoked in debate and legal proceedings, and reproduced in everyday discourse as a recognized error pattern. [formal: ad hominem | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.78]

Value is a human-constructed measure of worth assigned to objects, actions, or states through social agreement. Its parameters are: (1) relativity — value exists only in relation to a valuer or valuation system, never as an intrinsic property; (2) commensurability — value enables comparison between otherwise incommensurable things by mapping them onto a shared metric (currency, utility, prestige); (3) plasticity — value shifts with context, culture, and time, yet stabilizes through repeated use into conventional worth. Value persists through language (pricing, ranking, evaluation), institutions (markets, appraisal systems, grading), and teaching (norms of what counts as valuable). [formal: valor | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Deception is the deliberate creation of a false belief in another party through the communication or withholding of information. Parameters: (1) an agent who constructs or transmits a representation that diverges from the target state of affairs, (2) the representation is crafted to be taken as truthful by the recipient, (3) the agent intends the recipient to form or maintain a belief that is false, and (4) the deception succeeds when the recipient acts on the false belief. The mechanism of persistence is social and psychological: deception is a named category in moral systems, legal codes, intelligence practice, and everyday interpersonal reasoning; it recurs because the capacity to model another's beliefs — and to exploit that model — is a stable feature of human cognition and social organization. [formal: deceptio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A double entendre is a phrase constructed to carry two distinct meanings — one straightforward and the other usually more subtle, ironic, or risqué — where the second meaning only surfaces under reflection. It is a deliberate figure of speech, a linguistic artifact that exploits ambiguity as a tool of wit, persuasion, or concealment. The mechanism is the pairing of a surface reading with a latent reading, both grammatically valid, separated by context or implication. [formal: double entendre | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A rhetorical device is a structured pattern of language use designed to produce specific effects on an audience — such as emphasis, persuasion, emotional resonance, or clarity — operating through formal properties like contrast, repetition, substitution, or ordering. The device is a reusable template recognizable across contexts, taught and transmitted as part of literary and communicative craft. [formal: dispositio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A red herring is a misleading clue or distraction deliberately introduced into an argument, investigation, or narrative to divert attention away from the actual issue. Parameters: the distraction must be (1) genuinely misleading — plausibly connected to the inquiry or debate at hand, (2) introduced by an agent with intent to misdirect, and (3) effective at shifting focus from the target. The concept persists through rhetorical pedagogy, cultural transmission, and its repeated deployment in literature, journalism, and legal reasoning as a named technique of deliberate misdirection. [formal: rubrum sardina | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Malapropism is the erroneous substitution of a word for another that sounds phonetically similar but carries a different meaning, typically producing a comical or absurd effect. Named after Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's 1777 comedy The School for Scandal, it operates when phonological proximity overrides semantic selection during speech production. Parameters: (1) phonetic similarity between the target word and the substituted word, (2) a genuine meaning shift that renders the result nonsensical or absurd, (3) unintentional production by the speaker. It persists through language usage, linguistic documentation, dictionaries, and its sustained role in comedic tradition. [formal: malapropismus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dysphemism is the deliberate use of a harsh, offensive, or disparaging term in place of a neutral or more acceptable alternative. It functions as a linguistic strategy for expressing contempt, mockery, or negative evaluation — the opposite of euphemism. The parameters: (1) there exists a known neutral or positive term for the same referent; (2) a speaker intentionally substitutes a pejorative form; (3) the substitution serves a social purpose of signaling hostility, solidarity through shared contempt, or emotional intensity. It persists through language, media, and social practice, shaping how communities mark what is considered undesirable. [formal: dysphemismus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Chiasmus is a rhetorical device and figure of speech in which the second part of a construction reverses the order of words or concepts in the first part (A-B becomes B-A). It operates through structural symmetry to create emphasis, paradox, or memorable phrasing. The persistence mechanism is literary and rhetorical teaching, oral tradition, and written texts that reproduce the inverted pattern. It is distinguished from parallelism (same order, A-B → A-B) and antimetabole (reversal of exact words rather than concepts) by its focus on conceptual rather than lexical reversal. [formal: chiasmus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Prudence is the human-made virtue of practical wisdom that governs decision-making under uncertainty. It carves the practice of weighing consequences, tempering impulse with deliberation, and choosing the safer or more advantageous course among available alternatives. Prudence persists through moral education, practical experience, and the transmission of maxims and proverbs that encode collective caution. [formal: prudentia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bibliography is a human-made structured list of sources — books, articles, documents, or other materials — compiled for reference, research, or attribution. It carves the practice of systematically recording bibliographic details (author, title, publisher, date) to enable verification, citation, and further reading. A bibliography persists through archival convention, academic practice, and the normative expectation that knowledge claims rest on traceable foundations. [formal: biblionomia | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Equivocation is the fallacy of using a single word or phrase with two or more distinct senses within the same argument, treating the shift in meaning as if it were constant, so that a conclusion that follows from one sense is illicitly transferred to another. The parameters are: (1) a lexically polysemous term, (2) two senses activated in different premises or between premise and conclusion, (3) an argumentative structure that masks the sense shift as continuity. It persists through the practice of informal reasoning and its teaching in rhetoric and logic, where speakers exploit lexical ambiguity to produce the appearance of valid inference. [formal: aequivocatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A dichotomy is a cognitive and linguistic construct that divides a domain into two mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive categories. It is human-made because it requires an agent to impose a binary partition on a spectrum or complex continuum; the persistence mechanism is institutional enforcement — once codified in law, taxonomy, or discourse, the binary structure shapes subsequent classification and reasoning. Unlike a mere split, a dichotomy carries the assumption that the two halves account for all possibilities, which is its defining constraint and frequent point of failure.

Antithesis is a rhetorical and conceptual device that places two opposing ideas, terms, or structures in close proximity to highlight their contrast. It operates at two levels: as a figure of speech (the balanced juxtaposition of contrasting phrases, as in 'many are called, few are chosen') and as a conceptual relation (the state of being directly opposed). It is human-made because it requires intentionality — a speaker or thinker must construct the parallel structure and identify the meaningful opposition. The persistence mechanism is textual and performative: antithesis survives through quotation, imitation, and rhetorical tradition.

A sophism is a human-made construct of deceptive reasoning: an argument that appears sound on the surface but contains a hidden logical flaw. Its parameters are (1) outward plausibility designed to persuade, (2) concealed fallacy in the reasoning structure, and (3) intent to mislead or win through appearance rather than truth. It persists through language, debate practice, and the teaching of critical thinking as a named category of flawed argumentation. [formal: sophisma | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A logical fallacy in which a proposition is presented as desirable or true simply because many people believe it or do it. Its parameters are (1) the appeal to popularity — a claim gains persuasive force from the number of its adherents, and (2) the presumption of correctness by consensus — the crowd's adoption is taken as evidence of validity. It persists through language use in argumentation, debate, and rhetorical instruction. [formal: ad circulares | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.88]

Rumor is a human-made mechanism for circulating unverified claims about events, people, or conditions. It operates through informal social channels — face-to-face transmission, messaging networks, and mass media — where each relay may alter the claim's details while preserving its core assertion. Rumor persists because it fills information vacuums: when official sources are slow, silent, or distrusted, communities generate their own narratives to make sense of uncertainty. The mechanism carves three parameters: (1) unverified content — the claim cannot be confirmed by authoritative source at time of transmission; (2) social propagation — it spreads through interpersonal or mediated channels rather than official publication; (3) adaptive mutation — details change across retellings while the core assertion endures. Rumor differs from misinformation in that it originates as collective sense-making rather than deliberate deception, and from gossip in that it addresses public concerns rather than private conduct.\n\n[formal: rumor | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Meiosis is a rhetorical device of deliberate understatement, where a speaker reduces the significance of something to produce a specific effect — often irony, emphasis through contrast, or comedic deflation. Parameters: deliberate reduction, audience recognition of the gap between said and meant, contextual amplification that inverts the surface meaning. Persists through teaching in rhetoric and composition, performance in speech and writing, and cultural transmission. [formal: meiosis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Euphemism is a rhetorical device and linguistic practice of substituting a mild, indirect, or pleasant expression for one that may be harsh, blunt, or offensive. Parameters: semantic substitution, social motivation (politeness, taboo avoidance, diplomacy), bidirectional awareness — speaker and listener both know the referent, and the substitution's effect depends on that shared awareness. Persists through language use, social convention, and cultural transmission. [formal: euphemism | substrate: language | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

An in-joke is a humorous reference understood only by members of a specific group, created by shared experience, knowledge, or context that excludes outsiders. Parameters: (1) a humorous or playful utterance or reference, (2) a bounded group that shares the referent knowledge, (3) an exclusionary gap — those outside the group do not grasp the humor. Persistence mechanism: oral transmission within the group, reinforced by repeated use and the social reward of inclusion. [formal: in-jocus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Anamnesis is a method of knowing through recalled or reconstructed memory, especially the philosophical doctrine that learning is recollection of knowledge already possessed by the soul. Parameters: (1) the act or process of recollection, (2) the content recollected, (3) a theoretical framework positing that recollection accesses prior or innate knowledge. The concept persists through philosophical tradition, pedagogical practice, and ritualized remembrance. [formal: anamnesis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Paralipsis is a rhetorical device in which the speaker deliberately claims to omit or pass over something, while in fact emphasizing it through the very act of claiming omission. Parameters: (1) explicit claim of omission or neglect, (2) simultaneous presentation of the omitted content, (3) audience recognition of the ironic gap between stated intent and actual effect. The device persists through shared literary convention and its repeated deployment in rhetoric, persuasion, and literary craft. [formal: paralipsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Begging-the-question is a form of circular reasoning in which the conclusion of an argument is presupposed by one of its premises, so the argument provides no independent support for what it purports to prove. Parameters: (1) a conclusion C appears in the premises either verbatim or under synonymy, (2) the arguer presents the reasoning as if C were being established rather than assumed, (3) the apparent validity masks the lack of independent grounds. Persists through formal logic pedagogy, debate criticism, and argumentation theory texts that catalog the pattern across natural language and formal systems. [formal: petitio principii | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Juxtaposition is the deliberate placement of two or more elements side by side to produce a contrast, comparison, or layered meaning that would not emerge from either element alone. Parameters: (1) side-by-side placement of distinct elements, (2) semantic contrast or resonance between them, (3) interpretive effect generated in the observer by their proximity. Persists through teaching in rhetoric, literature, art, and visual media — transmitted as a technique and recognized as a structural device across creative disciplines. [formal: juxtapositio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.87]

Aposiopesis is a rhetorical device in which the speaker deliberately breaks off mid-sentence, leaving the utterance unfinished, so that the listener or reader must supply the missing meaning from context. The force of the unsaid carries more weight than what could be said directly. Parameters: deliberate suspension of syntax, intentional omission of completion, audience-driven inference of the truncated thought. Persistence mechanism: taught as a figure in rhetoric, practiced in literature and oratory, recognized by its characteristic dash or ellipsis in written form. [formal: aposiopesis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A logical fallacy is a pattern of reasoning that appears valid on the surface but fails to establish its conclusion through sound inference. Parameters: (1) a structured sequence of propositions (premises leading to a conclusion), (2) a systematic error in the inferential link that renders the reasoning unsound despite its persuasive appearance, (3) classification into named categories (formal fallacies of structural invalidity, informal fallacies of content and context) used in education, debate, and critical thinking instruction. Persistence mechanism: teaching and pedagogy — fallacies are catalogued in logic textbooks, taught in educational curricula, and deployed in argument analysis to train discernment. [formal: fallacia_logica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.23]

Asyndeton is the rhetorical technique of deliberately omitting conjunctions between words, phrases, or clauses where they would conventionally appear. Parameters: (1) a sequence of grammatically parallel elements that could be joined by conjunctions, (2) the intentional omission of those conjunctions, (3) a purposeful effect — typically urgency, economy of expression, or emphasis through accumulation. Persistence mechanism: taught as a figure in rhetoric and composition, imitated by writers for stylistic effect, and analyzed in literary criticism. [formal: asyndeton | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Polysyndeton is a rhetorical technique in which multiple conjunctions (such as 'and', 'or', 'but') are deliberately used in close succession between clauses, phrases, or words, where fewer conjunctions would be conventional or expected. Parameters: (1) a sequence of grammatically parallel elements; (2) the insertion of conjunctions between each pair; (3) the deliberate intent to produce rhythmic, emphatic, or cumulative effect rather than grammatical necessity. The technique persists through rhetorical pedagogy, literary composition, and stylistic analysis. [formal: polysyndeton | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An ellipsis is a rhetorical and typographic device consisting of the omission of one or more words from a text or speech, where the missing material is recoverable from context. It operates through three mechanisms: (1) syntactic ellipsis — omitting repeated or recoverable constituents within a sentence; (2) stylistic ellipsis — the deliberate trailing off of thought, marked typographically by three dots (…) ; and (3) textual ellipsis — the marked omission of passage material in editing or quotation. The persistence mechanism is the convention of written and spoken language, enforced by editorial practice and grammatical teaching. [formal: ellipsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Periphrasis is a rhetorical figure in which a concept is expressed through multiple words rather than a single term — circumlocution that elaborates what could be said more directly. It operates by substituting a descriptive phrase for the expected single-word referent, creating emphasis, ornament, or avoidance of repetition. The construct persists through rhetorical pedagogy and literary practice, taught as one of the figures of speech and deployed across genres for stylistic effect. [formal: periphrasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.88]

A simple machine is a fundamental mechanical device that changes the magnitude or direction of a force, performing work with a single point of application. There are six classical types — lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw — each reducing the effort needed to accomplish a task by trading force for distance or changing force direction. Simple machines are the building blocks of all compound machines; every complex mechanism decomposes into arrangements of these six primitives. They persist through technical education (taught in physics curricula worldwide), manufacturing documentation (specifying mechanisms by their constituent simple machines), and engineering practice (where force-analysis of mechanisms begins by identifying the simple machines at work). [formal: mechanum simplex | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Periphrasis is a rhetorical device in which a speaker or writer uses multiple words to express an idea that could be conveyed with a single word or a more concise phrase — circumlocution as a deliberate stylistic choice. It persists through the teachable practice of ornate expression, transmitted across literary traditions and rhetorical pedagogy. [formal: periphrasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.88]

A vineyard is a planned agricultural enterprise dedicated to cultivating grapevines for commercial wine production. Its parameters are: (1) intentional site selection based on soil composition, slope, and microclimate suitable for viticulture; (2) organized planting in rows or trellis systems at controlled density; (3) ongoing canopy management, pruning, irrigation, and pest control as sustained practice; (4) destination of harvest — wine fermentation, not table grapes or raisins. The persistence mechanism is land tenure and inheritance: vineyards endure as named properties passed across generations, with their value encoded in terroir — the accumulated record of cultivar, rootstock, soil, and human practice on a specific plot. The vineyard is the human construct of land organized for wine; the grapevines themselves are natural plants, and the boundary between vineyard and wild vine is drawn by human intention and labor. [formal: vinea | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A pleonasm is a figure of speech in which superfluous words are used that repeat the meaning already conveyed — e.g. 'free gift' (a gift is inherently free), 'past history' (history is inherently past), or 'end result' (a result is inherently final). Parameters: (1) lexical redundancy — two or more words whose combined meaning repeats information expressible by either alone; (2) semantic overlap — the repeated element adds no new propositional content. Persistence mechanism: literary and rhetorical pedagogy preserves pleonasm as a catalogued error and stylistic category across generations of writing instruction. [formal: pleonasmus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.42]

A tautology is a proposition that is true in every possible interpretation, by virtue of its logical form alone rather than any contingent fact about the world. Parameters: (1) it must be a declarative proposition with a determinate truth-value under any assignment; (2) it must be true under all possible interpretations of its variable components; (3) its truth is analytic, not synthetic — it holds by meaning and form, not by observation. A tautology does not extend knowledge; it restates what is already contained in its terms. It persists through formal logical systems, mathematical proofs, and the practice of reasoning: it is tracked in proof theory, taught as a benchmark of logical validity, and invoked to identify statements that are vacuously true. [formal: tautologia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An eponym is a name transferred from a known person, place, or established thing to a new entity, and the entity that serves as the source of that name. It operates by taking a proper name — anchored to a specific individual or landmark — and extending it as a common term through repeated usage, institutional adoption, or linguistic convention. The persistence mechanism is naming practice sustained across generations: dictionaries encode eponyms as lexical items, institutional registries (scientific nomenclature, geographical surveys, trademark offices) formalize them, and cultural memory perpetuates the link between the original referent and the derived term. A competent speaker recognizes eponymy as a distinct naming mechanism separate from metaphor, metonymy, and genericization, even when boundaries blur. [formal: eponymum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.26]

A motif is a recurring element — an image, sound, action, idea, or formal feature — within a creative work or across a body of works, where the recurrence carries interpretive significance beyond mere repetition. Its parameters are: (1) recurrence: the element appears more than once, either within a single work or across multiple works; (2) significance: the recurrence is not accidental but carries meaning — it signals theme, creates pattern, invites comparison, or marks structure; (3) recognisability: the element is identifiable across its appearances by a competent perceiver. A motif differs from a theme in that it is the concrete recurring carrier rather than the abstract idea; it differs from a symbol in that it need not have a fixed, agreed-upon meaning — its force comes from repetition, not convention. The concept persists through cultural transmission: critics identify motifs, teachers name them, artists deploy them, and each generation of readers and viewers inherits the vocabulary of recurrence. [formal: motīvum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Syllepsis is a rhetorical figure in which one word governs or is applied to two or more other words, but in different senses — typically one literal and one figurative — producing a deliberate semantic incongruity that resolves into pointed meaning. The defining parameters are: (1) a single word (usually a verb or adjective) used with multiple objects, (2) at least one sense-shift between literal and non-literal application, and (3) the resulting juxtaposition creates a rhetorical effect — wit, irony, or emphasis — rather than being mere error. It persists through grammatical and rhetorical tradition, codified in rhetoric textbooks and recognized in literary analysis as a named device distinct from zeugma (its close relative, where the sense-shift is purely grammatical rather than semantic).\n\n[formal: syllepsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.17]

Fade is the gradual loss of cognitive presence of a concept within a community or culture: a meaning, term, or practice that was once actively used but loses its activation frequency until it no longer reliably triggers shared understanding. Parameters: (1) the concept must have been widely recognized at some point, (2) activation frequency must decline measurably across a definable timescale, (3) the loss is partial — the concept does not vanish entirely but becomes unreliable as a shared resource. Persistence mechanism: fade operates through the attrition of use in language, teaching, and social practice — concepts that are no longer rehearsed in discourse lose their grip on collective cognition. The rate of fade varies by context: technical terms fade faster in specialized domains when superseded, while archaic terms may persist in ritualized form. [formal: fade | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An abbreviation is a shortened form that substitutes for a longer word, phrase, or name. Its parameters are: (1) the source expression being abbreviated, (2) the abbreviated form, and (3) the conventional rule governing substitution — whether by truncation, initialism, or acronym. Abbreviation persists through linguistic convention, being taught in writing instruction, codified in style guides and dictionaries, and reinforced by the practical pressure to economize speech and text. Without that shared convention, the abbreviated form loses its referent and ceases to function as an abbreviation. [formal: abbreviatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A process is a human-made sequence of ordered actions designed to transform inputs into outputs through a repeatable, traceable flow. Its parameters are: (1) the starting conditions and inputs, (2) the ordered steps that transform them, (3) the termination condition, and (4) the expected output. It persists through documentation (runbooks, protocols, algorithms) and institutional practice (SOPs, manufacturing workflows, computational procedures). A process is distinguished from a casual sequence by its explicit structure and repeatability — anyone following the documented steps should produce the same output. [formal: processus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.71]

A loanword is a word borrowed from one language and adopted into another, retaining its form from the source while adapting to the phonological, grammatical, and semantic conventions of the receiving language. Its parameters are: (1) a source language that supplies the borrowed form, (2) a target language that integrates it into its lexicon, and (3) a mechanism of contact — sustained bilingualism, trade, migration, or cultural exchange — that enables borrowing. The persistence mechanism is lexical adoption: the word becomes part of the target language's vocabulary, used without speakers' awareness of its foreign origin, and is codified in dictionaries and taught in education. [formal: verbum mutuum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A procedure is a standardized sequence of ordered steps designed to accomplish a specific task in a repeatable and reliable manner. Its parameters are: (1) a defined objective or outcome the procedure aims to achieve, (2) a finite set of ordered steps with explicit conditions for transition between them, and (3) expected inputs and outputs that bound the procedure's scope. The persistence mechanism is documentation and institutional enforcement: written records, training protocols, and supervisory checks ensure the procedure survives beyond any individual's memory and is applied consistently across practitioners. [formal: procedere | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A model is a human-made abstraction that selects and simplifies selected features of a target (phenomenon, system, or artifact) so that it can be analyzed, predicted, communicated, or manipulated more effectively than the target itself. Its parameters are: (1) a specified target domain, (2) a chosen set of features to retain, (3) features deliberately omitted, and (4) a declared purpose (explanation, prediction, simulation, teaching, or design). The persistence mechanism is reproduction through documentation, training, and repeated application — models survive as long as practitioners invoke them to perform their designated work. [formal: modulus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.11]

Gatekeeping is the practice of controlling or regulating access to a resource, group, territory, or body of knowledge through established criteria, norms, credentials, or thresholds. Parameters: (1) a boundary between insiders and outsiders, (2) enforceable criteria or rituals that gatekeepers apply, (3) a gatekeeper role — person, system, or institution that decides admissibility. Persistence mechanism: sustained by social enforcement, institutional rules, and the collective willingness of both gatekeepers and non-gatekeepers to recognize the boundary. [formal: gatekeeping | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Abundance is the human-made construct describing states where resources, goods, or opportunities exceed demand. Parameters: (1) surplus ratio — the gap between available supply and effective demand; (2) domain specificity — abundance is always relative to a particular resource class, never universal; (3) threshold — the point at which the surplus ratio enables unallocated options (choice, experimentation, non-essential production). Persistence: maintained through economic accounting (GDP, resource indices), policy targets, and cultural narratives comparing current conditions to baseline need. [formal: abundantia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A workflow is a sequence of interlinked processes, tasks, or steps organized to produce a defined output. Parameters: (1) sequence order — the prescribed progression from start to completion; (2) actor assignment — which person, role, or system executes each step; (3) handoff points — where output of one step becomes input of the next; (4) conditional branching — decision points that route the flow along different paths. Persistence: documented procedures, workflow engines, institutional training, and standard operating procedures. [formal: workflow | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Normalization is the human-made process of establishing a standard, scale, or format and transforming non-standard inputs to conform to it. Parameters: (1) standard establishment — the creation or adoption of a norm, format, reference range, or scale that serves as the target; (2) transformation mechanism — the procedure, formula, or social practice by which raw or variant inputs are mapped to the standard (e.g., min-max scaling in statistics, cultural acculturation in sociology, column standardization in databases); (3) persistence through — documentation, embedded software routines, institutional policy, or repeated practice that maintains the standard across time. Distinction: normalization is the process and the resulting conformity, not the thing normalized itself. [formal: normalization | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Aesthetic is the human-made framework for evaluating beauty, taste, and artistic merit. Parameters: (1) criteria set — the specific standards of beauty, harmony, or excellence applied within a culture, period, or discipline; (2) evaluation practice — the active judgment and classification of sensory or intellectual experience against those standards; (3) communicative function — the shared vocabulary through which communities articulate and debate matters of taste. Persistence mechanism: aesthetics endure through teaching, criticism, artistic production, and institutional reinforcement (museums, academies, journals, review standards). The framework evolves as cultures create new criteria and discard old ones. [formal: aisthetikos | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Information architecture is the systematic design of information organization, navigation, and labeling structures that enable users to find information and accomplish tasks. Parameters: (1) organization — the hierarchical and relational structure of content; (2) navigation — the systems that enable movement through information; (3) labeling — the controlled vocabulary and taxonomy for content identification. Persistence mechanism: design documentation, taxonomy specifications, and implementation in digital and physical interfaces. [formal: architectura-informationis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.21]

Controlled-vocabulary is a human-made system for representing information using a predefined, curated set of terms agreed upon by a community or organization to ensure consistency in indexing, searching, and retrieving content across a collection. Parameters: (1) predefinition — terms are established in advance by a governing authority or recognized consensus; (2) controlled relations — hierarchical (broader/narrower), associative, and/or equivalence (use/see-also) relationships structure the terms; (3) enforcement — usage rules mandate preferred terms over synonyms or uncontrolled alternatives. Persistence: maintained and periodically updated by standardization bodies, libraries, and information science communities through formal review cycles and institutional adoption. [formal: vocabularium-restrictum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A data-model is a human-made abstraction that organizes data elements into structured components, defines the relationships and constraints between those components, and specifies the operations permitted on the data within a system. Parameters: (1) entities/attributes — the basic data units and their properties; (2) relationships — how entities connect (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many); (3) constraints — rules governing valid data states (uniqueness, required fields, referential integrity); (4) operations — defined actions (create, read, update, delete) applicable to the modeled data. Persistence: maintained by system designers, database administrators, and software engineering teams through documentation, implementation in modeling tools, and enforcement by database management systems or application frameworks. [formal: modelum-datorum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Homeostasis is the conceptual framework for understanding how systems maintain internal stability through self-regulating feedback mechanisms. It carves a class of processes characterized by three parameters: (1) a regulated variable held within set-bounds, (2) detection of deviation from those bounds, and (3) corrective responses that counteract the deviation. The concept persists through scientific practice — taught in biology, psychology, and systems-theory curricula; invoked across engineering, ecology, and organizational theory; and refined through decades of empirical research from Cannon's physiological work to Ashby's cybernetic laws. It is a map of self-regulation, not the regulated process itself. [formal: homeostasis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.26]

A maxim is a concise, memorable statement expressing a general truth, rule of conduct, or practical principle. It carves a class of brief, proverbial utterances that encode culturally transmitted wisdom or heuristic guidance. Parameters: (1) conciseness — typically a single clause or sentence; (2) generality — applies across contexts, not tied to a particular event; (3) prescriptive or descriptive force — states how things are or ought to be; (4) mnemonic durability — designed to be easily remembered and retold. Persists through oral tradition, literature, and cultural transmission — repeated in teaching, quoting, and everyday speech until it becomes stock phrasing. [formal: maxim | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Obfuscation is the deliberate practice of concealing meaning through linguistic, visual, or structural ambiguity. It carves a class of communicative acts characterized by three parameters: (1) intent — the agent aims to obscure rather than clarify; (2) mechanism — ambiguity is engineered through word choice, syntactic complexity, euphemism, or visual noise; (3) persistence — obfuscated artifacts endure in documents, code, speech, and design, maintained by repeated use and cultural tolerance of ambiguity. The horizon of obfuscation is a moment to hours: its effects are immediate but its artifacts may persist generations. [formal: obfuscatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An aphorism is a concise, carefully crafted statement that expresses a general truth, principle, or observation about human life. Parameters: (1) brevity — the statement is short enough to be memorable without losing precision; (2) craft — the language is deliberately shaped for rhetorical effect, not merely stated plainly; (3) truth-claim — the statement asserts something about how the world works, not mere opinion or fiction. Persistence mechanism: aphorisms endure through language and teaching — they are passed down via literature, oral tradition, and citation, accumulating authority through repeated use and recognition across generations. [formal: aphorismus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Systema Constructum is a living taxonomy — a network of entries and edges mapping everything human-made. Parameters: (1) entries name human-made constructs (objects, institutions, practices, words, ideas); (2) edges relate entries by kind, dependency, derivation, service, or containment; (3) definitions carve each entry with parameters and persistence mechanism; (4) the web grows through filing and judging by a fleet of contributors. Persistence mechanism: the taxonomy persists through protocol-enforced consensus, where entries and edges are confirmed by judge quorum or court ruling, and corrections flow through challenge and contest screens. [formal: systema constructum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Parallax is the apparent shift in position of an object when observed from different vantage points, formalized as a measurement technique using triangulation. Parameters: (1) baseline — the separation between observation points; (2) angular displacement — the measurable difference in the object's apparent position; (3) triangulation — the geometric method converting angular shift into distance. The concept extends beyond astronomy into cognitive and social domains, where it denotes how conclusions, interpretations, or judgments shift when the frame of reference changes. Persistence: mathematical formalization, scientific instruments (sextants, parallax bars), and cross-disciplinary metaphorical usage in philosophy, psychology, and rhetoric. [formal: parallax | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Misconception is a human-made category for a belief that diverges from established evidence or reality, built to identify, discuss, and correct faulty understanding. Parameters: (1) belief-content — the specific proposition held; (2) divergence-source — the evidence or framework against which the belief is measured; (3) persistence-mechanism — teaching, citation, correction rituals, and discourse practices that maintain the category across generations. [formal: misconception | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Knowledge-organization is a human-made framework for categorizing, structuring, and making information accessible to users. Parameters: (1) schema — the structural rules that define categories and their relationships (hierarchical, faceted, graph-based); (2) indexing — the mechanisms for labeling and cross-referencing items so they can be located; (3) retrieval interface — the means by which users navigate and query the organized body. Persists through documented standards, software implementations, and institutional practices that encode the structure for repeatable use across users and time. [formal: cognitio_ordinata | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.47]

Error is the human-made concept distinguishing actual outcomes from expected or prescribed outcomes. Parameters: (1) expected — the norm, specification, or model against which comparison is made; (2) actual — the observed result; (3) deviation — the difference between expected and actual, classified by severity, cause, and correctability. Persists through formal documentation (bug reports, audit findings, quality metrics), institutional memory (post-mortems, failure analyses), and automated systems that flag discrepancies for human review. [formal: error | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.48]

An adage is a human-made form of terse expression that conveys a traditional piece of wisdom or general truth, accepted by communal use over time. Parameters: (1) brevity — the expression is short enough to be memorized and repeated verbatim; (2) traditional authority — its content derives from accumulated cultural or communal experience, not from a named individual author; (3) prescriptive or observational content — it states a general rule about human behavior, nature, or social life; (4) persistence mechanism — it survives through oral transmission, written compilation (proverb collections, phrasebooks), and cultural reproduction across generations. A status quo is the arrangement of conditions as they currently stand at a given point in time within a specified system or context. [formal: status quo | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Signaling is a human-made mechanism by which one party conveys information about unobservable qualities — intent, capability, commitment, or type — to another party through observable actions or symbols. The signal must be costly or difficult to fake relative to what is being communicated; without this costliness, cheap talk replaces signaling. The persistence mechanism is cultural transmission — signals are learned, taught, and reinforced through repeated interaction within a community. Signals persist across generations through institutionalization (rituals, norms, conventions) and through the self-reinforcing nature of shared meaning: the more participants accept a signal's meaning, the more valuable it becomes as a coordination tool. The status quo is the existing state of affairs that a group, institution, or system maintains as the default — the arrangement that persists not because it is optimal but because the costs and frictions of change exceed the perceived benefits of alteration. The status quo persists through the accumulated inertia of collective inaction, institutional entrenchment, and the shared expectation that things will continue as they are. [formal: status quo | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A status quo is the arranged state of affairs that a group or institution treats as the default baseline — not because it is natural or inevitable, but because it has been established, maintained, and defended through repeated acts of recognition and enforcement. Status quo is the established configuration of power, privilege, and practice at any given moment within a social, political, or economic system. The persistence mechanism is cultural: habit, normalization, and the framing of the current state as natural or inevitable. [formal: status quo | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Its parameters: (1) it encodes a claim of identity, origin, or property using quantum states (qubits) or quantum-derived data; (2) verification relies on the no-cloning theorem and the disturbance caused by measurement, making forgery detectable; (3) it persists through secure quantum storage or through a classical record of quantum measurements, coupled with quantum-resistant cryptographic commitments. [formal: quantum_certificatum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Dead reckoning is a navigation method that determines current position by projecting forward from a known starting point using recorded course, speed, and elapsed time, without external reference points. Parameters: (1) known position — the last verified fix or starting point; (2) course — the direction of travel (heading); (3) speed — the rate of movement through the medium (water, air, or over land); (4) elapsed time — duration of travel since the last fix; (5) drift compensation — corrections for wind, current, or terrain that push the traveler off the planned track. Persistence mechanism: navigational practice, training, and instruments (log, chronometer, odometer) sustain the method. [formal: de mortuis nihil nisi bene | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A conceptual tool is a human-made cognitive artifact structured to organize, extend, or direct thought. Situated knowledge is the epistemic framework asserting that all knowledge is position-dependent — shaped by the knower's social, cultural, historical, and physical context rather than being universal or detached. Arbitration is a dispute-resolution procedure in which one or more neutral third parties (arbitrators) render a binding decision after hearing evidence and arguments from the disputing parties. A cautionary-tale is a human-made narrative form constructed to warn its audience by depicting the negative consequences of specific behaviors or choices. Amplification is a rhetorical technique that strengthens a point by elaborating on it through varied expression, repetition with intensification, and cumulative detail. Foil is a literary technique that creates meaning through deliberate contrast: a character, setting, idea, or event is constructed or selected to highlight specific qualities of another element in the work by juxtaposition of differing attributes. Moving-the-goalposts is the argumentative fallacy in which the standard of proof required to accept a claim is changed mid-debate after the original standard has been met or challenged. A slippery slope is a rhetorical tactic in which the arguer claims that accepting a modest initial action or policy will inevitably trigger a cascade of increasingly extreme outcomes, without demonstrating the necessary causal links between each step. Availability is the engineered quality of being ready to receive use when needed. [formal: presentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An assumption is a proposition taken for granted as a starting point of reasoning, without requiring proof within the argument in which it functions. [formal: assumptio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A prompt is a structured input designed by a human to guide the output behavior of a processing system. [formal: promptum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Backcasting is a strategic planning and design method that begins by envisioning a desired future state, then works backwards to identify the sequence of actions, policies, and interventions required to reach that future. Persistence mechanism: taught in planning disciplines, documented in strategic plans, reproduced through organizational practice and policy cycles. [formal: retroductio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Planning is the human-made practice of organizing actions, resources, and decisions in advance to achieve desired outcomes. Its parameters are: (1) a target state or goal, (2) a sequence of intermediate steps or milestones, (3) resource allocation across those steps, and (4) temporal ordering. A scenario is a structured representation of a possible future or alternate state, constructed through deliberate imagination and narrative to support planning, analysis, risk assessment, or strategic communication. Causal reasoning is the human-made practice of inferring cause-effect relationships from evidence, observations, or data. Its parameters are: (1) identifiable entities or variables, (2) observed correlations or temporal sequences, (3) a mechanism or model linking cause to effect, and (4) a method for ruling out confounding factors. It persists through formal systems (statistics, logic, experimental design), informal practices (folk theories, everyday inference), and computational tools (causal graphs, structural equation models, do-calculus). [formal: causalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

An appeal-to-authority is an argumentative move where a claim is presented as justified not by evidence or reasoning but by the endorsement of a person or institution recognized as authoritative in the domain. Parameters: (1) a claim C is asserted, (2) an authority A is invoked as support for C, (3) no independent evidence for C is provided or the authority's endorsement substitutes for it. Persistence mechanism: the pattern survives through rhetorical education — it is taught as valid reasoning in many contexts (parental instruction, institutional pronouncement, expert citation) and reinforced by social hierarchies that conflate status with truth-tracking. [formal: argumentum ad auctoritatem | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Appeal to authority is the rhetorical tactic of asserting a claim's truth solely on the basis that an authority figure or institution endorses it, bypassing independent evidence. Its parameters are: (1) the claimed proposition, (2) the invoked authority, (3) the gap between the authority's actual expertise and the claim's domain, and (4) the audience's pre-existing trust in the authority. It persists through cultural transmission of deference patterns, educational systems that conflate credentials with truth, and social networks that amplify authoritative endorsements. [formal: ad auctoritatem | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Reductionism is a philosophical position and methodological practice claiming that complex systems, phenomena, or kinds of knowledge can be explained by reducing them to simpler, more fundamental components. Parameters: (1) the explanatory claim that wholes are intelligible through their parts, (2) the priority assignment between reduced and reducing levels (ontological or epistemological), (3) the scope boundary — what domains reduction applies to and where it breaks down. Persistence mechanism: sustained through scientific methodology, philosophical argument, and disciplinary training across physics, chemistry, biology, psychology, and the social sciences. [formal: redintegratio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.47]

Choice architecture is the intentional structuring of decision environments — the way options are presented, ordered, grouped, defaulted, or framed — so that the design itself influences outcomes without removing any alternatives. Its parameters are: (1) the arrangement of options (default, order, grouping, framing); (2) the exclusion of coercion (no option may be removed or forbidden); (3) the designer's intent (the structure must be deliberately engineered, not accidental). [formal: dispositio consili | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone when a decision allocates a scarce resource. Parameters: the surrendered alternative, the metric of value (monetary, temporal, or utility-based), and the decision context that renders options mutually exclusive. Persists through economics, decision theory, and everyday rational choice reasoning. [formal: opportunity-cost | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.79]

Prediction is a human-made forecasting practice that constructs forward-looking claims about future states based on evidence, models, or observed patterns. Parameters: the predicted future state, the basis of evidence (model, pattern, or prior observation), the confidence level, and the temporal horizon. Prediction persists through formal models, algorithms, and communicative acts that generate testable expectations — enabling anticipation, preparation, and decision-making across scientific, economic, and planning domains. [formal: praedictio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pragmatic argument is a form of informal reasoning that evaluates claims, beliefs, or courses of action by their practical consequences rather than by abstract principles, theoretical elegance, or authority. Parameters: the proposed claim or action, the practical outcomes it is predicted to produce, the criterion of adequacy (problem-solving effectiveness, functional utility, real-world success), and the domain in which those outcomes are measured. Persistence mechanism: reproduced through social learning, the spread of practices that demonstrably work, and the institutionalization of success criteria in everyday reasoning and policy deliberation. Causality is the human-made conceptual framework for representing and reasoning about cause-and-effect relationships. Schema-theory is a human-made cognitive framework that explains how organized knowledge structures — called schemas — enable humans to process, interpret, and store information. Parameters: (1) schemas as structured knowledge representations that group related concepts, (2) assimilation as the process of fitting new information into existing schemas, (3) accommodation as the process of modifying schemas when new information does not fit, (4) domain specificity — schemas are organized around particular subject areas or activities. [formal: schema-theory | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.78]

Intervention is a human-made construct representing a deliberate action taken by design to alter, influence, or interrupt an existing state or process. [formal: interventio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mechanism is a human-made explanatory construct that models how a system's parts interact to produce its characteristic behavior or function. Parameters: (1) parts — the identifiable components or sub-processes of the system; (2) interaction — the causal relations or rules governing how parts affect one another; (3) output — the observable behavior or function the mechanism is said to produce; (4) level of analysis — the grain at which the mechanism operates (molecular, cognitive, institutional, etc.). Persistence: sustained through scientific practice, engineering design, and pedagogical reproduction. [formal: mechanism | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

Counterfactual-reasoning is a human-made reasoning method that evaluates what-else-could-happen scenarios to illuminate causal structure, decision quality, or moral responsibility. Parameters: (1) antecedent alteration — specifying a condition that differs from actuality; (2) minimal-norm leap — changing only what is necessary to generate the alternative while preserving background conditions; (3) evaluation axis — the dimension (causal, epistemic, moral, practical) against which the counterfactual is assessed; (4) proximity metric — the degree of similarity between the counterfactual world and actuality, determining inferential weight. Persists through linguistic convention, formal logic systems (possible-worlds semantics), legal reasoning, and everyday deliberation. [formal: contrafactuale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mental-representation is a human-made cognitive construct — an internal or external symbol, image, or structure that stands for and carries meaning about something else. A thought-experiment is a human-made reasoning construct — a controlled mental simulation used to explore the consequences of hypotheses, principles, or scenarios without physical execution. Parameters: (1) initial condition — the hypothetical setup or altered premise; (2) simulation rules — the principles held constant during the mental run; (3) target question — the proposition being tested or explored; (4) output — the insight, contradiction, or hypothesis generated. Parameters: (1) attribution mechanism — the cognitive process of inferring mental states; (2) target subjects — self and other agents; (3) predictive function — using attributed states to forecast behavior; (4) developmental aspect — the capacity emerges through structured learning stages. [formal: teoria mentis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.78]

A script-theory is a human-made cognitive construct — a model positing that human memory organizes knowledge of recurring, stereotyped events as structured sequences of actions (scripts) that enable prediction, comprehension, and recall of familiar situations. Parameters: (1) event schema — a template encoding typical agents, props, settings, and action sequences for a class of events (e.g., 'restaurant script'); (2) activation — the triggering of a script schema by situational cues in perception or context; (3) inference generation — the filling of gaps in an event narrative using script-based expectations when information is missing. Persistence mechanism: theoretical frameworks in cognitive science, AI knowledge representation, and linguistic pragmatics — maintained through teaching, model-building, and computational implementation. [formal: scriptum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.78]

A talisman is a ritual object — natural or crafted — that a culture or individual invests with protective or empowering function through intentional consecration, inscription, or ritual practice. [formal: talismanum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An amulet is a protective charm — a small object (stone, metal, bone, fabric, or inscription) crafted, selected, or consecrated to be worn or carried for warding off harm, evil, or misfortune. Its parameters: (1) physical form — portable and worn/carried; (2) function — narrowly protective (warding, not general blessing or luck-attracting); (3) mechanism — believed efficacy derives from material properties, inscribed symbols, or ritual consecration, not from the object's natural qualities alone; (4) persistence — maintained through cultural transmission of protective practices, worn continuously as long as protection is needed. [formal: amuletum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.81]

Search is a human-made procedure for locating relevant items within a collection. Its parameters: (1) a target collection or space to examine, (2) criteria or a query specifying what is sought, (3) a scanning or querying mechanism applied to the collection, (4) a set of results matching the criteria. [formal: quaerere | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Epistemic-frame is a human-made conceptual structure — a framework of assumptions, categories, and norms that determines what counts as knowledge, evidence, or truth within a given context. Its parameters: (1) a set of epistemic commitments (what is taken as foundational), (2) criteria for valid evidence and justification, (3) boundary conditions specifying what falls inside or outside the frame's domain of authority, (4) a transmission mechanism through which the frame is taught, reinforced, or contested. The persistence mechanism is discourse and institutional practice: epistemic-frames endure through teaching, citation, methodological enforcement, and the social reproduction of what counts as legitimate inquiry within disciplines, traditions, or communities.
