Logarithm is the human-made mathematical concept that assigns to each positive real number x the exponent to which a chosen base b must be raised to produce x. Its parameters are: (1) a base b > 0, b ≠ 1; (2) an argument x > 0; (3) the unique value y such that b^y = x, written y = log_b(x). It persists through symbolic notation (log_b(x)), published tables, algorithmic computation in calculators and software, and formal mathematical education. The logarithm transforms multiplicative relationships into additive ones, making it indispensable for computation in navigation, astronomy, engineering, and the sciences. [formal: logarithmus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Nomography is the craft of designing nomograms — graphical calculating devices that represent mathematical relationships between variables through graduated scales arranged so that a straightedge, connector, or other alignment reveals the solution. A nomogram maps numerical quantities to positions on geometric scales (parallel, radial, curved, or combined) according to a specific algebraic or functional relationship, allowing users to read results by drawing a line or sliding a bridge. The parameters of a nomogram are the scale equations, their geometric layout, and the alignment rule that connects them; the persistence mechanism is transmission through engineering and technical drawing curricula, professional practice, and published reference tables — a practitioner learns the scale mathematics, constructs the chart, and distributes it for use. [formal: nomographia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cartogram is a thematic map in which geographic units (countries, regions, districts) are resized proportionally to a chosen statistical variable, transforming spatial relationships to encode quantitative data through area distortion rather than geographic fidelity. The construction requires: (1) a base map with defined geographic boundaries, (2) a statistical dataset providing values for each unit, (3) a rescaling algorithm that maps values to areas while preserving adjacency where possible. Cartograms are produced through sustained cartographic practice and published in atlases, reports, and academic literature. [formal: cartogramma | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diagram is a human-made visual representation that uses marks, lines, symbols, and spatial arrangements to convey structural, relational, or procedural information about a subject. Unlike a picture that depicts appearance, a diagram abstracts away visual detail to highlight organization, connections, sequences, or relationships among components. Its parameters are: (1) it is intentionally designed to encode information through visual grammar rather than aesthetic depiction; (2) it relies on conventions — color coding, line styles, geometric shapes, labels, and spatial positioning — that map visual features to conceptual relationships; (3) its meaning is decipherable through shared understanding of those conventions. Diagrams persist through reproduction, standardization of visual grammar, and their role in teaching, engineering, and scientific communication. [formal: diagramma | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.83]

A box plot (also called a box-and-whisker plot) is a human-made statistical diagram that summarizes the distribution of a dataset through five key values: the minimum, the first quartile (Q1), the median (Q2), the third quartile (Q3), and the maximum. It displays these values as a rectangular box spanning Q1 to Q3 (the interquartile range), with a line marking the median, and whiskers extending to show the range of non-outlier data. Individual points beyond the whiskers are plotted as outliers. Its parameters are: (1) it encodes five-number summaries into a standardized visual form invented by statistician John Tukey in 1977; (2) it is designed to reveal skewness, central tendency, spread, and outlier presence in a single compact view; (3) its conventions for outlier detection (typically 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles) are part of its operational definition. Box plots persist through their adoption in statistical software, scientific publishing, and data analysis pedagogy. [formal: box plot | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.84]

An isarithm is a human-made cartographic construct: a continuous line drawn on a map or chart that connects points sharing the same measured value of a quantitative variable (e.g., temperature, atmospheric pressure, elevation, salinity). The parameters that define an isarithm are: (1) a scalar field over a spatial domain, (2) an isoline at a specified interval value, and (3) interpolation between measured sample points where the field is not directly observed. The persistence mechanism is standardization in scientific charting — meteorological services, oceanographic surveys, and topographic agencies publish isarithmic maps at fixed intervals using agreed-upon conventions for line weight, labeling, and color. The parameters: (1) a continuous scalar field over a domain, (2) a chosen set of value intervals, (3) the drawn curve tracing where the field equals each chosen value. It persists as ink on paper, pixels on a screen, and instruction in cartography and geography.

A scatter plot is a graph that displays individual data points on a two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system, where each point's horizontal and vertical position encodes the values of two variables for that observation. The parameters: (1) a paired set of variables, (2) a coordinate system with labeled axes, (3) a mark placed at each variable pair's intersection. It persists as ink on paper, pixels on a display, and a standard fixture of statistical pedagogy.

A parallel coordinates plot is a data visualization technique that represents multivariate data by displaying each variable on its own vertical axis, with all axes arranged horizontally and data points connected by lines across axes to reveal multivariate patterns and correlations. The parameters: (1) each axis represents one variable, (2) data values are mapped proportionally along each axis, (3) lines connect points across axes for each observation. The persistence mechanism: graphical convention codified in statistical graphics literature and implemented in data analysis software. [formal: parallelium | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Persistence is maintained through version-control histories, automated test suites that verify behavioral invariance, and coding conventions that encode the catalog of recognized refactorings. [formal: restructuratio interna | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.99]

The ladder is used in taxonomy, ontology engineering, and knowledge organization to ensure every item can be placed within a broader categorical framework without redundant leaps. Persistence mechanism: encoded in taxonomic databases, ontologies, and classification systems maintained by human institutions. [formal: scala | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Parameters: (1) truth-evaluable content, (2) identity conditions independent of linguistic form, (3) role as subject of propositional attitudes (belief, doubt, assertion). The persistence mechanism is graphic rendering through charting libraries and visualization software, maintained by standard conventions for bubble-size scaling and axis labeling. [formal: bubble-chartum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A treemap is a human-made data visualization technique that represents hierarchical (tree-structured) data as a set of nested rectangles. An ontological category is a human-made classification scheme used to partition reality into fundamental types of entities within an ontology. A venn diagram is a human-made diagram that represents sets and their logical relationships using overlapping geometric shapes — most commonly circles in a two-dimensional plane. Each set is depicted as a closed curve, and the spatial overlap between curves encodes set membership: regions where curves intersect represent elements belonging to multiple sets simultaneously, while non-overlapping regions denote elements unique to a single set. The construction persists through mathematical notation, educational materials, and digital rendering tools that compute exact intersection areas. [formal: diagramma vennum | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A violin plot is a data visualization that displays the distribution of numerical data across one or more categories by combining a box plot with a kernel density estimate (KDE). Parameters: (1) a box-plot core showing median as a central mark, interquartile range as the box, and whiskers extending to 1.5×IQR; (2) mirrored KDE curves on each side of the box, where the width at any value reflects the estimated density — wide sections indicate high probability mass, narrow sections indicate rarity. Persistence mechanism: the violin plot persists as a reproducible rendering instruction in statistical software (R, Python/Matplotlib, ggplot2), in published papers and textbooks, and in data-analysis curricula — it survives through code, print, and teaching. A competent speaker calls it a data visualization. [formal: violina-graphia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.06]

A scatter plot matrix is a data visualization composed of a grid of individual scatter plots arranged in rows and columns, where each plot shows the relationship between two variables from a larger set. Parameters: (1) the variable set defining the grid dimensions, (2) the data matrix providing observations for each cell, (3) visual encodings (position, color, shape) for data points within each cell. Persists through software implementations, published figures, and pedagogical teaching of multivariate analysis. [formal: matrixes dispersio punctata | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A dot plot is a data visualization technique that represents quantitative values as discrete dots positioned along a categorical axis. Parameters: (1) a single categorical variable defining the grouping dimension, (2) a quantitative variable mapped to vertical position, (3) optional jitter or stacking when multiple observations share the same category. The method encodes value through vertical displacement alone, omitting area or length encoding. [formal: plotum punctorum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A waterfall chart is a data visualization technique that displays sequentially ordered values as a series of bars whose heights represent individual positive or negative contributions to a running total. Parameters: (1) a running total that accumulates across categories, (2) discrete bars encoding additive or subtractive contributions, (3) a connective line showing the progression from baseline to final value. Persists through mark placement and color-coded directional encoding (typically green for gains, red for losses). [formal: cataractarius | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A sunburst diagram is a hierarchical data visualization that encodes nested categories as concentric rings, where each ring represents a depth level and the angular span of a segment indicates its proportion within its parent category. Parameters: (1) a tree-structured hierarchy with parent-child relationships, (2) concentric rings encoding depth levels, (3) angular encoding for within-category proportions. A stem plot is a data visualization technique that displays quantitative values as vertical stems rising from a shared baseline, where each stem's height represents a value and the stem's thickness or count encodes frequency. Parameters: (1) a numeric axis mapping height to value, (2) discrete stems positioned at category or bin locations, (3) count encoding via multiple stacked stems per position. Persists through mark placement on a shared baseline with uniform stem width. [formal: caulescens | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

A contour plot is a method of visualizing three-dimensional data on a two-dimensional plane by drawing lines (contours or isolines) that connect points of equal value. It takes a scalar function of two variables and renders it as a set of level curves, each labeled with its value; the spacing and density of contours encode the gradient steepness. The persistence mechanism is the plotted image or interactive renderer, which remains a stable artifact until replaced. [formal: contouratus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A contour plot is a two-dimensional visualization that represents three-dimensional data by drawing contour lines (isolines) — curves connecting points of equal value — across a coordinate plane. A contour plot is a two-dimensional visualization that represents three-dimensional scalar data by drawing contour lines (isolines) — curves connecting points of equal value — across a coordinate plane. Error bar is a graphical indicator placed on a data point in a chart or plot that represents the estimated uncertainty, variability, or confidence interval of that measured or reported value. Parameters: (1) anchored at a plotted data point or mean value; (2) extends along one axis (typically vertical, sometimes horizontal) to show the range of uncertainty; (3) the length of the bar corresponds to a specific statistical quantity — standard deviation, standard error, or a confidence interval — which must be stated in the chart legend or caption; (4) rendered as a line with terminal caps (I-beam shape). Persistence mechanism: established convention in scientific plotting and technical communication, embedded in every major charting library (matplotlib, ggplot, d3) as a standard chart element. [formal: error bar | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Word cloud is a data visualization in which words from a text corpus are rendered as graphical elements whose size (and optionally color) is proportional to their frequency or weight in the source text. Parameters: (1) input is a collection of tokens from a text corpus with associated counts or weights; (2) visual encoding maps frequency to font size and optionally to color hue; (3) words are arranged on a two-dimensional plane with placement constrained by a shape or bounding box, words non-overlapping; (4) a legend or scale may indicate the frequency-to-size mapping. Persistence mechanism: widely adopted convention in text analysis dashboards and editorial graphics, implemented in charting libraries (d3-cloud, wordcloud2.js) and publishing tools. [formal: nubilum verborum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A streamgraph is a variation of a stacked area chart in which the layers are displaced around a central baseline rather than a flat axis, producing a flowing, organic appearance. Parameters: (1) continuous x-axis representing time or an ordinal dimension, (2) one or more quantitative series stacked as layers, (3) a displaced baseline that centers the flow. A lollipop chart is a data visualization that represents values as horizontal or vertical lines terminating in filled circles (the 'lollipop head'), combining the axis structure of a bar chart with the point emphasis of a dot plot. Parameters: (1) categorical axis defining categories and their ordering, (2) numerical axis encoding magnitude as position along the stem, (3) stems rendered as lines from the axis origin to the value, (4) heads rendered as circles at the value position whose radius encodes no additional data. The persistence mechanism is charting software and data visualization libraries that render the glyph from structured data. [formal: lollipop chart | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.50]

A bump chart is a data visualization that displays changes in relative rank ordering across ordered dimensions (typically time periods or groups) using lines that rise and fall as items shift in rank. Parameters: (1) an ordered axis (usually ordinal such as time periods) defining the sequence of comparisons, (2) a rank axis encoding position in ordering rather than absolute value, (3) lines tracking each item's rank across the ordered dimension, (4) labels identifying the ranked items. The persistence mechanism is charting software and data visualization libraries that render the rank lines from ranked data. [formal: bump chart | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.50]

An error bar is a data visualization element that represents the uncertainty or variability of a measured value using a line segment (with terminal caps) extending above and/or below a data point. Parameters: (1) a central value (mean, median, or observation), (2) a measure of spread (standard deviation, confidence interval, or standard error), (3) direction (symmetric, asymmetric, one-sided). A spider chart (also called a radar chart or web chart) is a data visualization that displays multivariate data on a two-dimensional chart with three or more quantitative variables represented on axes radiating from a common origin. Each variable gets its own axis, evenly angularly spaced, and data values are plotted along each axis and connected to form a polygon. The parameters are: (1) the number of variables (axes), (2) the scale range per axis, and (3) the data points mapped onto the polygon vertices. It persists through software libraries and charting tools that render the geometric layout from structured tabular data. [formal: aranea | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

A gantt chart is a data visualization that displays a project schedule as horizontal bars aligned to a time axis, where each bar represents a task with its start date, duration, and end date. The parameters are: (1) the task list with assigned time bounds, (2) the time scale and granularity of the axis, and (3) dependency markers linking tasks that must be sequenced. It persists through project management software and scheduling tools that maintain the bar-based timeline representation from structured task data. [formal: guntum | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

A forest plot is a data visualization used in meta-analysis to display the estimated effects of interventions across multiple studies. Its parameters are: (1) a vertical line of no effect, (2) individual study results shown as markers with horizontal lines representing confidence intervals, (3) a summary diamond or line at the bottom aggregating all studies. Each row corresponds to one study, with numerical data typically listed beside the plot. It persists as a standard figure type in systematic review publications. [formal: forest plot | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A chord diagram is a data visualization that shows relationships and flow between entities using a circular layout. Entities are placed around the perimeter of a circle as arcs, and ribbons connecting arcs represent the magnitude of flow or relationship strength between entity pairs. The parameters are: (1) the entity set and their arc positions, (2) the adjacency matrix encoding pairwise flows, and (3) the ribbon width proportional to flow magnitude. It persists through interactive visualization libraries and charting frameworks that render the circular arc-and-ribbon geometry from structured relational data. [formal: chorda | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

A dot density map is a data visualization that represents quantitative values through a pattern of dots distributed across a geographic or categorical area, where dot density encodes magnitude. Its parameters are: (1) a base area or category serving as the canvas, (2) a quantitative value mapped to dot count or density, (3) a symbol (typically a circle/dot) placed at quasi-random positions within each sub-region proportional to the value, (4) a legend mapping dot count to magnitude. The persistence mechanism is the visual encoding convention maintained through cartographic practice, statistical graphics libraries, and information design education. [formal: dot-density-mappa | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mosaic plot is a data visualization for exploring relationships between two or more categorical variables. Its parameters are: (1) categorical variables that partition a contingency table into rectangular cells, (2) cell frequencies or proportions encoded as the area of each rectangle, (3) optional color or shading to encode residuals from independence. The mosaic is constructed by recursively subdividing a unit square so that each rectangle's area is proportional to its cell count, then partitioning each child rectangle according to conditional distributions. It persists through rendering in statistical visualization libraries (e.g., R's vcd, ggplot2 extensions). [formal: mosaicus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A data visualization element that encodes uncertainty or variability around a measured or estimated value using a geometric mark — typically a line segment with terminal caps extending from a central point — where the length of the mark corresponds to a confidence interval, standard deviation, or standard error. Its parameters are: (1) the central estimate or measurement, (2) the interval type (confidence, standard, error), and (3) the encoding direction (vertical, horizontal, or bidirectional). A data visualization layout that arranges multiple small visualizations in a grid structure, where each panel displays the same type of graphic for a different subset of the data, sliced by one or more categorical variables. A data visualization technique that displays distributions for several groups as overlapping density curves arranged vertically, creating a landscape-like appearance of mountain ridges, designed to reveal patterns of change in distributions across ordered categories or time. A stacked bar chart is a data visualization technique in which rectangular bars are subdivided into colored segments, each representing a proportional part of a whole. An error bar is a visual encoding element used in data visualization that represents the variability or uncertainty of a measured or estimated value. It appears as a line segment (vertical or horizontal) extending from a data point, where the length of the bar corresponds to a specified statistical measure — typically a confidence interval, standard deviation, or standard error — allowing viewers to assess the precision of the reported value at a glance. An alluvial diagram is a data visualization technique that represents flows or transitions between categories over sequential stages. [formal: alluvial diagram | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A facet grid is a data visualization layout that arranges multiple subplots in a two-dimensional grid, where rows and columns of the grid encode different categorical variables and each cell displays a view of the data filtered to that combination of categories. It enables comparison across all cross-tabulated groups simultaneously by sharing axes within rows or columns, designed to reveal interactions between categorical variables. It persists through the structural encoding of grid position as category combination and shared axes as dimensional alignment. [formal: facet grid | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

A small multiple is a data visualization design pattern that displays the same type of chart or graph multiple times, each showing a different subset or segment of the data, arranged in a grid or sequence for direct visual comparison. The technique leverages the human visual system's ability to detect differences across similar visual encodings, designed to reveal patterns, trends, or anomalies that would be obscured in a single overloaded chart. [formal: small multiple | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

A faceted visualization is a data visualization technique that splits a dataset by one or more categorical variables and displays a separate chart for each subset, enabling comparison across categories by showing what the data looks like under different conditions. Unlike a single chart with encoded category distinctions, faceting uses distinct visual spaces so that each subset gets its own full visual treatment, designed to reveal how patterns, distributions, or relationships vary across category levels. A sunburst chart is a data visualization technique that displays hierarchical data using concentric circles. Each ring represents one level of the tree hierarchy, with the root at the center. A boot is a type of footwear that encloses the entire foot and extends upward over the ankle or higher, typically reaching the calf, knee, or thigh. A hexbin plot is a two-dimensional data visualization that bins scattered points into a grid of regular hexagons, encoding density through color or shading so clusters and voids in dense point clouds become visible at a glance. A swarm plot is a data visualization for categorical scatter data that positions each point along an axis according to its value while jittering perpendicular to avoid overlap, producing a natural density shape that preserves every individual observation without binning. A raincloud plot is a composite data visualization that displays a distribution by layering three elements vertically: (1) a box plot showing quartiles and whiskers, (2) a half-violin showing kernel density estimate on one side, and (3) a raincloud of jittered raw data points below the violin. The parameters are: the dataset to visualize, the bandwidth for kernel density estimation, and the jitter amplitude for point dispersion. It persists as a rendered graphical display produced by statistical visualization software such as the 'raincloudplots' Python package or the 'rainclouds' R package, enabling researchers to see both aggregate statistics and individual observations simultaneously. A qq plot (quantile-quantile plot) is a diagnostic scatter plot used to compare whether two data sets follow a common distribution. It plots the quantiles of one data set against the quantiles of another; if the points fall approximately along a straight reference line, the two distributions are similar. Its parameters are: the two data sets (or one data set and a theoretical distribution), the quantile mapping function (typically probability plotting positions), and the reference line (either a theoretical straight line or a fitted line through sample quantiles). The persistence mechanism is the plotting convention — standardized by Tukey (1977) and codified in statistical software packages, reproduced identically across disciplines. [formal: quantile-quantile plot | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A likelihood ratio is a statistical measure that quantifies how much more likely a set of observations is under one hypothesis than under another. It is computed as the ratio of the likelihood of the data given H₁ to the likelihood of the data given H₀, where H₁ and H₀ are two competing hypotheses. Likelihood ratios form the basis of the likelihood-ratio test, Neyman-Pearson lemma-based optimal hypothesis testing, and Bayesian updating via Bayes' theorem. The measure operates through calculation from probability models fitted to data, persisted in statistical practice through computational tools and published analyses. [formal: ratio verisimilitudinis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A likert scale is a psychometric instrument for measuring attitudes and opinions through structured response options. It presents respondents with a series of statements and asks them to indicate their level of agreement using a symmetric ordinal scale, typically with five or seven points ranging from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree.' The parameters are the number of response points, the verbal labels for each point, and the set of statements being rated. It persists through standardized administration, cross-population comparison, and meta-analysis of aggregated scores. [formal: scala likertiana | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

An odds ratio is a statistical measure quantifying the strength of association between two binary variables by comparing the odds of an outcome under one condition to the odds under another. It is computed as the ratio of (odds of outcome given exposure A) to (odds of outcome given exposure B), or equivalently as the cross-product ratio from a 2x2 contingency table. The parameters are the two binary variables, the reference category, and the direction of comparison. It persists through statistical reporting, meta-analysis, and evidence-based practice. [formal: oratio oddsiorum | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

The primary function is to allow rapid assessment of multivariate relationships by scanning the matrix. Parameters: number of variables (n cells), encoding choice (color or scatter), variable ordering (can be reordered by clustering). Persistence mechanism: rendered by statistical software libraries (R, Python, Tableau) and reproduced in scientific publications. [formal: correlogram | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A dendrogram is a tree-diagram data visualization that encodes hierarchical relationships among a set of entities through nested branching structure. Its parameters are: clustering method (agglomerative vs divisive, or specific linkage criterion), distance or similarity metric, and rendering orientation (vertical, horizontal, radial). It persists through statistical computing environments and visualization file formats. [formal: dendrogram | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A radial chart is a data visualization in which data values are encoded as positions, lengths, or areas along circular paths radiating from a central origin. Common variants include radial bar charts, radial histograms, and circular scatter plots. The form reveals cyclical patterns, enables magnitude comparison across angular sectors, and suits hierarchical or temporal data with inherent cycles. It is constructed by mapping data values to angular and radial coordinates in polar space. [formal: charta radialis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A premise is a proposition — a declarative statement — accepted as true for the sake of argument or reasoning. It serves as the starting point from which inference proceeds, either to derive conclusions (in deductive argument) or to test hypotheses (in practical reasoning). A premise may be explicit (stated in the argument) or implicit (assumed but unstated). The concept of premise is a human-made construct of logic and argumentation: it carves out those propositions that function as the foundation of inference rather than as conclusions or intermediate inferences. Its parameters are: (1) it must be a proposition capable of truth or falsity, (2) it must serve as a starting point for an inference chain, and (3) it is held fixed for the duration of the reasoning. It persists through language (being stated or understood), through the teaching of logic and critical thinking, and through sustained practice in argumentation across disciplines from philosophy to mathematics to law. [formal: praemissa | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A standard error is a statistical measure of the precision of a sample estimate — specifically, the estimated standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic (typically the mean). [formal: error standardis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Standard error is a statistical estimate of the variability of a sample statistic across repeated random sampling from the same population. Parameters: sample size n, population variance σ² (or its estimate s²), sampling distribution shape. Persistence mechanism: computed from sample data using the formula SE = σ/√n (or s/√n), propagated through academic reporting, peer review, and data analysis conventions, preserved in textbooks and statistical software documentation. [formal: standard-error | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.23]

A correlation coefficient is a human-made statistical measure that quantifies the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables. Parameters: the pair of variables (X, Y), the sample size n, and the coefficient type (Pearson's r for linear relationships, Spearman's rho for rank-based, or Kendall's tau for concordance). The coefficient ranges from -1 (perfect negative correlation) through 0 (no correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation). Persistence mechanism: mathematical formula encoded in statistical textbooks, computational libraries, and pedagogical practice across disciplines. The concept persists through formal mathematical notation and its operationalization in data analysis software. [formal: correlatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A summary is a condensed restatement of a longer work, preserving its essential content and structure while omitting detail. Information design is the deliberate practice of structuring the visual and spatial presentation of information so that it can be perceived, understood, and acted upon by a user. Misinformation is the social category applied to information claims that a community determines to be false or inaccurate. Curating is the practice of selecting, organizing, and presenting items — artifacts, information, content, or experiences — for a defined audience according to stated criteria. Provocation is a deliberate act or stimulus designed to elicit a reaction, challenge assumptions, or initiate a process. A black swan is a cognitive heuristic for reasoning about low-probability, high-impact events. It identifies events satisfying three criteria: (1) rarity — the event lies outside normal expectations and cannot be reliably predicted by existing knowledge or models; (2) extreme impact — the event carries consequences that dwarf those of ordinary events; (3) retrospective predictability — after the event occurs, human reconstruction makes it appear explainable or predictable in hindsight. The black swan heuristic corrects for systematic underweighting of tail outcomes in probabilistic reasoning by forcing explicit consideration of extreme, previously unimaginable events. It persists through narrative, teaching, and adoption across disciplines — finance, history, science, and risk management — where it functions as a corrective to overconfidence in predictive models and standard statistical assumptions. [formal: black-swanus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

Self-deception is the cognitive practice of maintaining a belief while evading, distorting, or rationalizing away evidence that contradicts it. Parameters: (1) a held belief, (2) available contrary evidence, (3) a mechanism of evidential avoidance or rationalization that operates at or below the subject's awareness, and (4) the subject's own perspective as the site where belief and evidence conflict. The map tracks a pattern that psychology calls motivated reasoning, confirmation bias, or denial; philosophy debates whether genuine self-deception requires intentionality or is structurally impossible. A human-made document format that condenses the key findings, recommendations, and data of a longer report into a brief, decision-ready overview. A chart is a human-made visual representation that encodes data, information, or statistics into graphical elements (lines, bars, areas, symbols, points) arranged on a coordinate system to communicate quantitative relationships or patterns to a reader. Debiasing is a class of deliberate interventions designed to reduce the impact of cognitive biases on judgment and decision-making. Its parameters are: (1) a target bias or heuristic (e.g. anchoring, confirmation bias, availability), (2) a decision context in which the bias operates, and (3) a specific technique applied to interrupt the bias's influence — such as requiring consideration of alternative hypotheses, introducing accountability, using checklists, or training in statistical reasoning. Debiasing differs from general error-correction in that it targets systematic, predictable errors rooted in human cognitive architecture rather than random mistakes. The persistence mechanism is institutionalization: debiasing procedures are embedded in decision aids, training curricula, organizational protocols, and software tools that enforce bias-aware procedures. [formal: debiasing | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

A cognitive bias in which adding a third option (the decoy) that is asymmetrically dominated — worse than one option but not the other — shifts preference toward the option that dominates the decoy. The decoy is designed by choice architects to make a target option appear superior by comparison, even though it was not objectively improved. Parameters: requires a choice set of at least three options with asymmetric dominance. Persistence mechanism: reproduced in laboratory experiments and deployed in commercial pricing strategies across markets. [formal: decoy effect | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

A cognitive bias in which people systematically prefer the current state of affairs. When considering change, the status quo is disproportionately favored — any departure from the current state is perceived as a loss rather than a potential gain, creating inertia in decision-making even when change would be beneficial. The bias operates through loss aversion (losses loom larger than equivalent gains) and creates resistance to change in personal, organizational, and policy contexts. Persistence: modeled and taught in behavioral economics, decision theory, and policy analysis; documented in Kahneman, Tversky, and Samuelson prospect theory and subsequent experimental work. [formal: status quo bias | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A model of decision-making in which agents produce satisficing outcomes — decisions that are good enough — rather than optimal ones, bounded by three constraints: (1) limited cognitive capacity for processing information, (2) incomplete or imperfect information about alternatives and their consequences, and (3) finite time available to make the decision. The model carves bounded rationality from rational choice theory by specifying parameters for cognitive load, information quality, and time pressure that determine the satisficing threshold. It persists through academic teaching (economics, psychology, organizational theory), computational modeling, and policy design that incorporates realistic cognitive limits. [formal: rationalitas limitata | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.1]

A decision strategy in which an agent selects the first alternative that satisfies a minimum threshold of acceptability, rather than continuing search to find the optimal solution. Parameters: (1) a satisficing threshold below which options are rejected, (2) a search process that terminates upon finding a satisfactory option, (3) bounded information processing capacity that limits exhaustive search. Persists through teaching in behavioral economics and organizational theory, repeated use in human decision-making practice, and implementation in AI algorithms that implement satisficing search. [formal: satisfacere | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

A psychological concept describing the declining quality of decisions after extended periods of decision-making. Parameters: (1) cumulative decision count — the number of choices already made in the session, (2) decision complexity — the cognitive load per individual decision, (3) domain — the area of decision-making (financial, moral, mundane). Persistence mechanism: empirical research in social psychology, teaching in behavioral economics, application in policy design (choice architecture, default options). The concept maps how finite cognitive resources are depleted through repeated acts of will and judgment, producing a measurable degradation in subsequent decision quality. [formal: defectio facultatum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A human-made psychological research program that identifies and catalogs systematic deviations from rational decision-making by mapping cognitive shortcuts (heuristics) to their predictable errors (biases). Parameters: (1) a named heuristic — a mental shortcut such as availability, representativeness, or anchoring, (2) the corresponding bias — the predictable error pattern the heuristic generates, (3) the domain of application — the decision context in which the heuristic-bias pair operates. [formal: heuristicae et prauiudicia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

A psychological framework describing how the quality of decisions deteriorates after an extended period of decision-making, as the mental effort of repeated choices depletes the capacity for further deliberate judgment. A psychological framework describing the phenomenon where exposure to an excessive number of options impairs decision quality, increases decision time, and reduces post-choice satisfaction. Parameters: (1) a defined set of alternatives exceeding a cognitive threshold, (2) measurable degradation in choice quality or satisfaction relative to reduced sets, (3) an explanatory model mapping option count to decision performance. Persistence mechanism: taught as a concept in behavioral economics and consumer psychology, reproduced through academic literature, experimental protocols, and applied frameworks for choice architecture. [formal: overload | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A psychological construct describing how the perception of insufficient resources—money, time, food, or social connection—captures cognitive bandwidth, narrows attention to immediate shortages (tunneling), and produces systematic shifts in judgment and decision-making. Parameters: resource domain (monetary, temporal, material, social), intensity threshold (when perceived deficit becomes chronic), and cognitive effect magnitude (degree of bandwidth depletion). A cognitive phenomenon constructed to describe situations where the volume or complexity of incoming information exceeds an individual's capacity to process it effectively. A human-made cognitive act of selecting among alternatives, constructed as a formalizable process for resolving uncertainty through preference evaluation. A human-made cognitive model describing the state of exhausted mental resources after sustained cognitive engagement. [formal: habitudo | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Self-regulation is a human-made psychological construct describing the systematic process by which individuals monitor, evaluate, and modify their own thoughts, emotions, and behaviors to achieve desired outcomes or conform to standards. [formal: self-regulatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

dual-task is a cognitive psychology paradigm in which subjects perform two or more tasks simultaneously, and the resulting performance decrement relative to single-task performance is quantified as the dual-task cost. Parameters: (1) two tasks each independently performable, (2) simultaneous or near-simultaneous presentation, (3) measurable output on each task (reaction time, accuracy, or both), (4) a single-task baseline for comparison. The persistence mechanism is the loop's structural recording — via wiring, code, procedures, or social norms — that carries the output signal back to the input across time. [formal: feedback loop | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.40]

Epistemic-trust is the practice of granting informational authority to another agent or system as a reliable source of knowledge. Representativeness-heuristic is a cognitive model of judgment-by-similarity in which people assess the likelihood of an event or category membership by how much it resembles a prototype or typical case, while neglecting statistically relevant information such as base rates and sample sizes. Its parameters are: (1) similarity metric — perceptual, categorical, or causal resemblance to a prototype; (2) base-rate neglect — systematic underweighting of prior probabilities; (3) sample-size insensitivity — failure to account for the reliability of small samples. It persists through psychological theory (Kahneman and Tversky), behavioral economics, and decision-making training programs. [formal: representativeness | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Belief-formation is a human-made cognitive process describing how agents integrate new information with existing representations to produce stable propositional attitudes. Parameters: (1) input channel — the mode by which information enters (perception, testimony, inference); (2) existing belief state — the prior network of representations against which new data is weighted; (3) update rule — the criterion by which information crosses the threshold from received to believed. The persistence mechanism is language (shared vocabulary for belief states), teaching (transmission of evidential standards), and cognitive science (systematic study of belief revision). [formal: formatio credulitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Attentional-control is the cognitive mechanism that selects, sustains, and shifts focused mental resources toward relevant stimuli or goals while suppressing distraction. [formal: attentional control | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.91]

Heuristic-systematic model is a dual-process framework describing how people process persuasive information — either through effortful, systematic evaluation of argument quality or through heuristic shortcuts like source credibility, message length, or consensus cues. Persistence mechanism: academic theory in social psychology and communication studies, textbook transmission, and applied frameworks in advertising, risk communication, and health messaging that operationalize the model's predictions. [formal: heuristic-systematic processing | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.92]

Cognitive flexibility is the psychological construct for the capacity to switch between mental sets, adapt to novel or changing task demands, and reorganize thinking when conditions shift. It persists through standardized measurement (Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, task-switching paradigms), clinical implementation (CBT flexibility protocols, mindfulness-based set-shifting), and the ongoing research literature that refines its operationalization across domains. [formal: flexibilibilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Force is the human-made concept in physics that quantifies interaction capable of changing an object's state of motion. Its parameters are: magnitude (measured in newtons, where 1 N = 1 kg⋅m/s²), direction (a vector quantity), and point of application. Force operates through Newton's laws of motion — specifically, F = dp/dt, the rate of change of momentum. The concept persists through mathematical formalism (vector calculus within classical and relativistic mechanics), experimental verification (force sensors, accelerometers, inertial measurements), and engineering practice (structural analysis, dynamics simulation). The boundaries of the map are drawn by what interactions can be modeled as momentum transfer; the territory maps gravity, electromagnetism, contact forces, and pressure gradients into this single conceptual framework. [formal: vis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Inhibitory control is the human-made concept in cognitive psychology denoting the executive capacity to deliberately suppress a dominant, automatic, or prepotent response in favor of a less automatic but more goal-appropriate one. It persists through standardized paradigms (Go/No-Go, Stop-Signal, Stroop tasks), institutional clinical practice (ADHD and executive-function assessment), and the research literature that maps its neural substrates in the prefrontal cortex. [formal: inhibitio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cognitive appraisal is a psychological construct that models how individuals evaluate and interpret situations in terms of their personal significance and relevance to well-being. The framework was developed as a theoretical model in cognitive psychology and stress research to explain why identical events produce different emotional and physiological responses across individuals or contexts. The construct persists through formal psychological theory, empirical measurement via self-report instruments and physiological protocols, and clinical application in stress management and cognitive-behavioral therapy. [formal: cognitiva-appellatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An expression is a group of words whose meaning is conventional rather than purely compositional — the whole carries semantic weight that exceeds (or diverges from) the sum of its parts. Parameters: semantic convention (degree to which meaning is fixed vs. freely recomputed from constituents), syntactic fixedness (how tightly the structure is constrained — frozen idioms admit no substitution, semi-fixed slots allow variation), register (formal to colloquial usage domains).
