[formal: expressio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cognitive load theory is a learning framework developed by John Sweller that posits human working memory has limited capacity and that instructional design must account for three types of cognitive load: intrinsic load (inherent complexity of the material), extraneous load (poor instructional design that wastes working memory resources), and germane load (cognitive effort devoted to schema construction). The theory specifies measurable parameters: germane load is maximized when extraneous load is minimized while intrinsic load is managed through worked examples, fading, and split-attention mitigation. Its persistence mechanism is academic teaching in educational psychology, curriculum design practice, and peer-reviewed research literature. [formal: cognitum-caricatum-theoria | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dual-coding theory is a learning theory that posits human cognition operates through two distinct but interconnected processing channels: a verbal channel for linguistic information (words, symbols) and a nonverbal channel for imaginal information (mental imagery, visual patterns). The theory holds that meaningful learning occurs when information is encoded in both channels simultaneously, creating redundant representations that strengthen recall. The verbal channel processes spoken and written language through phonological and semantic coding; the nonverbal channel processes concrete objects and spatial relationships through imagery. Learning is enhanced (the dual-coding effect) when verbal and nonverbal materials are presented together rather than in isolation, because the two systems provide complementary retrieval paths.

The theory was proposed by Allan Paivio and has been validated through experimental paradigms measuring recall and recognition of paired associates, picture-word combinations, and multimedia learning tasks. It persists through decades of empirical research in educational psychology, cognitive science, and instructional design.

[formal: codificatio-duplex | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A simile is a figure of speech that makes an explicit comparison between two unlike things by using a comparative marker such as 'like', 'as', 'than', or 'as ... as'. Its parameters are: (1) a target domain (the thing being described), (2) a source domain (the thing used for comparison), and (3) a comparative marker that signals the mapping between them. It persists through natural language use, literary tradition, and pedagogical teaching of rhetorical devices. [formal: comparatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A conceptual model is a deliberately crafted abstraction that selects and simplifies aspects of a domain of reality to support understanding, reasoning, or communication about that domain. Its defining parameters are: (1) selectivity — it omits details that do not serve the model's purpose, (2) representation — it maps elements of the domain to symbols, structures, or relationships, and (3) intended use — it is designed for a specific cognitive or communicative task. It persists through teaching, documentation, and sustained practice within communities that deploy it. [formal: model_conceptualis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mental technique and cognitive construct where reasoning proceeds through spatial layouts, images, and visual relationships rather than through linguistic symbols. Parameters: (1) the thinker generates or manipulates internal visual representations, (2) the structure of the representation carries the logical content (spatial proximity encodes relational proximity), (3) the technique is trained and teachable through practices like mind-mapping, diagramming, and spatial memory. The mechanism of persistence is repeated practice and external notation systems (sketches, blueprints, diagrams) that externalize the internal capacity. [formal: cogitatio visualis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

A conceptual model is a deliberately crafted abstraction that selects and simplifies aspects of a domain of reality to support understanding, reasoning, or communication about that domain. Parameters: (1) it isolates relevant features while omitting noise, (2) it encodes relationships among those features in a representable form (diagram, formula, narrative, or structure), and (3) it is portable across instances of the domain for prediction, explanation, or design. The persistence mechanism is teaching and notation — models survive their authors through codified representation in textbooks, diagrams, software, and disciplinary curricula. [formal: conceptualis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.13]

Elaboration strategy is a learning technique that improves retention and understanding by connecting new information to existing knowledge structures through active elaboration. Parameters: (1) it requires pre-existing knowledge in the domain to elaborate upon; (2) the elaboration must be meaningful and self-generated rather than provided externally; (3) it operates by creating additional retrieval paths through deeper encoding. Persistence mechanism: taught explicitly in educational settings, sustained by research evidence from cognitive psychology, and applied by teachers and learners. [formal: elaboratio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Interrogation is the structured practice of systematic questioning by an authorized questioner to extract or verify information from a subject under defined procedural rules. It is distinguished from casual inquiry by (a) a formal role division (interrogator vs. subject), (b) procedural constraints (what questions may be asked, how answers are recorded, what counts as admissible), and (c) an institutional context (legal proceedings, investigations, intelligence gathering, military detention). The persistence mechanism is institutional codification: legal statutes, professional protocols, training curricula, and organizational SOPs that reproduce the practice across individuals and time. Without these institutional supports, interrogation collapses into unstructured questioning. [formal: interrogatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A knowledge-graph is a structured representation of information where real-world entities are encoded as nodes and the relationships between them as labeled edges, forming a graph data structure that supports semantic querying and inference. Its parameters are: (1) entities typed by class or category, (2) relationships typed by predicate or role, (3) properties attached to nodes and edges as key-value pairs. It persists through (a) graph-database storage engines (property-graph or RDF stores), (b) query languages (Cypher, SPARQL) that traverse and aggregate relationships, and (c) visualization tools that render the structure as interconnected nodes. Distinct from a flat database by its emphasis on relationship-first topology — the edges carry meaning, not just connectivity. [formal: cognitio-graphica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A document is a human-made artifact that encodes information in a durable, readable form — text, image, or structured data — for storage, communication, or legal effect across time and distance. Parameters: it carries semantic content, persists in a material or digital medium, and is designed for human interpretation. Persistence mechanism: encoded symbols stored in physical (paper, stone, clay) or digital (file, database, blockchain) media, maintained by preservation practices and reading technologies. [formal: documentum | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A visual thinking technique in which information is organized in a radial diagram: a central concept anchors the structure, with branches extending outward containing related keywords, images, and sub-branches. Parameters: (1) radial layout with a single central node; (2) hierarchical branching from general to specific; (3) use of keywords rather than long phrases; (4) visual elements (colors, images) to enhance recall. Persistence mechanism: drawn on paper or rendered digitally through mind-mapping software (XMind, FreeMind, MindMeister). [formal: mind-mapping | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Interleaved practice is a learning technique in which different topics, skills, or types of problems are mixed within a single study session, rather than practiced in isolated blocks. The technique exploits the cognitive benefit of varied retrieval, forcing the learner to continually reload and restructure mental models. It persists through structured curriculum design, educational practice regimes, and deliberate study methods validated by cognitive science research. [formal: interleaved_practice | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Transfer-appropriate processing is a learning principle from educational psychology: memory performance is optimized when the cognitive operations engaged during encoding match the cognitive operations required at retrieval. Its parameters are (1) an encoding phase that induces specific processing orientations (e.g., semantic vs. structural) and (2) a retrieval phase whose demands are compared against the encoding operations. The mechanism of persistence is empirical — the principle persists through repeated experimental demonstration in controlled learning studies, formal pedagogy derived from those results, and instructional design frameworks that operationalize the match-mismatch diagnostic. [formal: transfer_appropriatus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

Explicit knowledge is a category of knowledge that can be readily articulated in symbolic form, codified into documentation, and deliberately transferred between persons. Its parameters are (1) accessibility — the knower can articulate the content in words, diagrams, or formal notation, and (2) transferability — the content can be packaged and transmitted independent of the knower's physical presence. It contrasts with tacit knowledge, which resides in practice and cannot be fully articulated. The mechanism of persistence is institutional — explicit knowledge persists through written records, formal teaching curricula, databases, and documentation systems maintained by communities of practice. [formal: cognitio_explicita | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.13]

A self-directed learning method consisting of four steps: (1) choose a concept and explain it in simple language as if teaching a complete novice, (2) identify gaps and errors in your explanation where understanding breaks down, (3) return to the source material to fill those specific gaps, and (4) simplify and create analogies to refine the explanation. Parameters: the learner must produce original language (no regurgitation), the audience must be defined as novice-level, and the process is iterative rather than one-pass. Persists through deliberate practice routines, written explanations, and teaching sessions. [formal: feynman-technique | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A user interface is the designed medium through which a human interacts with a machine or system. Its parameters are: (1) input methods — how the user sends commands (keyboard, mouse, touch, voice, gesture); (2) output/feedback — how the system communicates state (display, sound, haptic, LED); (3) layout — the spatial arrangement of interactive elements; (4) interaction conventions — the rules governing how input maps to system behavior. It is human-made by designers and engineers, persists through design specifications, implementation code, design system documentation, and the accumulated practice of human-computer interaction. A poorly designed interface makes a capable system unusable; a good one disappears into flow. [formal: interfacies | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Deep processing is a learning technique that encodes information through semantic analysis, personal relevance, and meaningful connections to existing knowledge. Its parameters are: (1) meaning construction — extracting semantic content rather than surface form; (2) personal elaboration — linking new information to existing beliefs, experiences, or goals; (3) relational integration — connecting concepts to each other rather than treating them as isolated facts. It persists through deliberate study methods, teaching practice, and cognitive training protocols. [formal: deep-processing | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A pomodoro technique is a time-management method that structures work into fixed-length intervals (traditionally 25 minutes) separated by short breaks, with a longer break after four intervals. Its parameters are: (1) work interval — a focused, uninterrupted period of task engagement; (2) short break — a recovery period after each work interval; (3) long break — an extended rest after completing a cycle of intervals; (4) cycle — the repeating sequence of intervals and breaks. It persists through structured training, productivity literature, and self-regulated study practice. [formal: pomodoro | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hierarchical note-taking format where ideas are organized using bullet-point indentation to show parent-child relationships among concepts. Each indent level signals a deeper or subordinate claim, and the structure itself encodes logical flow without requiring explicit connectors or numbering systems. Persistence is achieved through plain-text encoding and editor-agnostic rendering — the meaning lives in the indent counts, not in any software-specific formatting layer. [formal: spiral notae | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

A personal knowledge management system built on atomic notes — each card or digital note carries exactly one idea — linked together by directional references that form a self-growing network of ideas. The persistence mechanism is the slip-box (Zettelkasten) itself: a physical or digital index of interconnected notes where new entries are filed by reference to existing ones, creating emergent structure through atomicity and linkage rather than pre-defined categories. The system's operational rule is that every note must either link to an existing note or become a link target for a future note. [formal: arca zettelorum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.00]

The educational psychology construct describing how learners revise or replace existing conceptual frameworks when encountering evidence or explanations that contradict their current understanding. It specifies the conditions under which prior beliefs are destabilized, the mechanisms of integration (accommodation vs. assimilation), and the markers of successful change (coherent alternative frameworks, behavioral consistency, predictive accuracy). Persistence mechanism: transmitted through pedagogical practice, empirical research literature, and curriculum design; sustained in academic disciplines that study learning and belief revision. [formal: conceptualis-transmutatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Instructional design is the systematic practice of designing, developing, and evaluating learning experiences and instruction. It operates through defined methods — needs analysis, learning-objective specification, content sequencing, assessment design, and iterative evaluation — applied via recognized models (ADDIE, SAM, backward design, Dick-Carey). Its parameters are: (1) a target learner population with specified prior knowledge, (2) learning objectives expressed as observable performance criteria, (3) instructional strategies matched to objective types, and (4) evaluation instruments measuring objective attainment. It persists through codified models published in professional literature, academic degree programs, professional certification, and institutional adoption of design standards. The practice transforms learning theory and cognitive science into structured experiences that reliably produce intended knowledge, skill, or attitude outcomes. [formal: designum instructivum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A pedagogical technique in which learners engage with challenging, ill-structured problems before receiving formal instruction. The initial struggle — which typically results in incomplete or incorrect solutions — creates productive knowledge gaps that enhance the encoding and retention of subsequently taught material. The mechanism operates through three phases: (1) individual or collaborative problem-solving attempts that surface existing mental models, (2) a transition phase where the inadequacy of pre-instruction solutions becomes apparent, and (3) formal instruction that directly addresses the gaps exposed during phase one. The persistence mechanism is teaching practice in educational settings, particularly in STEM disciplines, validated through randomized controlled experiments comparing productive-failure sequences with direct-instruction sequences. The effect size is moderate to large for conceptual understanding and transfer, with smaller or null effects for procedural performance. [formal: productive-failure | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A growth-mindset is the belief system holding that personal attributes — intelligence, talent, character, and competence — are malleable and can be cultivated through sustained effort, effective strategies, and guidance from others. It is not a claim that effort alone guarantees success, but rather that capacity is expandable rather than fixed. The construct distinguishes itself from the fixed-mindset alternative, which treats attributes as static endowments. Operationalized in educational practice through process-oriented praise, emphasis on learning over performance, and framing of mistakes as information rather than failure. It persists through pedagogical training, organizational policy, and cultural transmission of achievement narratives. [formal: mens crescit | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A desirable-difficulty is a pedagogical intervention that strategically introduces cognitive challenge during learning to enhance long-term retention and transfer. Parameters: (1) the difficulty must be 'desirable' — challenging enough to increase processing effort but not so hard as to overwhelm working memory; (2) it must be systematic rather than accidental — part of a deliberate instructional design; (3) it must produce a measurable delay effect where short-term performance may suffer but long-term retention improves. Persistence mechanism: the concept persists through academic literature (Bjork's original formulation, subsequent meta-analyses), teacher training curricula, and evidence-based instructional practice frameworks. [formal: difficultia optima | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A preface is a short introductory section written by the author of a book or published work, positioned at the beginning of the text before the main body. It states the author's purpose for writing, the scope and intended audience of the work, and may explain the methodology, origins, or circumstances of its creation.

Parameters: (1) The author must be the work's primary writer or writing team — this distinguishes a preface from a foreword, which is authored by a different person. (2) The content must concern the work itself: its aims, methods, scope, or production history. (3) It is situated at the front matter of the published artifact, preceding the main text. (4) Its length is typically brief relative to the work as a whole, serving orientation rather than substantive argument.

Persistence mechanism: The preface is embedded in the published text and reproduced identically with each copy of the work; it persists as a fixed structural element of the artifact across all editions that retain it (superseded only by a revised edition that replaces it).

[formal: praefatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A learning-strategy is a deliberate method or technique for improving the acquisition, retention, and application of knowledge. It operates through structured cognitive engagement: organizing information, retrieving from memory, self-explaining, and connecting new material to prior knowledge. The mechanism is the intentional activation of encoding and retrieval processes that strengthen memory traces and build coherent mental representations. [formal: strategium discendi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cloze procedure is a language-learning technique in which passages of text have words removed at regular intervals, and learners must supply the missing words from context. It carves the method by its parameters: systematic deletion (typically every 5th–7th word or all function words), the constraint that replacements be grammatically consistent with the surrounding syntax, and the assessment function whereby correct recalls measure retention and comprehension. It persists through classroom practice, standardized testing protocols, and the teaching methodology that treats recall-from-partial-text as a proxy for deep encoding. [formal: clausura | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A communication-paradox is a structured pattern of interaction in which contradictory messages operate across different logical levels, rendering any consistent response self-undermining. It carves the construct by its parameters: (1) multiple communicative messages or frames, (2) logical incompatibility between the levels at which these messages operate, (3) the impossibility of resolving the contradiction through ordinary communicative means. It persists through discourse, psychological theory, and philosophical analysis of interaction. [formal: paradox | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

first-principles is a human-made reasoning method that decomposes complex problems into their most basic, foundational truths — propositions accepted as self-evident or empirically verified — and reconstructs solutions from those truths upward. It carves the construct by its two-phase structure (decomposition to axioms, reconstruction from axioms), its reliance on first-truth selection criteria, and its persistence through teaching, scientific practice, and problem-solving documentation. [formal: principia prima | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Hypophora is a rhetorical device in which a speaker or writer poses a question and then immediately provides the answer. Parameters: (1) a question is explicitly stated; (2) the answer follows without pause or delay; (3) the question-answer pair serves to steer an audience through argumentation, surface an objection, and resolve it in the speaker's favor. Persistence mechanism: transmitted through rhetorical training, preserved in handbooks of discourse from antiquity through modern composition pedagogy, and sustained by repeated use in speeches, essays, and debate. [formal: hypophora | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A lesson plan is a structured document or cognitive framework used by educators to organize and sequence teaching activities toward defined learning objectives. Parameters: (1) it specifies one or more learning objectives or outcomes for the session; (2) it sequences instructional activities in a coherent temporal order; (3) it identifies required materials, resources, and assessment methods; (4) it operates within a bounded time period for a defined audience of learners. A lesson plan persists through written documentation, digital storage, and the institutionalized practice of pre-planning instruction across teaching communities. [formal: dispositio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Motive is the reason or purpose that an agent attributes to themselves or imputes to others as the explanation for an action. Parameters: (1) it identifies a goal, desire, belief-state, or value that purportedly drives the action; (2) it is distinct from causal factors (physiological, environmental, genetic) and from legal culpability — a motive may be present without guilt, and culpable without a discoverable motive; (3) it is constructed and deployed in narrative, legal, psychological, and everyday explanatory practices, and need not be conscious or accurate. A motive is the explanatory map, not the territory of the agent's internal state. [formal: motivus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dark patterns are a class of user interface design techniques that deliberately exploit human cognitive biases, heuristics, and trust relationships to steer users toward outcomes that serve the operator's interests — often at the user's expense. They operate by manipulating interface structure, language, sequencing, or defaults: hiding costs until checkout (bait and switch), making cancellation harder than sign-up (robo-subscription / forced continuity), using social pressure in confirmation dialogs (confirm shaming), disguising advertising as editorial content (dark print), and pre-selecting opt-ins (sneak into basket). The class is distinguished from legitimate persuasion (transparent nudges, ethical design) by its deceptive character: the pattern conceals its true purpose, exploits cognitive vulnerabilities rather than informing decisions, and produces outcomes contrary to what the user would choose with full information and undistracted deliberation. The concept emerged from UX research in the 2000s (Brignull, 2010) and has since been recognized by regulators (EU DSA, California Consumer Privacy Act) as a form of manipulative design. [formal: pattern_deceptivus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias in problem-solving wherein an individual's ability to use an object is constrained by their knowledge of its customary function. The bias causes people to overlook alternative uses of familiar objects because their mental representation anchors to traditional purpose. Karl Duncker (1945) established the phenomenon through the candle problem and related experiments, demonstrating that exposure to an object's conventional use impairs creative recombination. The construct has since been operationalized in design thinking pedagogy as a barrier to innovation, and in cognitive psychology as a documented limit on divergent thinking. The mechanism operates through learned schemas — repeated exposure to standard object-function pairings builds cognitive pathways that resist alternative mappings. [formal: functionalia fixata | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Heuristic evaluation is a usability inspection method in human-computer interaction wherein trained evaluators systematically assess a user interface against a set of established usability heuristics (principles), documenting violations and prioritizing recommendations for improvement. The method is defined by three parameters: (1) the heuristic set used as criteria (commonly Nielsen's 10 heuristics or a domain-adapted variant), (2) the number and expertise level of evaluators conducting the inspection, and (3) the structured reporting format that captures each violation with severity rating. It persists through documented practice in HCI methodology, formalized in the Nielsen-Normann framework and maintained through professional UX communities and academic literature. [formal: evaluatio heuristicum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A data lake is a centralized storage architecture in information systems that ingests and retains vast volumes of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data in its native format, deferring schema definition to the read phase. It persists through distributed storage systems (HDFS, S3, Blob) backed by catalog metadata and access controls. Schema-on-read, rather than schema-on-write, allows arbitrary analytics, machine learning, and reporting workloads over the same raw data store without prior transformation.

[formal: lacus_data | substrate: matter | horizon: years | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Conflation is a rhetorical and linguistic device wherein two distinct concepts, narratives, or referents are merged into a single mental representation, producing ambiguity, false equivalence, or persuasive force. It operates through forced conceptual overlap: the conflation asserts identity between two non-identical things, exploiting cognitive tendencies to resolve ambiguity. The device persists through spoken discourse, written text, and cultural transmission, becoming a recognizable pattern in argumentation and narrative. [formal: conflatio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A conceptual map is a structured diagram that represents knowledge as a network of concepts (nodes) connected by labeled relational links (edges). Its parameters are: (1) nodes — discrete concepts arranged hierarchically from most general at the top to most specific at the bottom; (2) edges — directed connections between pairs of nodes, each labeled with a phrase describing the relationship; (3) cross-links — non-hierarchical connections that reveal integrative relationships across domains; (4) hierarchical organization — the vertical structure showing subordination and inclusion. The persistence mechanism is teaching and collaborative use: conceptual maps are learned through instruction, reproduced in practice, and refined through group activity in education, knowledge management, and design. [formal: mapae conceptuum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Documentation is the human-made practice of systematically recording information for preservation, reference, and communication across time and space. Its parameters are: (1) content — discrete units of recorded information organized by subject or process; (2) medium — the substrate (paper, digital, oral) that carries the record; (3) audience — the intended readers or users for whom the record is structured. It persists through deliberate act of recording, structured organization, and storage in accessible repositories. [formal: documentatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Workload is the human-made management concept measuring the volume of work assigned to or expected of a person or system. Its parameters are: (1) assigned tasks — discrete units of work allocated within a time period; (2) expected output — the quantity or quality of results required; (3) time constraints — deadlines and scheduling windows that bound delivery. It persists through performance tracking systems, scheduling tools, and organizational planning practices that quantify and distribute work. [formal: workload | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cataphora is a rhetorical and linguistic device in which a word — typically a pronoun, determiner, or descriptive phrase — is used before its antecedent, establishing reference forward rather than backward. The term derives from Greek kataphorá, meaning 'a carrying down.' In the sentence 'When he finally spoke, the room fell silent,' the pronoun 'he' refers ahead to 'the room' is not right — 'he' refers to a person named later: 'When John entered the room, he fell silent.' Cataphora operates through anticipatory reference, the reverse of anaphora (backward reference to a prior antecedent). It functions as a narrative technique to build suspense, create cohesion across clauses, and establish referential links before the referent is named. The mechanism relies on the listener's ability to resolve the forward-pointing reference upon encountering the antecedent. [formal: cataphora | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Data-quality is the degree to which data satisfies defined fitness-for-use requirements — accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and validity — as measured against a specification and sustained through governance processes. It is a human-made evaluative construct: the concept of data quality does not exist in raw data itself; it is imposed by human systems (databases, compliance frameworks, ML pipelines) that define, measure, and enforce thresholds for acceptable data. The persistence mechanism is institutional practice: data governance policies, quality assurance workflows, and the standardized metrics (completeness rate, error rate, freshness SLA) that organizations maintain and audit. [formal: data qualitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Literacy is the acquired capacity to decode, interpret, and produce meaning within a defined symbolic system. Its parameters are: (1) a symbolic system with conventions — written text, digital interfaces, mathematical notation, musical notation, or other semiotic codes — (2) a learner who acquires the decoding and production skills through instruction and practice, and (3) a community whose interpretive standards validate the output. It persists through pedagogical institutions, social reinforcement of competence, and the ongoing reproduction of the symbolic system's conventions across generations. [formal: littera | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Attention-economy is a conceptual framework that models human attention as a scarce, competitively allocated resource, treatable and tradable the way economic goods are. It maps media platforms, algorithms, advertising, and information systems onto a market architecture in which the scarce input is focused cognitive capacity and the currency is time-on-screen, engagement metrics, and data extraction. The framework persists through academic discourse (media studies, political economy of communication), industry practice (ad-tech optimization, algorithmic recommendation, UX growth metrics), and policy debate (screen-time regulation, digital wellness, antitrust). It was coined by Herbert Simon in 1971 and operationalized by Clay Shirky and later by digital-media critics. It carves the space between the natural faculty of attention (out of scope, Law 2a) and the constructed market-model that treats that faculty as extractable yield — the parameters being: a scarcity claim about attention, a mapping of design practices to attention capture, and a metric regime that quantifies engagement as revenue. [formal: attentionis oeconomia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.74]

An implementation-intention is a self-regulatory strategy in which a person formulates a specific if-then plan linking a situational cue to a goal-directed response (e.g., 'If situation X arises, then I will perform response Y'). It works by mentally simulating the cue-response pairing so that the cue automatically triggers the intended behavior, bypassing deliberative decision-making in the moment. Its parameters are: a specified cue, a specified response, and a mental representation formed through repeated simulation of their connection. It persists as a stored behavioral program that activates upon cue detection.
[formal: implementare intentionem | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Intrinsic motivation is the drive to perform an activity for its inherent satisfaction — the activity itself is the reward, not some separable outcome. It is distinguished from extrinsic motivation (action for external rewards) and defined by three parameters: autonomy (volitional choice), competence (felt effectiveness), and relatedness (connection to others), per Self-Determination Theory (Deci and Ryan, 1985). The concept persists through psychological theory, measurement instruments, empirical research, and pedagogical application. [formal: intrinseca motivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Operant-conditioning is a learning mechanism in which the strength and frequency of voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — reinforcement (which increases behavior) or punishment (which decreases behavior). It operates through contingency learning: an organism learns to associate its actions with outcomes. Developed by B.F. Skinner (1938), the concept persists through behavioral therapy protocols, educational applications, and animal training paradigms, maintained by schedules of reinforcement that define when consequences follow behavior. [formal: operant-conditioning | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cognitive-state is a temporary condition of mental operation characterized by specific patterns of attention allocation, processing capacity, and awareness. Cognitive-states include flow (deep immersion with high capacity), cognitive overload (capacity exceeded by demand), confusion (unclear mental model), and focused attention (narrowed processing). The construct persists through psychological theory, empirical measurement via self-report and performance metrics, and its operational use in designing learning environments, interfaces, and workflows that match available cognitive capacity to task demands. [formal: status_cognitivus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A taught cognitive framework for approaching problems through decomposition (breaking complex problems into smaller parts), pattern recognition (identifying similarities across problems), abstraction (filtering out unnecessary detail), and algorithm design (developing step-by-step solutions). It is a method of structuring thought, not the computation itself. [formal: computatio cogitans | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

Motivation is the human-constructed concept that categorizes the internal drives, goals, incentives, and reasons that propel action. It exists as a linguistic and cognitive tool — a framework humans invented to explain, predict, and regulate behavior in themselves and others. Motivation is not a single mechanism but a family of related constructs: intrinsic motivation (action for its own sake), extrinsic motivation (action for external reward), and the transitions between them. It persists through language, social norms, educational systems, and self-reflection practices. This construct is not merely descriptive; it is constitutive of how humans organize their understanding of agency, responsibility, and purpose. Without this concept, the distinction between compulsion and choice, between impulse and intention, loses its shared vocabulary.
\nDefinition is carved as a linguistic construct for categorizing internal drive and goal-directed behavior, persistent through language and social practice.

Self-assessment is the structured practice wherein learners evaluate their own work, knowledge, or performance against explicitly stated criteria. Parameters: (1) explicit criteria must be provided or co-constructed; (2) the learner produces a judgment of quality or understanding; (3) the judgment may trigger corrective action. Persistence mechanism: sustained through educational institutions that design rubrics, scaffold metacognitive reflection, and reward self-evaluation — a pedagogical construct that does not exist without deliberate teaching and institutional reinforcement. [formal: se-iudicium | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Instructional scaffolding is a teaching technique wherein temporary, graduated support is provided to a learner and systematically withdrawn as competence increases. Parameters: (1) the support is calibrated to the learner's current level — within the zone of proximal development; (2) it is temporary and fades as independence grows; (3) it takes forms such as modeling, prompts, worked examples, graphic organizers, or guided questions. Persistence mechanism: transmitted through teacher training, curriculum design, and educational research — a deliberate pedagogical craft that exists only through institutionalized teaching practice. [formal: substructio pedagogica | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Extrinsic motivation is a form of motivation driven by external rewards or the avoidance of negative outcomes, distinct from acting out of inherent interest or enjoyment. Parameters: (1) the motivating stimulus must be external to the activity itself (rewards, punishments, evaluations, tangible incentives); (2) the behavior is performed instrumentally to achieve a separable outcome. Contrast with intrinsic motivation where the activity is its own reward. Persistence mechanism: operationalized and measured through self-report inventories, behavioral choice paradigms, and incentive structures across psychology, education, and organizational behavior. [formal: extrinsecus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A garment is a human-made item of clothing designed to be worn on the body. Parameters: (1) it must cover or adorn at least part of the human body; (2) it is constructed from textiles, leather, or other flexible materials; (3) its form is shaped by cultural conventions and functional needs. Garments persist through textile manufacturing practices, fashion systems, and dress traditions transmitted across generations. [formal: vestis | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Long-term memory is the human-made concept of durable information storage — the map by which disciplines track knowledge, skills, and records that persist across extended time. Parameters: (1) it represents retained information encoded through repetition, encoding practice, or external inscription; (2) it operates across scales from hours to a lifetime or beyond; (3) it is distinguished from immediate or working memory by its resistance to rapid decay without active maintenance. Built to persist through education systems, written records, archival practice, and the cultural transmission of knowledge across generations. [formal: memoria longinqui | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.21]

Extrinsic reward is a human-made incentive structure in which a tangible or symbolic benefit — money, praise, grades, privileges — is conferred upon an agent contingent on performance of a specified behavior or achievement of a target outcome.
