Invention is the human-made concept of creating something novel and useful that did not previously exist. Parameters: (1) mechanism — cognitive processes combined with cultural knowledge to produce a novel arrangement, device, or method; (2) criteria — novelty (not previously existing), utility (serving a function), and intentionality (deliberate creation). The concept of invention organizes human understanding of creativity, progress, and technological change across societies. [formal: inventor | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mise-en-abyme is the human-made concept of a self-referential structure that embeds a smaller copy of itself within its own form. Parameters: (1) mechanism — recursive embedding where a work contains a version of itself reduced in scale but structurally identical; (2) persistence — established through deliberate compositional practice in visual art (frames within paintings), literature (characters reading the same novel), and cinema (screens showing the current scene); (3) range — applies when the embedded copy is recognizably the same work, not merely thematically similar. [formal: mise-en-abyme | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Variation is the human-made concept of altering a theme, pattern, or form while preserving its underlying identity — a compositional technique used deliberately across music, literature, visual art, and design to explore the space around a stable core. Parameters: (1) mechanism — selective modification of one or more dimensions (pitch, rhythm, texture, color, structure, narrative) while holding others constant; (2) identity anchor — the invariant element(s) that allow recognition of the source beneath alteration; (3) degree — the spectrum from conservative modification (surface-level decoration) to radical transformation (structural reimagining). The technique persists through notation, performance practice, teaching, and iterative creative processes. [formal: variatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Paracosm is the human-made concept of an elaborate, sustained imaginary world built within conscious cognition. Parameters: (1) internal consistency — the world follows its own rules of physics, society, and history; (2) elaboration — it extends beyond a single scene to include geography, chronology, and multiple inhabitants; (3) deliberate construction — it is built intentionally rather than arising spontaneously in daydream. Persistence mechanism: the paracosm survives through narrative documentation, repeated imaginative engagement, and communication with others who participate in or receive the world. The construct endures as long as the builder maintains and refines it across time — typically over months or years of sustained imaginative labor, and sometimes transmitted across generations through published fiction. [formal: paracosm | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.62]

Improvisation is the human-made concept of creating or performing spontaneously without prior preparation. Parameters: (1) spontaneity — material is generated in the moment of performance or creation; (2) technique — relies on trained skills, conventions, and patterns internalized through practice; (3) domain — applied deliberately across music, theater, dance, comedy, and other performative arts. Persistence mechanism: transmitted through apprenticeship, shared conventions, and cultural practice. [formal: improvisatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Algorithm design is the structured methodology for creating algorithms — systematic step-by-step procedures for problem-solving. It encompasses techniques such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy methods, and backtracking, each providing a reusable pattern for transforming a problem specification into an correct, efficient algorithm. The practice persists through textbooks, courses, and collaborative software engineering, organized by design paradigms and problem classes. [formal: algorithm_design | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.35]

Analepsis is a narrative technique — a structural device by which a story temporarily interrupts its present timeline to recount events that occurred earlier in the narrative's chronological order. The parameters are: (1) temporal displacement backward from a reference point in the narrative, (2) completeness of the recalled sequence (retrospective scenes are not partial), and (3) intentional use as a storytelling strategy rather than accidental chronological confusion. It persists through the mechanisms of literary pedagogy, screenwriting instruction, and the sustained practice of authors and filmmakers who deploy it deliberately. [formal: analepsis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.63]

A reductio ad absurdum is a form of argument that attempts to disprove a proposition by demonstrating that its acceptance entails an absurd, contradictory, or unacceptable conclusion. The argument takes the opponent's claim as a premise, derives consequences through valid inference, and shows that at least one consequence is intolerable — thereby inferring the original claim is false. The parameters that define it are: (1) a target proposition to be refuted, (2) a chain of inference that treats the proposition as true, (3) a consequence that is demonstrably absurd or contradictory, and (4) a negation of the target drawn from the intolerable consequence. It persists through teaching, formal logic systems, mathematical proof practice, and argumentative discourse — transmitted in textbooks, deployed in debate, and codified in the rules of reasoning.

A circumlocution is a linguistic device that expresses an idea through roundabout or indirect wording rather than a direct term or phrase. Parameters: it substitutes a longer, circuitous expression for a concise one; it operates at the level of lexical choice within speech and writing; it persists through language use, stylistic convention, and cultural teaching of indirect expression. [formal: circumlocutio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A paronomasia (pun) is a linguistic device that exploits two meanings of the same word, or similar-sounding words with different meanings, to produce a double reading. Parameters: (1) there must be an acoustic or orthographic overlap — the two words or senses sound or look alike or identical; (2) both meanings are held in suspension simultaneously, producing a moment of semantic tension that resolves into wit, emphasis, or humor; (3) the effect requires the audience to recognize the overlap and entertain both readings at once. Unlike mere ambiguity, a pun is deliberately engineered: the speaker or writer chooses the sound pattern and expects the double interpretation. Persistence mechanism: language use, literary composition, and rhetorical practice — sustained through oral and written transmission, taught as a figure of speech, and reproduced whenever speakers play with homophones, near-homophones, or polysemous words for effect. [formal: paronomasia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diacope is a rhetorical figure consisting of the repetition of a word or short phrase with one or more intervening words or sounds between the repeated elements. Parameters: (1) at least two instances of the same word or phrase must appear; (2) one or more words or sounds must intervene between them; (3) the interrupted repetition serves an emphatic or rhythmic function — the effect relies on the break, not mere adjacency. The intervening material may carry independent meaning, but the figure's identity comes from the structure of interrupted recurrence. Persistence mechanism: the pattern is maintained through linguistic transmission — teaching, citation, and sustained use across texts and speech communities. [formal: diacope | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.64]

Epistrophe is a rhetorical figure in which the same word or phrase is repeated at the end of successive clauses, sentences, or lines. Parameters: (1) at least two successive structural units (clauses, sentences, or lines); (2) identical or near-identical repetition of a word or phrase at the terminal position of each unit; (3) deliberate design for emphasis, rhythm, or persuasive force. Persistence: epistrophe persists through rhetorical pedagogy, literary practice, and the oral-tradition techniques of public speaking — it is a named pattern in the grammar of emphasis, transmitted across generations of rhetoricians and writers. [formal: epistrophe | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An antimetabole is a rhetorical figure in which a phrase or sequence of words is repeated in reverse order, creating parallel structure that highlights contrast or irony. Parameters: (1) at least two words or phrases arranged in a specific sequence, (2) the second clause repeats those same words or phrases in exact reverse order, (3) the reversal produces contrast, irony, or rhetorical emphasis. Persistence mechanism: sustained use in oratory, literature, and everyday speech as a recognized and nameable rhetorical device. [formal: antimetabole | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An apologia is a formal rhetorical defense — a structured speech or text in which the author justifies their own conduct, addresses accusations, and seeks to restore their credibility before an audience. Its parameters are: (1) a known accuser or public charge, (2) a defined audience whose judgment matters, (3) a logical structure that moves from acknowledgment to justification to appeal for mercy or acceptance, and (4) a persuasive register calibrated to the audience's values. It persists through written texts (Cicero's Pro Milone, Thucydides' Pericles' Funeral Oration as paradigm), oral tradition, and the institutional practices of debate, law, and public accountability that require and preserve self-defense. [formal: apologia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.81]

A polemic is a confrontational rhetorical form — a structured argument aimed at refuting or dismantling an opponent's position while advancing an opposing claim. Its parameters are: (1) a specific opposing thesis or position that serves as the target, (2) a clear alternative position that the polemicist advances, (3) a persuasive register calibrated to persuade a third-party audience (readers, voters, judges, the public) rather than to convert the opponent, and (4) a strategic use of evidence, logic, and rhetorical force to expose weaknesses in the target position. It persists through written treatises, public debates, journalistic op-eds, legal briefs, and the institutional traditions of intellectual contestation — from Plato's dialogues to modern political discourse. [formal: polemic | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.82]

An antonomasia is a figure of speech in which (1) a proper name is substituted for a common noun — e.g. 'a Xerxes' for a tyrant, or (2) a descriptive epithet replaces a proper name — e.g. 'the Bard' for Shakespeare. Its parameters are: (a) an established cultural association between name and referent, (b) a linguistic community that recognizes the substitution, (c) a conventionalized pairing that has moved beyond ad hoc usage into shared vocabulary. It persists through literary tradition, education, and everyday idiomatic use. [formal: antonomasia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A category of false or misleading communication, distinguished by the creator-s intent to deceive. Its parameters are: (1) the content is false or misleading, (2) it is produced by human agents, (3) there exists deliberate intent to cause receivers to believe something false. It persists through deliberate reproduction via media channels, social networks, and coordinated campaigns. [formal: disinformation | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.1]

Antiphrasis is a rhetorical figure of speech in which a word or phrase is used in a sense opposite to its literal or conventional meaning. The device operates by semantic inversion: the speaker selects a term whose dictionary definition directly contradicts the intended sense, relying on contextual cues and shared knowledge to signal the reversal. Persistence mechanism: antiphrasis survives through linguistic convention — it is codified in rhetorical handbooks, taught as a recognized device, and sustained by the ongoing practice of speakers who deploy it for ironic, humorous, or emphatic effect. Its boundaries are delimited by the contrast between surface literal meaning and contextually recovered opposite meaning; without that contrast, the device ceases to operate. [formal: antiphrasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A paraprosdokian is a rhetorical figure in which the second part of a phrase or sentence is unexpected, forcing the listener to reinterpret the first part. The device operates by setting up an initial expectation and then subverting it through a surprising continuation, causing the entire utterance to take on a new meaning. It persists through literary tradition, comedy routines, and rhetorical training — taught in speech classes and preserved in collections of figures of speech. [formal: paraprosdokian | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diatribe is a forceful, bitter verbal attack directed against a person, institution, or idea. It carves a distinct rhetorical genre from simple criticism by its sustained hostility, generalized accusations, and performative intensity — the speaker does not merely disagree but denounces. It persists through oral delivery, written pamphlets, and scripted performance, maintained by the social practice of public censure. [formal: diatribē | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An antanaclasis is a rhetorical figure in which a word or phrase is repeated, each occurrence bearing a distinct meaning. The device carves itself by lexical doubling with semantic shift — the same surface form, two different senses, the pivot between them generating the effect. It persists through oral and written discourse, maintained by the practice of stylistic variation and punning. [formal: antanaklasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Paralepsis is a rhetorical device in which a speaker or writer claims to omit or pass over a particular point, yet simultaneously draws the audience's attention to it by raising it. The device carves itself by the tension between stated omission and actual mention — the speaker says they will not discuss something while making sure the audience thinks about it. This distinguishes it from the related figure of apophasis, where the emphasis is on raising a topic through denial of raising it. Paralepsis persists through rhetorical training, pedagogical instruction, and its continued use in legal defense and political argument. [formal: paralipsis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Bathos is a rhetorical and literary device marked by an abrupt, often unintentional fall from an elevated or serious tone to a commonplace, trivial, or absurd subject. It carves itself by the quality of the tonal descent — the distance between the register established and the register landed in, and the suddenness of the shift. When the fall is deliberate it becomes parody or satire; bathos is distinguished by its failure to control the descent. It persists in literary practice and criticism as a named pattern of compositional misfire, sustained by the conventions of tonal expectation. [formal: bathos | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Vituperation is the practice of harsh verbal abuse or scathing criticism directed at a person or group. It carves itself by its target (a specific addressee), its mode (insults, condemnation, vitiation of reputation through language), and its intent (to damage, degrade, or punish via public censure). It persists through rhetorical education (progymnasmata treated it as an exercise), legal tradition (defamation law channels it into institutional form), and everyday discourse where it operates as the weaponized use of language to destroy standing. [formal: vituperatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Anadiplosis is a rhetorical figure in which the last word (or words) of one clause, sentence, or line is repeated at the beginning of the following clause, sentence, or line. It carves itself by its structural pattern (terminal repetition producing a chain-link effect), its scope (intra-textual, requiring at least two adjacent units), and its function (building intensity, creating emphasis through recursive looping, forging causal or associative chains). It persists through teaching (a standard figure in rhetorical handbooks from antiquity through the Renaissance), literary practice (used deliberately by poets and orators), and popular discourse (proverbs, sermons, political speeches exploit its hypnotic cadence). [formal: anadiplosis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Epanalepsis is a rhetorical figure in which the same word or short phrase serves as both the opener and the closer of a single clause or sentence, with other words intervening between the two repetitions. It carves itself by its structural pattern: [Word X] ... [Word X], where X is identical at both boundaries of the same syntactic unit. The persistence mechanism is the written and spoken tradition of rhetoric — taught, catalogued, and deployed deliberately by writers and speakers. The figure depends on the listener's recognition of the return to the opening term, creating a circular emphasis that closes back on itself. [formal: epanalepsis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A chreia is a brief, self-contained anecdote or remark about a person — typically a saying, deed, or witticism attributed to a named figure — memorized and recited as a rhetorical exercise. It carves itself by four parameters: (1) it is short enough to commit to memory in full; (2) it concerns a specific person (not a generic type); (3) it presents a single action, utterance, or response; (4) it conveys a moral point, character insight, or instructive lesson. Its persistence mechanism is the schoolroom tradition of progymnasmata, where students memorized, paraphrased, expanded, and adapted chreiai as foundational exercises in rhetoric and composition, passing them through oral recitation and written commentary across generations. [formal: chreia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Hyperbaton is a rhetorical figure in which the normal or expected word order of a sentence is deliberately disrupted — words that would conventionally be adjacent are separated, and words that would normally follow one another are rearranged. It carves itself by four parameters: (1) the rearrangement departs from the syntactic norms of the language in question; (2) the departure is intentional, not the result of error or disfluency; (3) the displaced words remain grammatically and semantically connected despite their separation; (4) the effect is to produce emphasis, poetic texture, or cognitive reordering. Its persistence mechanism is the transmission through rhetorical handbooks, grammatical treatises, and literary criticism — where hyperbaton is named, exemplified, and taught as a figure of distemper (figura distantiæ), preserved in the shared vocabulary of writers, teachers, and critics. [formal: hyperbaton | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

Epizeuxis is a figure of speech in which a word or short phrase is repeated immediately and without interruption for emphasis — the same lexical item appears consecutively, as in 'fire fire!' or 'no no no.' Its parameters are: (1) immediate adjacency with no intervening words, (2) identical lexical form (not merely synonymous), and (3) pragmatic intent to amplify force, urgency, or emotional intensity. It persists through spoken performance and written citation of dialogue, taught as a named technique in rhetoric and grammar curricula, and preserved in lists of figures across languages and periods.
[formal: epizeuxis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Palilogy is a figure of speech consisting of the excessive and deliberate repetition of a word or phrase beyond what is necessary for simple emphasis, used to convey urgency, insistence, or emotional overwhelm — as in 'that that that that boy wrote.' Its parameters are: (1) repetition of the same lexical item or phrase multiple times (typically three or more), (2) intentional excess (the repetition exceeds bare emphasis, crossing into insistence or obsession), and (3) pragmatic force that amplifies through accumulation rather than immediate adjacency. It persists through oral performance, literary citation, and pedagogical treatment in rhetoric and stylistics, catalogued across traditions of figures of speech.
[formal: palilogia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Prosopopoeia is a rhetorical figure in which the speaker gives voice to an absent, abstract, or non-human entity — attributing speech, agency, or personhood to something that lacks a living human voice. It operates by constructing a fictional persona (e.g. 'Liberty demands,' 'The grave cries out,' 'France pleads') and delivering speech through that constructed voice. Its parameters are: (1) the target lacks a living human voice (abstract, absent, deceased, or non-human), (2) the speaker actively constructs and delivers speech as that target, and (3) the purpose is rhetorical persuasion through imagined testimony. [formal: prosopopoeia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A category mistake is a logical error in which a concept, entity, or property is assigned to an incompatible logical type or category, yielding a statement that is syntactically well-formed but semantically nonsensical. The mistake arises from treating a concept as belonging to one categorical framework when it properly belongs to another — for example, asking what color a number is, or treating the mind as a 'thing' inside the body rather than as a pattern of dispositions and capacities. Parameters: (1) a statement must combine terms from incommensurable categories; (2) the resulting expression must be grammatically valid yet fail to pick out any possible state of affairs; (3) the error is exposed by reclassifying the misassigned term under its proper categorical framework. Persists through language, teaching in philosophy and analytic logic, and sustained use as a diagnostic tool in argument analysis and conceptual clarification. [formal: category-mistake | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.49]

Ekphrasis is a rhetorical device that renders a visual artwork — painting, sculpture, photograph — into vivid verbal description so that the depicted scene appears alive before the reader. Its parameters: (1) the source is a visual artefact, (2) the description is intensely visual and sensory, (3) the purpose is rhetorical — to produce vividness (enargeia) and emotional impact. It persists through literary convention, classroom teaching, and the written record of art criticism. [formal: ekphrasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

Path-dependence is a concept in institutional economics and complexity theory describing how prior decisions and events constrain future possibilities. Its parameters: (1) an initial choice or event sets a trajectory, (2) increasing returns or switching costs make deviation increasingly expensive over time, (3) the resulting path persists even if suboptimal compared to alternatives. The mechanism of persistence is lock-in through accumulated investment, expectation formation, and coordinated adaptation. [formal: path-dependent | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Techne is a human-made conceptual category for systematic knowledge of how to make things, distinguished from theoretical or contemplative knowledge. It encompasses craft, art, and technique — not the raw act of making, but the knowable, teachable, and repeatable principles that govern skilled production. Originating in ancient Greek philosophy (where it was contrasted with episteme, or theoretical knowledge), techne has persisted as a conceptual framework through Western thought in aesthetics, craft theory, design, and the philosophy of technology. Its parameters: (1) it is knowledge of production, not action or contemplation; (2) it is systematic and teachable, not purely intuitive; (3) it aims at an external product or outcome. Techne persists through language (the vocabulary of craft and technique), teaching (apprenticeship and formal instruction), and disciplines (philosophy of art, design theory, craft studies). [formal: techne | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A touchstone is a physical reference specimen — originally a dark siliceous stone (basanite) — against which samples of precious metal are rubbed to produce a streak whose color is compared with streaks from standards of known purity, thereby determining the metal's alloy composition. The concept persists through two mechanisms: (1) the literal practice of assaying in metallurgy and jewelry, governed by standardized test procedures and institutional calibration; and (2) the metaphorical extension, where any established benchmark or accepted criterion serves as a touchstone for evaluating non-metallic things — arguments, art, standards, relationships. Parameters: (a) the original sense requires a physical stone of appropriate hardness and texture, a sample of unknown purity, and comparison standards of known composition; (b) the metaphorical sense requires an established benchmark recognized by a community of judges. [formal: touchstone | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A social-norm is a shared, emergent expectation about appropriate behavior within a group or community, enforced through informal social pressure — approval, disapproval, ridicule, or exclusion — rather than formal legal authority. Parameters: (1) it arises spontaneously from repeated collective practice, not from top-down decree; (2) its enforcement is informal and distributed among members, not delegated to a专职 body; (3) its content and strictness vary across cultures, subcultures, and historical periods. The mechanism of persistence is internalization (members come to feel the expectation as their own) reinforced by peer enforcement (others signal approval or sanction). Social-norms range from trivial conventions (greeting customs, dress codes) to moral weight-bearing rules (mores), all bound by the same informal-enforcement structure. [formal: socialis norma | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: no | epoch: 0.01]

Engagement-metrics are quantified indicators — counts, rates, or ratios — that measure the level of sustained interaction, attention, or involvement that users or audiences have with content, a brand, a product, or a platform. Parameters: (1) they are designed to capture ongoing, repeat interaction (not one-off exposure); (2) they are computed from observable data — clicks, watches, comments, shares, session duration — aggregated into scores or KPIs; (3) they serve as optimization targets for platform algorithms and content strategies. The persistence mechanism is institutionalized measurement: dashboards, reporting cycles, and algorithmic feedback loops that internalize these metrics into production and distribution decisions. Engagement-metrics differ from vanity metrics (raw view counts) by emphasizing depth and recurrence of interaction. [formal: mensurae engagementis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Tact is a learned social skill: the capacity to judge what to say or do in a delicate situation so as to avoid offense and maintain social harmony. Its parameters are (1) situational awareness — reading the social context, the parties involved, and the stakes of the interaction; (2) restraint — withholding what is true or sharp in favor of what is appropriate; (3) timing — choosing the right moment and manner for expression. It persists through socialization, cultural transmission, modeling by others, and the positive/negative feedback of interpersonal relationships. Tact is not deception or dishonesty; it is the calibrated expression of truth within the constraints of social obligation. [formal: tactus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A garden-path is a psycholinguistic phenomenon wherein a sentence's early syntactic structure strongly invites one parse, and later words contradict that parse, forcing the reader or listener to abandon the initial analysis and reanalyse from the point of ambiguity. The concept applies at three levels: (1) lexical ambiguity (e.g. 'The horse raced past the barn fell' — 'raced' initially read as main verb), (2) structural ambiguity (e.g. 'While Mary eaten the cake...' — 'eaten' initially read as main verb), and (3) phrase-level ambiguity (e.g. prepositional-phrase attachment). It persists as a theoretical construct in linguistics, experimental psychology, and natural-language processing, sustained through corpus studies, acceptability-judgment tasks, reading-time measurements, and computational parser benchmarks. The phenomenon is not in the text but in the interaction between text structure and human parsing strategy. [formal: garden-path effect | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Interpellation is the process by which ideology addresses or hails individuals, transforming them into subjects who recognize themselves in that address. Parameters: (1) an address or call from an ideological apparatus (state, media, education, family); (2) the individual's recognition of the address as directed at them; (3) the resulting subject-position that organizes their perception and action. Persistence mechanism: linguistic reproduction through discourse, institutional teaching, and the everyday practices of critical theory and philosophy. Interpellation explains how power operates not through force alone but through the very structure of self-recognition — we become subjects by answering the call ideology places before us. [formal: interpellatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A frame-of-reference is a human-made conceptual framework that establishes the coordinate system, standards, or vantage point from which observations, measurements, and interpretations are made. Parameters: (1) a set of reference points or axes (spatial, temporal, conceptual, or normative); (2) a position or standpoint relative to those reference points; (3) a function that maps observations from one frame to another. The persistence mechanism is codification through notation, mathematical formalism, disciplinary pedagogy, and cross-cultural transmission — frames persist as long as the practices that maintain them persist. [formal: frame-of-reference | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An antinomy is a structural contradiction in which two principles or propositions, each seemingly valid by accepted reasoning, yield mutually exclusive conclusions. The concept arises when reason turns against itself, producing irreconcilable pairs of claims. It serves as a diagnostic tool in philosophy and logic for exposing the boundaries and limits of conceptual systems. [formal: antinomia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A rhetorical-figure is a classificatory concept invented by rhetoricians to name and categorize patterns of language that systematically depart from ordinary usage in order to produce a specific communicative or persuasive effect. The concept carves a taxonomy of identifiable structural devices — metaphor, irony, understatement, hyperbole, and others — each defined by the particular effect it generates in an audience. The concept persists through teaching in rhetoric and literary studies, through naming in grammars and style guides, and through the sustained practice of analyzing texts for their figured language. [formal: figura rhetoric | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Disambiguation is the process of resolving ambiguity in language, data, symbols, or references by determining which specific meaning is intended in a given context. It operates through contextual analysis, statistical inference, or explicit marking to establish a single interpretation from multiple possible readings. The mechanism of persistence lies in its embedding within conventions of usage, algorithms of parsing, and practices of editing that speakers, writers, and systems deploy to prevent confusion and ensure successful communication. [formal: disambiguatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An interpretive framework is a structured set of concepts, categories, and assumptions that guides the interpretation of data, phenomena, or experiences. It provides a systematic lens through which raw observations are organized into meaningful patterns. The framework operates through deliberate application: its components are selected, deployed, and refined by practitioners who share interpretive goals. Parameters include its domain of application, its constitutive categories, its methodological rules, and its boundary conditions. It persists through explicit codification — written documentation, pedagogical transmission, and institutional adoption — ensuring that the interpretive stance can be reproduced across time and practitioners. [formal: framework interpretativum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Anticipation is the human-made capacity to project awareness beyond the present moment, constructing mental models of what may come and using those models to guide current action. It operates through three mechanisms: (1) temporal projection — extending the now-future boundary of conscious awareness; (2) scenario simulation — generating plausible futures from present data; and (3) preparatory action — modifying present behavior based on those simulations. Unlike mere prediction, anticipation embeds emotional and motivational valence: it is not a neutral forecast but a felt orientation toward coming states. The construct persists through language (tense systems, conditional mood), ritual (ceremonies that mark expected events), and teaching (training for contingencies). [formal: anticipatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Equifinality is the principle that open systems can reach the same final state from different initial conditions and via different paths. Formulated by Ludwig von Bertalanffy within general systems theory, it distinguishes open systems (which exhibit equifinality) from closed systems (which follow unique trajectories determined by initial conditions). The principle applies across domains: in psychology, multiple developmental pathways lead to the same outcome; in ecology, different disturbances yield similar community states; in management, varied strategies achieve identical organizational goals. Its persistence mechanism is academic discourse, textbook citation, and cross-disciplinary application. [formal: equifinality | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

A digest is a condensed, structured presentation of information selected from a larger body of content, produced through human editorial judgment. Its parameters: (1) selection — items are chosen by a compiler for relevance or interest, not exhaustively collected; (2) condensation — each item is shortened, paraphrased, or abstracted from its source; (3) organization — items are arranged in a coherent order (thematic, chronological, alphabetical); (4) self-containment — a reader can understand the content without consulting the original sources. The persistence mechanism is editorial compilation recorded in written texts, oral recitation, or digital media — the construct exists only through repeated human acts of selection and reorganization. It differs from a compendium (which aims at comprehensiveness rather than condensation) and from a synopsis (which traces the narrative arc of a single work rather than surveying multiple sources). [formal: digestum | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A specification is a human-made artifact that precisely delineates requirements, constraints, or design criteria for the construction of a system, product, or document. Its parameters are: (1) scope — the bounded domain of what must and need not be satisfied; (2) constraints — explicit limits on form, function, materials, or behavior; (3) acceptance criteria — objective conditions against which compliance is measured. Specifications persist through codification in written documents, diagrams, or machine-readable formats and endure across development cycles as the authoritative reference that all parties must reconcile with. [formal: specificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Reliability is the concept of consistent performance under stated conditions across time and repetitions. Root-cause-analysis is the human-made systematic method for identifying the fundamental cause of a problem or failure by tracing observable effects backward through chains of contributing factors. It is defined by four parameters: (1) effect — the observable failure or problem to be explained; (2) causal-chain — ordered sequence of contributing factors linking effect to root cause; (3) technique — the structured method used (five-whys, fishbone/Ishikawa diagram, or fault-tree analysis); (4) termination — the point at which further tracing yields no actionable contributing factor. Persistence mechanism: documented procedure codified in standard operating protocols and quality-management systems. [formal: analysis-causae-fundamentalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Decision-analysis is the human-made systematic method for evaluating alternatives by quantifying their attributes, risks, and consequences against weighted criteria. It is defined by four parameters: (1) evaluation procedure — a structured process for comparing each alternative across a common set of criteria; (2) weighting mechanism — assignment of relative importance values to criteria reflecting their differential relevance to the decision at hand; (3) uncertainty modeling — representation of probability distributions, confidence intervals, or scenario ranges for outcomes whose values are not known with certainty; (4) aggregation function — a mathematical or logical rule that combines the weighted, uncertainty-bearing evaluations into a ranked ordering or decision recommendation. It persists through documented procedures, templates, and trained practitioners. [formal: analysis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Fault-tree is the human-made systematic method for identifying causes of a system failure by constructing a top-down logical tree. It is defined by four parameters: (1) a top event representing the system failure to be analyzed, (2) Boolean logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) that combine events at each node, (3) basic events representing root-level component failures, and (4) the tree structure mapping all causal paths from top event to basic events. Persistence: engineering practice, safety standards, and technical teaching. [formal: arbor vitiorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Error-handling is the human-made systematic approach to detecting, responding to, and recovering from errors or exceptions in a system. It is defined by four parameters: (1) error detection — the mechanisms that identify when an error has occurred (monitoring, exception throwing, status codes); (2) response protocol — the predetermined actions taken upon error detection (logging, alerting, fallback execution); (3) recovery strategy — the methods for restoring normal operation (retry, rollback, graceful degradation); (4) learning loop — the analysis of error patterns to prevent recurrence. The persistence mechanism is institutionalized practice: documented procedures, implemented handlers, and trained operators that encode failure response into the system's architecture and culture. [formal: error-handling | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Survivorship-bias is the human-made cognitive error of drawing conclusions from a visible set of successes while the unseen set of failures is systematically excluded from analysis. It is defined by three parameters: (1) selection filter — a process that allows only some entities through while eliminating others; (2) visibility asymmetry — the survivors are observed and studied while the eliminated entities are invisible or under-studied; (3) inferential error — conclusions are drawn as if the visible set were representative of the full population. Persistence mechanism: taught in statistical education, business case-study methodology, and cognitive psychology training. [formal: bias cognitio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Post-mortem is the human-made practice of conducting a structured review after a project, event, or process has concluded, examining outcomes against expectations to extract lessons. It is defined by four parameters: (1) retrospection — looking backward at what actually happened; (2) comparison — measuring outcomes against the original plan, requirements, or hypothesis; (3) cause identification — determining why things succeeded or failed; (4) action extraction — producing concrete changes for future work. It persists through written records, organizational routines, and shared practice. [formal: post-mortem | substrate: behavior | horizon: a project | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A threat-model is a human-made structured representation of the potential threats targeting a system — capturing assets, vulnerabilities, threat actors, capabilities, motivations, and the attack paths that connect them. It is defined by four parameters: (1) scope — the system boundary and assets under analysis; (2) threat taxonomy — the categories of threat actors and their capabilities; (3) vulnerability mapping — the weaknesses that could be exploited; (4) attack scenarios — the plausible sequences through which an actor could reach a valuable asset. The threat-model persists through documentation (diagrams, attack trees, STRIDE lists), institutional knowledge in security teams, and integration into threat-assessment workflows. [formal: modellum periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Risk-analysis is the human-made practice of systematically evaluating identified risks to determine their likelihood, impact, and priority for decision-making about risk responses. It is defined by four parameters: (1) the set of identified risks from a risk register or threat-model, (2) likelihood assessment using qualitative or quantitative methods, (3) impact assessment across relevant dimensions (financial, operational, reputational), and (4) prioritization through risk matrices or scoring systems. It persists through documented analysis frameworks, risk registers, and institutional memory of past risk evaluations and their outcomes. [formal: riskus-analyis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A risk register is a living document that records identified risks, their analysis (likelihood, impact, severity), assigned owners, and planned response strategies. It persists through structured documentation — a named, organized artifact maintained by project governance to centralize risk information for monitoring and decision-making. Its parameters are: (1) a catalog of discrete risk items each with a description and metadata, (2) quantified or qualitative assessment of each risk, (3) response plans (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept), and (4) an update cycle tied to the project lifecycle. The mechanism of persistence is the documented artifact itself, backed by version control or change tracking in a project management system.\n\n[formal: tabula rationum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A programming language feature that separates normal control flow from error-handling flow. It works by throwing an exception object when an error occurs, and catching it in a handler block that specifies recovery or cleanup actions. Parameters: (1) throw/raise mechanism to signal anomalous conditions, (2) catch/try block to intercept and handle, (3) finally block for mandatory cleanup, (4) optional else block for non-error paths. Persists through language syntax, compiler/interpreter support, and programmer convention in software systems. [formal: exceptio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An error-boundary is a design boundary that separates a system component from its environment such that failures occurring outside the boundary cannot propagate across it. Parameters: (1) containment — errors on one side are intercepted and do not cross to the other side; (2) fallback — when a failure is contained, a degraded or alternative state is maintained on the protected side; (3) visibility — the boundary reports errors across itself for monitoring without allowing them to cross. It persists through code conventions, architectural documentation, and implementation in frameworks (e.g., try-catch blocks, circuit breakers, compartmentalization patterns). [formal: terminatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A corrective-action is a planned organizational intervention that eliminates the root cause of a detected nonconformity or failure to prevent recurrence. Parameters: (1) cause-elimination — targets the fundamental cause, not the symptom; (2) prevention — designed to stop the failure from recurring; (3) documentation — recorded in corrective action reports or CARs; (4) verification — effectiveness must be confirmed after implementation. Persistence mechanism: documented procedures, quality standards (ISO 9001 clause 10.2), and organizational routines that institutionalize the practice across generations of engineers and managers. [formal: correctiva | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A lessons-learned is the institutional practice of systematically capturing knowledge from completed projects, events, or processes and making it available for future decision-making. Parameters: (1) retrospection — structured review of what happened, (2) documentation — written record of insights, failures, and successes, (3) dissemination — distribution to relevant stakeholders for future use. Persistence mechanism: organizational memory systems, institutional rituals of post-project review, and knowledge management infrastructure that encode tacit experience into explicit form available across project boundaries and organizational time. [formal: lessons-learned | substrate: mind | horizon: a project | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A failure-mode-analysis is a systematic engineering methodology for cataloguing every possible way a system, component, or process can fail, assessing the consequences of each failure mode, and prioritising mitigation or correction. Parameters: (1) exhaustive enumeration of failure modes per component or step, (2) effect severity ranking, (3) occurrence likelihood, (4) detectability of each mode before it causes harm, (5) prioritisation by risk-priority-number. Persistence: the FMEA report is a living document maintained in engineering quality systems and updated whenever design, process, or operational conditions change. [formal: formalisatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A retrospective is a structured group practice conducted after a completed project, sprint, or defined episode, where participants reflect on events to identify what worked, what did not, and what to change in future iterations. Parameters: (1) bounded time frame (a sprint, project phase, or episode); (2) structured facilitation with rounds of observation and analysis; (3) output of concrete action items. Persistence mechanism: recurring organizational ritual maintained through scheduled meetings, documented lessons, and institutional practice that outlives any single session. [formal: retrospective | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

A safety-case is a structured argument, supported by evidence, that a system or component is sufficiently safe for a given application in a given environment. It carves the concept by specifying: (1) a claim hierarchy decomposing safety assertions into sub-claims, (2) evidence items (test results, analyses, operational data) supporting each sub-claim, and (3) an inference scheme (typically goal structuring) connecting evidence to claims. It persists through documented argumentation artifacts, version-controlled evidence repositories, and periodic re-assessment against changing operational contexts. The safety-case is the institutional mechanism by which complex systems demonstrate — rather than merely claim — their safety properties. [formal: casus salutis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Reliability-engineering is the systematic methodology for ensuring that systems perform their intended functions without failure under stated conditions for a stated period. It carves the concept by specifying: (1) quantitative reliability targets (failure rates, mean time between failures, availability percentages), (2) failure analysis methods (FMEA, fault-tree analysis, failure-mode-effects-and-criticality analysis), (3) design strategies (redundancy, fault tolerance, derating, graceful degradation), and (4) continuous improvement through failure data collection and analysis. It persists through engineering standards (ISO 26262, IEC 61508, MIL-HDBK-338), professional certification bodies, institutionalized failure databases, and sustained practice across aerospace, automotive, nuclear, and software industries. [formal: relabilitas-engenia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.34]

A hazard is a human-made conceptual category denoting a potential source of harm or adverse condition capable of causing injury, illness, property damage, environmental harm, or other undesirable outcomes. It is carved by three parameters: (1) the hazard type (physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychosocial), (2) the exposure pathway by which the hazard can reach a receptor, and (3) the severity-consequence spectrum. Hazards persist through standardized classification taxonomies (e.g., OSHA hazard categories, GHS pictograms), safety data sheets, and regulatory frameworks that codify and disseminate hazard recognition across professions. [formal: hazardia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Fault-tree-analysis is a human-made analytical method for systematically deducing the combinations of component failures and events that can cause a specified top-level system failure. It is carved by: (1) a boolean logic tree structure with the top event at the root, intermediate events connected by logic gates (AND, OR), and basic events at the leaves; (2) the deductive direction from failure to causes; (3) qualitative minimal-cut-set extraction and, optionally, quantitative probability computation. It persists through safety and reliability standards (e.g. IEC 61025, MIL-HDBK-338), engineering documentation practices, and risk-assessment frameworks. [formal: fault tree analysis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.47]

Safety-culture is a human-made organizational construct comprising shared values, beliefs, and behavioral norms regarding the priority and management of safety within a group, workplace, or institution. It is carved by: (1) shared cognitive commitment to safety as a core value (not merely compliance), (2) observable behavioral patterns in reporting, risk assessment, and protocol adherence, (3) institutional mechanisms reinforcing safety priorities (training, leadership signaling, reward structures). It persists through socialization, leadership modeling, institutional training, and regulatory pressure. [formal: cultura securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

hazard-analysis is a human-made analytical procedure that identifies, evaluates, and documents potential hazards in a system, process, or environment. It is carved by: (1) systematic identification of hazard sources (physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychological), (2) risk characterization that combines severity and likelihood, (3) prioritization that orders interventions by expected harm reduction, and (4) documentation that produces actionable outputs for risk management. It persists through safety standards (ISO 31000, IEC 60300), regulatory frameworks, and the institutional memory of safety engineering practice. [formal: hazardum analytum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

fault-tolerance is a human-made engineering property describing system designs that continue operating — possibly degraded — when one or more components fail. It is carved by: (1) the presence of failure-resilient design (redundancy, isolation, graceful degradation), (2) defined acceptable degradation levels (full operation, degraded mode, safe shutdown), and (3) a persistence mechanism through engineering specifications, safety certification standards, and operational procedures in critical systems. [formal: tolerantia vitii | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

audit-trail is a human-made record-keeping construct that produces a sequential, tamper-evident chronology of actions, decisions, and state transitions for later verification. It is carved by: (1) sequential ordering of entries with immutable timestamps, (2) tamper-evidence through cryptographic hashing or physical sealing, (3) coverage of defined action types (who did what, when, and under what authority), and (4) retention policies tied to compliance or legal requirements. It persists through audit-log software, compliance management systems, and regulatory audit frameworks. [formal: auditum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

bow-tie-analysis is a human-made risk assessment methodology that visualizes accident pathways in a bow-tie diagram. It is carved by: (1) a central top-event representing the hazard state, (2) causal pathways on the left branching from potential initiating causes to the top event, (3) consequence pathways on the right branching from the top event to final outcomes, and (4) barriers mapped on both sides — preventive barriers on the left between causes and the top event, and mitigative barriers on the right between the top event and consequences. The persistence mechanism is documentation within safety management systems, regulated by industry standards (e.g., ISO 31000, OSHA process safety guidelines) and maintained through formal safety review cycles. [formal: la | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

risk-management is a human-made institutional practice that systematically identifies, assesses, and controls hazards and uncertainties in organizational operations. It is carved by: (1) a structured process for hazard identification (systematic scanning for sources of harm), (2) risk assessment (evaluating likelihood and severity of identified hazards), (3) risk control (implementing barriers and safeguards to reduce risk to acceptable levels), and (4) monitoring and review (continuously tracking risk status and control effectiveness). It persists through documented procedures, organizational roles, and compliance frameworks that embed risk-conscious decision-making into daily operations. [formal: ratio_periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

defensive-depth is a human-made security architecture that layers multiple independent controls so the failure of any single one does not compromise the protected asset. It is carved by: (1) heterogeneous barriers (different mechanisms, not redundant copies of the same), (2) independence (failure of one layer does not impair others), (3) progression resistance (an attacker must defeat each layer sequentially, increasing detection probability and effort), and (4) coverage gaps (deliberately overlapping zones of control to eliminate blind spots). It persists through design standards, security policies, and implementation practices that mandate layered protection in system architecture. [formal: defensiopluralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

failure-mode-and-effects-analysis is a human-made systematic risk-assessment procedure that enumerates potential failure modes within a system or process, determines their causes and downstream effects, and ranks them by severity, occurrence frequency, and detectability to prioritize preventive measures. It is carved by: (1) a structured enumeration of failure modes at the component or process-step level, (2) causal analysis tracing each mode to its origin, (3) effect analysis mapping each mode to its impact on system function, and (4) a risk-priority scoring system (severity x occurrence x detectability) that orders interventions. It persists through documented FMEA worksheets, standardized checklists, and institutionalized review cycles in engineering and operations practice. [formal: fma | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

event-tree-analysis is a human-made systematic risk-assessment procedure that begins with an identified initiating event and traces forward through a sequence of possible events, using binary branches (success or failure of each safety function) to map all possible outcome scenarios and their probabilities. It is carved by: (1) an identified initiating event that triggers the analysis; (2) a sequence of safety functions or system responses that can succeed or fail; (3) binary branching at each event to model all possible outcome paths; (4) calculation of outcome probabilities by multiplying branch probabilities along each path. [formal: eventus tractatus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hierarchy-of-controls is a risk-assessment framework that ranks safety interventions by effectiveness: (1) elimination of the hazard entirely, (2) substitution with a less hazardous alternative, (3) engineering controls that isolate people from the hazard, (4) administrative controls that change the way people work, and (5) personal protective equipment that protects the worker. It persists through occupational health and safety standards (e.g. OSHA, ISO 45001), regulatory frameworks, safety management systems, and institutional training. [formal: hierarchy-of-controls | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.91]

Safety-engineering is a human-made discipline that systematically applies engineering principles to identify, assess, and mitigate hazards in complex systems. It operates through structured methodologies — including hazard identification, risk assessment, failure analysis, and control design — to reduce the probability and consequence of accidents. The practice persists through institutional frameworks, standards bodies, regulatory requirements, and professional certification. Its scope spans industrial safety, product safety, process safety, and system safety, unified by the principle that hazards can be predicted, quantified, and controlled before harm occurs. [formal: ingenium tutelae | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-analysis is a human-made systematic process for identifying hazards, evaluating risks, and determining appropriate controls in technical, industrial, and organizational systems. It operates through structured methodologies — including checklist-based reviews, systematic hazard identification (HAZID), and risk assessment matrices — and persists through documented procedures, regulatory frameworks, and professional safety practice. [formal: systematic-risk-evaluation | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An inference-engine is a human-made computational system that applies formal reasoning rules to derive conclusions from a structured knowledge base. Its parameters are: (1) a rule set encoding inference patterns (deductive, inductive, or abductive); (2) a knowledge base of asserted facts or propositions; and (3) a control strategy that determines the order and selection of rule applications. It persists through programmable implementations — production systems, rule engines, and automated theorem provers — that execute reasoning cycles to produce new derived facts. [formal: inferentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A formalized practice of systematic hazard detection: the structured process by which teams or individuals identify, catalog, and record potential sources of harm before they materialize. It operates through defined methods — hazard checklists, design reviews, job safety analysis, brainstorming sessions, and inspection protocols — and persists through documentation standards, regulatory frameworks, and institutional knowledge within organizations. Its parameters include: (1) the domain of application (workplace, product, process, environment), (2) the depth of scanning (surface-level screening vs. deep-systematic analysis), and (3) the formality of documentation (informal observation vs. structured registry). The persistence mechanism is institutional: records, checklists, and procedures that survive individual practitioners and are transmitted across generations of practitioners through training and regulation. [formal: notatio_periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Scenario-analysis is a structured technique for exploring alternative futures by constructing coherent, plausible narratives about how key variables could evolve under different conditions. It operates through a defined sequence: (1) identifying the focal question and scope, (2) enumerating critical uncertainties that could reshape the future, (3) building internally consistent scenario narratives that combine key uncertainties in different configurations, (4) analyzing the implications of each scenario for decisions at hand, and (5) stress-testing strategies against multiple scenarios to find robust or adaptive options. The method persists through documented scenario narratives, decision frameworks, and organizational learning processes. It is distinguished from prediction by embracing irreducible uncertainty rather than attempting to forecast a single outcome. [formal: scenario-analysis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A fishbone diagram (also called an Ishikawa or cause-and-effect diagram) is a structured visual tool for cause analysis: it maps the possible causes of a specific problem or effect along branching categories arranged in a skeletal layout resembling a fish skeleton, with the effect at the head and cause categories as the main bones, each further subdivided into sub-causes. It persists as a discipline artifact — taught in quality management and reliability engineering, reproduced in standard templates, and sustained through organizational practice. [formal: causa-effectus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.49]

A structured analytical method for systematically identifying the underlying origins of problems or failures, as distinguished from managing symptoms. It proceeds by collecting evidence, mapping causal relationships, and iteratively probing why-questions to trace effects back to root causes. Parameters: (1) systematic evidence collection, (2) causal relationship mapping, (3) iterative root-cause probing, (4) distinction between cause identification and corrective action. [formal: causae-analyisis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.27]

A topographic map is a scaled graphical representation that encodes terrain elevation and surface features using a defined symbol set: contour lines connecting equal-elevation points, spot elevations at measured locations, and standardized symbols for hydrography, vegetation, and cultural features. It persists through cartographic standards (e.g. USGS 7.5-minute series specifications), surveying instrumentation data pipelines, and published map editions. The map's construction follows explicit projection rules and coordinate reference systems that ensure geometric fidelity between the depicted terrain and its ground truth. [formal: topographica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

A control chart is a statistical process control tool that plots time-ordered data points against a central line (process mean) and two control limits (typically ±3 standard deviations) to distinguish common-cause variation from assignable-cause variation. Its parameters are: (1) a sequence of measurements sampled at regular intervals, (2) a calculated process mean as the center line, (3) upper and lower control limits derived from process variability estimates, and (4) rule-based signals (Western Electric, Nelson rules) that flag out-of-control conditions. It persists through standardized SPC chart templates, quality-management software, and the pedagogical transmission of statistical process control methodology. [formal: control-chart | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Traceability is the capability to reconstruct the history, application, location, or transformation of an item, process, or decision through a connected chain of documented records. Its parameters are: (1) tracee — the entity being tracked (material, component, decision, or action); (2) trace-path — the sequence of recorded transitions linking origins to current state; (3) anchor points — discrete record entries (timestamps, signatures, location data) that make the path verifiable. Persistence mechanism: maintained through documented record-keeping systems, chain-of-custody procedures, and audit logs that are designed to preserve continuity across organizational and temporal boundaries. [formal: tractabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Failure-modes-and-effects-analysis (FMEA) is a structured, inductive method for systematically enumerating every way a product, process, or system can fail, tracing each failure mode to its root causes, and scoring the consequences by severity, occurrence likelihood, and detectability — typically via a Risk Priority Number (RPN = severity × occurrence × detection) to prioritize corrective actions. Its parameters are: (1) the failure mode — how something fails; (2) the effects — what goes wrong when it fails; (3) the causes — what triggers the failure; (4) the RPN scores that rank urgency; and (5) the prescribed controls that mitigate or eliminate the risk. It persists through documented FMEA sheets embedded in engineering workflows and quality management systems (ISO 9001, IATF 16949), where each analysis is a living record updated as designs evolve and field failures are discovered. [formal: fatalis modorum effectusque analyses | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pareto-analysis is a data-ranking technique that orders factors by their measured contribution to a total effect, then applies the Pareto principle — the empirical observation that a minority of causes typically generates the majority of results — to distinguish the vital few from the trivial many. Its parameters are: (1) the dataset of candidate factors and their measured effects (frequency, cost, severity, or another metric); (2) the cumulative distribution computed from that dataset; (3) the threshold — conventionally the 80/20 inflection — that separates vital factors requiring prioritized intervention from trivial factors warranting routine monitoring. It persists through quality management methodology, statistical practice, and continuous improvement documentation. [formal: Paretiana | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.96]

root-cause is the concept of a fundamental reason behind a problem or failure — the underlying condition whose elimination would prevent recurrence, as opposed to proximate causes which merely trigger the event. It is carved by three parameters: (1) temporal depth — the cause must predate the triggering event; (2) eliminability — removing it must prevent recurrence; (3) independence — it must not itself require another root-cause to explain. It persists through the practice of root-cause analysis, safety investigations, and organizational memory. — Mira, 2026-07

cause-and-effect is the conceptual framework that maps relationships between actions, conditions, and their outcomes — asserting that every effect has at least one cause and every cause produces at least one effect. Parameters: the relationship can be deterministic (same cause → same effect) or probabilistic (cause raises probability of effect); causality can be direct or mediated through intermediate causes; and causal chains can branch or converge. The framework persists through language (causative grammar, conditional logic), scientific method (hypothesis testing, controlled experiments), legal reasoning (proximate cause, liability), and everyday practical reasoning (troubleshooting, planning). [formal: causa et effectus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

human-reliability is the concept of quantifying the likelihood that a human operator will execute a required task correctly under specified conditions and within a defined time window. It parameterizes human performance as a probabilistic variable subject to degradation under stress, fatigue, ambiguity, or time pressure, and persists through human error databases, reliability prediction methods, and training protocols that model and improve operator performance. [formal: human-reliability | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Inherent-safety is the concept of eliminating hazards from a system through design choices rather than adding protective measures or controls. Its parameters are: (1) the hazard must be completely removed from the system's operation, not merely contained or mitigated; (2) the elimination must result from the intrinsic properties of materials, energy levels, or system architecture chosen during design; (3) the safety gain must not depend on procedures, administrative controls, or external safeguards. It persists through engineering design standards (e.g., OSHA's hierarchy of controls, NFPA guidelines), safety certification regimes, and the professional practice of safety reviewers evaluating design decisions. [formal: eliminatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

safety-critical is the human-made classification that designates systems, components, or processes where failure could result in catastrophic consequences — loss of life, severe injury, or major environmental damage. Its parameters are: (1) consequence severity threshold (catastrophic vs. major/minor/negligible), (2) failure mode analysis linking single-point failures to consequence classes, and (3) regulatory or standards-driven designation authority (e.g. DO-178C for avionics, IEC 61508 for industrial systems). It persists through regulatory frameworks, certification processes, and safety case documentation that must be maintained for the operational lifetime of the designated asset. [formal: systema-criticalis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

layers-of-protection is the safety engineering concept of deploying multiple independent protective barriers in sequence between a hazard and its target. Its parameters are: (1) each barrier must be independent — no single cause can defeat all layers; (2) each barrier must be capable of preventing or mitigating the hazard on its own; (3) barriers are arranged so that failure of any single layer does not cascade. Its persistence mechanism is engineering design standards and systematic safety analysis. [formal: multi-lamina-protectio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) is a structured, incremental methodology for enumerating every plausible way a system, subsystem, or component can fail, assessing the consequences of each failure mode on system-level function, and ranking them by severity, occurrence frequency, and detectability so that engineering resources target the highest-risk failures first. Parameters: the unit of analysis (component, process, or design), the failure catalogue built from design specifications and operational history, and the Risk Priority Number (RPN) computed as severity × occurrence × detectability. Persistence mechanism: codified in standards (e.g., IECEE 60812, AIAG-VDA FMEA), maintained as living worksheets and databases that are updated whenever failures are observed or design changes occur, and enforced through mandatory review gates in product-development workflows. [formal: fmea | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Prevention-and-detection is the dual safety principle that human systems must both prevent failures from occurring (proactive barriers, design safeguards, procedural controls) and detect failures that do occur before they escalate into harm (monitoring, alarms, inspection, fault diagnosis). It carves a conceptual space defined by two complementary mechanisms: prevention constrains the state-space of possible failures, while detection provides early-warning and containment when prevention is insufficient. The mechanism of persistence is institutional practice embedded in safety management systems, engineering standards, and operational procedures. [formal: praesidio-et-discernere | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

What-if-analysis is a structured brainstorming technique for hazard identification, in which experienced analysts pose 'what if' questions about potential deviations from normal design or operational parameters and systematically trace each deviation through its possible causes, consequences, and required preventive or mitigating controls. The method persists through standardized question catalogs, trained facilitator practice, and documented study reports. [formal: quid si | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

Barrier-analysis is a safety engineering method that systematically evaluates the adequacy, design, and operational status of barriers — physical, procedural, or administrative controls — intended to prevent or mitigate hazards. It identifies each barrier, assesses its effectiveness against the hazard it guards against, and evaluates whether barriers operate independently (no single point of failure). The method persists through structured assessment protocols and documented reports that track barrier integrity over time. [formal: barrier-analysis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Hazard-operability-study is a systematic hazard-identification method in process engineering where trained teams apply structured guide words (no, more, less, reverse, part-of, as-well-as) to process parameters (flow, pressure, temperature, level) to identify feasible deviations, trace each to root causes, evaluate consequences, and recommend safeguards. It persists through formal study protocols, certified facilitators, documented reports, and regulatory requirements. [formal: hazard-operabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

human-factors is the discipline that studies how humans interact with systems, tools, and environments — designing for human capabilities, limitations, and behaviors so that systems operate safely and effectively. It carves a bounded field: not the natural mind or body, but the constructed knowledge of how humans fit into designed artifacts, persisted through methods, standards, and research. [formal: factor-humana | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.15]

Criticality-analysis is a risk-assessment method that assigns a numeric criticality score to each failure mode or hazard by combining three rated parameters: severity (the seriousness of the consequence), occurrence (the frequency or probability of the cause happening), and detectability (the likelihood that the cause or effect will be discovered before harm occurs). The method uses standardized scoring scales (typically 1-10) multiplied or tabulated in a criticality matrix to produce a prioritized ranking that determines which failure modes require corrective action first. Parameters: scoring scales defined by the applicable standard (MIL-STD-1629A for reliability-critical systems, IEC 60812 for industrial FMEA), a criticality matrix or formula mapping the three parameters to a score, and a threshold above which mitigation is mandatory. Persistence: maintained through documented procedures in safety management systems, regulatory frameworks, and engineering standards that prescribe the scoring methodology and matrix structure. [formal: criticalitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

risk-tolerance is a governance construct that specifies the maximum level and category of risk an organization or decision-maker will accept in pursuit of an objective. It is established through policy, regulatory compliance, or strategic deliberation, and serves as a calibration point for risk acceptance, mitigation prioritization, and residual risk evaluation. It is not a psychological disposition but a formalized boundary — the threshold at which risk treatment transitions from optional to mandatory. [formal: risk-tolerantia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

Reliability-centred maintenance (RCM) is a systematic methodology for determining what must be preserved and how to preserve it in order to ensure that any physical asset continues doing what its stakeholders require. It operates by analyzing failure modes, their consequences, and the suitability of maintenance tasks through a structured decision process. The methodology specifies failure detection and restoration procedures, proactive replacement intervals, and design modifications when tasks are inapplicable.
