[formal: rcm | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A hazard-log is a structured register maintained to record identified hazards, their assessment status, and the controls applied or planned. It is parameterized by: (1) a unique identifier for each recorded hazard, (2) a description of the hazard and its potential consequences, (3) a risk rating derived from severity and likelihood, (4) a status field tracking whether the hazard is open, under review, or closed, and (5) a reference to the control measures assigned to each entry. The hazard-log persists as a living document that is updated throughout the lifecycle of a system or project, enabling systematic hazard management and auditability. It is sustained by organized review practices and integrated into risk assessment workflows. [formal: periclitatio periculorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A decision-support-system (DSS) is a human-made information system designed to assist decision-makers in compiling information from raw data, documents, personal knowledge, and models to identify and solve problems and make decisions. It is parameterized by: (1) input data sources (structured databases, unstructured documents, or real-time feeds), (2) analytical models (statistical, optimization, simulation, or heuristic) that transform inputs into actionable insights, (3) an interactive interface allowing users to explore scenarios and adjust parameters, and (4) an output mechanism presenting findings in a form suitable for judgment. A DSS persists through software architecture, database schemas, and user training — it endures as long as its models, data pipelines, and interfaces are maintained. It extends human cognition in structured problem-solving contexts where decisions involve uncertainty, multiple criteria, or complex trade-offs. [formal: systema adiuvantis deliberationem | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Forensics is the disciplined practice of investigating phenomena — whether crimes, system failures, digital artefacts, or historical events — by applying systematic methods of evidence collection, analysis, and documentation. Its parameters are: (1) a question requiring factual resolution, (2) methods that produce reproducible and chain-of-custody-traceable results, (3) findings structured to be admissible before an authoritative audience (court, regulator, or peer body). It persists through institutionalized training protocols, standardized methodologies (chemical analysis, digital recovery, fingerprint comparison, document examination), and professional bodies that certify practitioners and maintain accreditation. The practice extends across domains — criminal forensics, digital forensics, engineering forensics, archaeological forensics — unified by the methodological commitment to evidence over conjecture. [formal: forensis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Functional-analysis is a structured engineering practice that decomposes a system into its required functions — what it must do — and represents those functions in hierarchical function models (function trees) and functional flow diagrams. It is parameterized by: (1) the system boundary being analysed, (2) the abstraction level of functional decomposition, (3) the function verbs that describe actions performed (e.g., 'transmit', 'contain', 'convert'), and (4) the functional links between inputs, outputs, and energy/material flows. It persists through function models maintained in engineering standards (e.g., V-Model function analysis, FAST diagrams) and CAD/PLM function modelling tools used in product development. [formal: analisys functionalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Risk-acceptance is the structured decision process by which an organization determines that identified risks are tolerable within its risk appetite, or that the cost of further mitigation exceeds the benefit. It operates through defined acceptance criteria, formal sign-off by authorized decision-makers, and documented risk acceptance records that specify residual risks, review intervals, and expiry conditions. The persistence mechanism is the formal risk acceptance documentation maintained within the organization's risk management system and subject to periodic review. [formal: acceptatio periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.1]

A safety-assessment is a systematic evaluation of known or potential hazards, the adequacy of existing controls, and the acceptability of residual risk. It operates through a sequence: identifying hazards, evaluating the likelihood and severity of harm, reviewing existing control measures, and determining whether risk remains below an acceptable threshold. The mechanism of persistence is procedural — codified into standards, checklists, and reporting protocols that organizations maintain and update across generations of operations and incidents. [formal: securitas iudicium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Process-safety is the organized practice of preventing catastrophic releases of toxic, flammable, explosive, or energy-rich materials from industrial facilities. It operates through hazard identification, risk assessment, barrier management, and organizational controls across the facility lifecycle. Its parameters scope: any process handling materials at quantities or conditions beyond normal handling thresholds; any facility where a loss of containment could cause multiple fatalities or widespread harm. Persistence mechanism: institutionalized through engineering curricula (chemical/process safety courses), professional certifications (CSP, CGP), regulatory frameworks (OSHA PSM, SEVESO), corporate management-of-change systems, and incident-investigation feedback loops that update procedures and training. The practice is explicit, taught, audited, and continuously revised through near-miss and incident learning cycles. [formal: processualis securitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

hazard-and-operability (HAZOP) is a structured, systematic examination methodology for identifying process deviations that could lead to hazards or operability issues. It operates through a structured team session: a multidisciplinary team reviews a process P&ID or procedure node-by-node, applies standardized guide words (NO, MORE, LESS, REVERSE, PART_OF, AS_WELL_AS, OTHER_THAN) to process parameters (FLOW, PRESSURE, TEMPERATURE, LEVEL, COMPOSITION), and analyzes each deviation's causes, consequences, and existing safeguards. The mechanism of persistence is through documented HAZOP studies that form part of an organization's risk management record and are revisited when processes change. [formal: hazard-and-operability | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A risk-matrix is a grid-based visualization that maps hazards or risk events onto cells defined by axes of likelihood and consequence, producing a colour-coded heat map that prioritises which risks require treatment. It carves the risk landscape into discrete bands (e.g. low, medium, high) so that decision-makers can compare disparate threats on a shared scale and allocate resources accordingly. The mechanism of persistence is institutional: it lives in risk registers, governance frameworks, and audit processes where the matrix structure standardises how organisations rank, communicate, and escalate risk across departments. [formal: matrix periculum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Consequence-analysis is the systematic evaluation of what happens when a hazard or threat materialises — it identifies and quantifies the impacts on people, assets, operations, and reputation that follow from a realised risk event. It carves the post-occurrence phase of risk management by distinguishing between direct impacts (immediate physical or financial damage) and secondary cascading effects (supply-chain disruption, regulatory response, reputational harm). The persistence mechanism is procedural: consequence-analyses are produced during risk assessments, safety studies, and business-impact evaluations, and the outputs feed into risk-treatment decisions, emergency planning, and insurance underwriting. [formal: consequentiae estimatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-barrier is a physical or procedural control deliberately engineered into a system to prevent, mitigate, or detect hazards before they cause harm. Barriers are categorised by function: prevention barriers stop initiating events, mitigation barriers reduce consequence severity, and detection barriers provide early warning. They operate through engineered controls (physical guards, interlocks), administrative controls (procedures, permits), or personal protective equipment. Barriers persist through formal implementation in safety management systems, documented in hazard analyses and verified by inspection and testing. [formal: clausula safety | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Functional-safety is the discipline of ensuring that safety-related control systems perform their required functions correctly under all specified conditions, including fault states. It is defined by quantified performance targets (safety integrity levels) applied through a lifecycle of hazard analysis, requirements specification, design implementation, validation testing, and ongoing monitoring. The persistence mechanism is standardization (IEC 61508 series) and third-party certification of safety instrumented systems. [formal: functional-safety | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A human-made classification system that quantifies the reliability of safety-related control systems, assigning discrete integrity levels (SIL 1 through SIL 4) based on probabilistic failure criteria. Each level specifies a range of probability of dangerous failure per hour (PFH) for random hardware faults, with SIL 4 being the most stringent. The system is defined by IEC 61508 and sector-specific standards (e.g. IEC 61511 for process industry), persisting through international standardization bodies, regulatory mandates, and industry certification regimes. A SIL assignment dictates the required architecture, diagnostics, and verification rigor of the safety instrumented function it governs — higher SIL demands redundant channels, diverse implementations, and more thorough validation.\n\n[formal: safety_integralis_gradus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-instrumented-system is an instrumented system consisting of sensors, a logic solver, and final elements, designed to execute one or more safety functions to put or keep a process in a safe state when specified predetermined conditions are violated. Each safety function is assigned a safety integrity level (SIL 1–4) based on required risk reduction. The system is designed, implemented, operated, and maintained according to a systematic and managed lifecycle per IEC 61508/61511. [formal: systema instrumentatum securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

A safety-function is a formally specified function that a safety-related system must execute to achieve or maintain a safe state upon detection of a specific hazard or hazardous event. It is defined by four parameters: (1) the hazard it addresses, (2) the safe state it targets, (3) its required performance level (e.g., SIL rating or Performance Level), and (4) its required response time. A safety-function persists through its specification in safety requirements documents, its implementation in safety-related control systems (sensors, logic solvers, final elements), and its validation against IEC 61508 or ISO 13849 standards. [formal: safety_function | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A process-hazard-analysis (PHA) is a structured safety-engineering practice that identifies, evaluates, and controls hazards in industrial chemical and manufacturing processes. It operates through discrete, repeatable sessions using standardized techniques—HAZOP (hazard-and-operability study), What-If questioning, checklist review, and failure-mode-and-effects analysis—each producing a documented finding of hazard scenario, contributing causes, existing safeguards, and recommended action. The mechanism of persistence is regulatory mandate (OSHA 1910.119, EU COMAH/Seveso III) and professional-safety engineering practice, which requires periodic revalidation (typically every 5 years) and retention of findings in the facility's process-safety information system. [formal: processus hazardous analysisis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-report is a formal regulatory document submitted by an industrial operator to demonstrate ongoing compliance with process-safety legislation such as the EU COMAH/Seveso III directive or national equivalents. It specifies the organizational and technical measures implemented to prevent major accidents involving hazardous substances, describes the safety-management system in place, and presents the results of internal audits and periodic reassessments. The definition rests on four parameters: (1) the legislative trigger that mandates its submission, (2) the prescribed content structure defined by the competent authority, (3) a fixed submission interval (typically 3–5 years depending on jurisdiction and hazard classification), and (4) independent external verification by a qualified safety assessor. Persistence is secured through legal requirement and archival enforcement by the regulatory body. [formal: relatios securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-sign is a visual communication system that uses standardized symbols, colors, shapes, and text to convey safety-related messages instantly and across language barriers. It is organized by five parameters: (1) hazard type communicated — warning, prohibition, mandatory action, emergency information, or safe condition; (2) color coding scheme — red for prohibition and fire equipment, yellow for warning of hazards, green for safe condition and emergency exits, blue for mandatory actions; (3) symbolic language — pictograms standardized by ISO 7010 and national equivalents to ensure cross-lingual recognition; (4) physical specification — dimensions, mounting height, photometric requirements ensuring visibility at the necessary distance; (5) regulatory context — mandatory application per OSHA 1910.145, ISO 3864, and EN 701 in workplaces handling hazardous materials or equipment. The concept persists through international standardization (ISO, ILO), national occupational safety regulations, the commercial production industry, and the training curricula of safety professionals. Its persistence mechanism is the institutional embedding of standards into law, the manufacturing infrastructure for standardized signs, and the visual conditioning of workers who encounter these symbols daily.\n\n[formal: safety-sign | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-critical-system is a engineered system whose failure mode, malfunction, or improper operation can directly cause serious injury, death, significant environmental damage, or major economic loss. It is defined by four parameters: (1) consequence severity — the worst-case outcome if the system fails; (2) failure probability — the statistical likelihood of failure on demand or during continuous operation; (3) safety integrity level (SIL) — the performance requirement assigned through risk assessment; (4) operational envelope — the range of conditions under which the system must maintain its safety function. It persists through regulatory mandates (IEC 61508, IEC 61511, API RP 752), certification regimes, and continuous lifecycle management from design through decommissioning. [formal: systema-criticum-safety | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-critical-system is an engineered system — comprising hardware, software, and operating procedures — whose failure, malfunction, or improper operation can directly cause serious injury, death, significant environmental damage, or major economic loss. It is defined by five parameters: (1) consequence severity — the system's failure mode maps to one or more of injury, death, environmental harm, or major economic loss; (2) criticality determination — its safety criticality is established through formal hazard analysis methods (e.g., HAZOP, FMEA, fault-tree analysis) rather than heuristic judgment; (3) lifecycle governance — the system is subject to rigorous design, validation, testing, and maintenance regimes that exceed standard engineering practice; (4) safety functions — it executes one or more safety functions that bring the process to or maintain a safe state when detected conditions warrant; (5) regulatory mandate — it exists within a framework of statutory or industry-mandated safety requirements. The system persists through documentation, institutionalized safety practices, certification regimes, and physical implementation — not as an idea but as a managed artifact whose continued operation is actively verified. [formal: systema securitatis critica | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-instrumented-function is a safety function executed by an instrumented system — comprising sensors, logic solvers, and final elements — that automatically brings a process to a safe state when specific hazardous conditions are detected. Parameters: (1) safety integrity level (SIL) rating 1–4 defining performance requirements, (2) defined safe state, (3) specified response time, (4) continuous diagnostics and testing regime. Persists through calibration, proof testing, and maintenance schedules per IEC 61508/61511 standards. [formal: instrumentum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hazard-registry is a human-created structured catalog of all identified hazards within a facility, process, or project, recording each hazard's characteristics, risk ratings, and assigned control measures. It persists as a living document maintained through organized review cycles, serving as the authoritative traceability backbone for safety management. The registry enables systematic hazard identification, cross-referencing of controls, and audit compliance by providing a single source of truth for all hazard-related information.[formal: inventarium | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

A fail-safe is a design approach in which a system is engineered to respond to a detected failure or fault by automatically transitioning into a predefined state that minimizes potential harm. The defining parameters are: (1) a failure detection mechanism (sensors, monitoring, or intrinsic system behavior), (2) a designated safe state (e.g., powered-down, isolated, or contained), and (3) a failover path that operates without requiring human intervention. It persists through engineering design standards (e.g., IEC 61508, AS9100), safety codes, regulatory requirements, and the sustained practice of safety-conscious engineering across industries. [formal: latens | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Lockout-tagout is a safety procedure for controlling hazardous energy sources during maintenance, repair, or servicing of equipment. Its parameters are: (1) preparation — identify all energy sources and notify affected workers; (2) shutdown — turn off equipment per approved procedures; (3) isolation — apply physical isolating devices (valves, switches, breakers); (4) lockout — secure each isolating device with a unique authorized lock; (5) tagging — affix a tag stating the worker's identity, date, and reason; (6) verification — confirm zero-energy state by attempting to operate the equipment; (7) release — remove locks and tags only by the authorized worker who applied them. It persists through occupational safety regulations (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147), corporate safety programs, and training regimens. [formal: lockout-tagout | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An emergency shutdown (ESD) system is a safety-critical engineered system that automatically or manually halts a process when predefined dangerous conditions are detected. Its parameters are: (1) detection — sensors and logic circuits continuously monitor process variables against safety limits; (2) decision — a safety instrumented system evaluates whether conditions warrant shutdown; (3) action — actuators move equipment to a safe state (valve closure, motor stop, pressure relief); (4) restoration — a defined procedure governs safe restart only after hazard clearance. Persistence mechanism: engineering design standards (IEC 61511, API RP 14C), regulatory mandates (OSHA PSM), and operational training. [formal: emergium | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-requirement is a human-made specification that states what a system, subsystem, or component must achieve to maintain risk at an acceptable level. Its parameters are: (1) origin — derived from safety goals through systematic hazard analysis and risk assessment; (2) form — traceable, verifiable statements with assigned safety integrity levels (SIL); (3) lifecycle — maintained through design, implementation, operation, and decommissioning via configuration management. The persistence mechanism is formal documentation within safety case artefacts and quality management systems. [formal: necessarium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-management-system is a structured organizational framework built to direct and control safety performance through systematic planning, execution, review, and improvement cycles. Its parameters are: (1) structure — the governance hierarchy, defined roles, accountabilities, and resources allocated to safety; (2) planning — systematic hazard identification, risk assessment, legal compliance review, and safety objective-setting; (3) implementation — documented operating procedures, training programs, emergency preparedness plans, and operational controls; (4) checking — performance monitoring, measurement, auditing, incident investigation, and corrective action tracking; (5) management review — periodic top-management evaluation of system suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness. The system persists through institutionalization: embedded in organizational governance, codified in procedures, enforced by audits, and sustained by management accountability cycles that close the plan-do-check-act loop. [formal: systema safety | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

personal-protective-equipment (PPE) is human-made equipment worn or carried by workers to create a barrier between the body and workplace hazards. Its parameters are: (1) scope of protection — classified by body region (head, eyes, respiratory, hands, feet, full-body) and hazard type (chemical, physical, biological, radiological); (2) performance standards — certified against tested thresholds for penetration, permeation, impact resistance, or filtration efficiency; (3) replacement cycle — determined by degradation indicators, service life, or single-use design. Its persistence mechanism is regulatory certification (OSHA, EN, ISO standards) and occupational practice that mandates selection based on hazard assessment. [formal: protectio personalis | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-audit is a structured, systematic examination of a workplace, system, or process to evaluate whether safety measures are adequate, properly implemented, and effective at controlling risks. Its parameters are: (1) scope — defined by the area, system, or process under review; (2) methodology — uses checklists, observation, document review, and interviews; (3) output — a report with findings, non-conformances, and corrective action recommendations; (4) frequency — scheduled at intervals set by the safety management system, plus ad hoc audits triggered by incidents or changes. It persists through documented audit trails, recorded findings, and corrective-action follow-up cycles that close the feedback loop. [formal: examinatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A structured instructional practice that builds and maintains competency in recognizing workplace hazards, following safety procedures, and responding to emergencies. It operates through designed curriculum and repetition — the mechanism is pedagogical: learners acquire situational awareness and procedural memory through exercises, drills, and feedback loops. The practice persists via institutional scheduling, certification cycles, and regulatory mandates that require periodic re-training. [formal: instructio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-interlock is a mechanical, electrical, or software mechanism that enforces a condition prerequisite to equipment or system operation: the device or logic checks for the presence of specified safety conditions (guards in place, pressure within limits, permissions granted) before allowing activation, and actively blocks or disables operation if any condition is unsatisfied. It persists through engineered hardware (physical key switches, limit sensors, mechanical linkages), firmware-enforced logic (PLC interlock routines), or regulatory-mandated control sequences that cannot be bypassed without intentional override. Unlike a safety device that responds to a hazard after it occurs, an interlock prevents the hazardous condition from arising by constraining the sequence of operations. [formal: interlockum | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-policy is a formal document or statement that defines an organization's safety intentions, principles, and directional commitments. It operates by establishing measurable safety objectives, assigning accountability for safety performance, and providing the authoritative mandate under which all safety procedures, standards, and management systems derive their legitimacy. The mechanism of persistence is institutional — codified through governance processes, version-controlled documentation, and periodic review cycles that ensure the policy remains current with operational changes. [formal: politia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-standards are formal specifications developed through recognized standardization bodies or consensus processes that establish required safety criteria, procedures, and performance levels. They operate by providing measurable benchmarks and prescriptive requirements that organizations adopt to ensure consistent safety outcomes. Standards may be mandatory (regulatory) or voluntary (industry best practice), and persist through formal publication, periodic revision cycles, and institutional adoption. [formal: norma | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-drill is a simulated emergency exercise organized by human institutions to practice and validate emergency response procedures. It works by creating controlled, time-bound scenarios that mimic real hazards, allowing participants to rehearse roles, test communication chains, and identify gaps in their safety-management systems without actual risk. The exercise persists through structured documentation (after-action reports, corrective action plans), institutional memory embedded in training curricula, and the organizational routines that schedule periodic drills. [formal: exercitium securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.51]

A hazard-assessment is the human-made systematic practice of examining identified hazards to determine their likelihood of occurrence, the severity of their potential consequences, and the adequacy of existing controls. It operates by applying structured methods (checklists, fault trees, bow-tie analysis, what-if scenarios) to evaluate risk factors and prioritize mitigation actions. The practice persists through documented procedures, regulatory requirements, and the organizational routines of risk management that mandate periodic reassessment as conditions change. [formal: periclitatio periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.52]

Redundancy is a design strategy in which duplicate or backup components are intentionally incorporated into a system so that if any single component fails, the system as a whole continues to operate or transitions to a safe state. It operates through deliberate duplication of critical paths, power supplies, control systems, or safety functions — the parameter being that the backup must be functionally independent enough to survive the failure mode affecting the primary. Redundancy persists through engineering documentation, design standards, and regulatory requirements that mandate its use in safety-critical domains. [formal: redundantia | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A permit-to-work is a human-made formal authorization procedure that controls entry into and execution of hazardous work activities. It operates by requiring documented risk assessment, verification of controls, and explicit approval from an authorized person before work begins. The system persists through written permits (physical or electronic) that specify scope, hazards, controls, duration, and responsible parties, and through organizational policies that mandate their use. It is maintained by safety-management systems and enforced by organizational authority structures. [formal: permitum-laboris | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Management-of-change is a human-made formal review process that evaluates the safety, operational, and regulatory implications of proposed changes to an industrial or organizational system before implementation. It operates by requiring documented hazard identification, risk assessment of the change, approval by authorized personnel, communication to affected parties, and update of relevant procedures and training records. [formal: administratio mutationis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Hazard-recognition is a human-made systematic observation procedure that identifies potential dangers in a work environment or system before they manifest as incidents. It operates through trained perceptual patterns, checklists, and structured hazard-identification methods that convert ambient conditions into flagged risks. The procedure persists through training curricula, standard operating procedures, safety briefings, and documented observation protocols. [formal: cognitio_periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.81]

A job-safety-analysis (JSA) is a human-made structured hazard-identification procedure that breaks a work task into discrete sequential steps, examines each step for potential hazards, and prescribes controls before the work begins. Its parameters are: (1) step-by-step decomposition of a specific job, (2) hazard identification per step (mechanical, chemical, ergonomic, environmental), and (3) control prescription — elimination, engineering controls, administrative controls, or PPE — in order of hierarchy. It persists through standardized checklists, documented procedures, and recurrent training that embed the practice in organizational routines. The procedure is operational at the moment of task initiation: if the JSA is removed, the organized pre-task hazard review stops operating entirely, even though workers may still perform the job unsafely by habit or expediency. [formal: procedura | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-observation is a human-made systematic procedure for watching work activities, conditions, and behaviors to identify hazards, unsafe practices, and near-misses in real time. It operates through trained observer protocols that follow structured routes or stationary watch positions, using standardized checklists or behavioral criteria to flag deviations from safe practice. The mechanism of persistence is the observer's documented findings, which feed into corrective-action systems and safety-data aggregation. [formal: observatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-observation is a human-made systematic behavioral practice in which trained observers watch work activities, conditions, and behaviors to identify hazards, unsafe practices, and near-misses in real time before they escalate into incidents. It persists through organizational procedures that mandate scheduled observation rounds, documented reporting protocols, and feedback loops that close identified gaps. [formal: observatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

near-miss is a human-made safety concept that names and categorizes unintended events which almost resulted in harm, damage, or operational failure but were averted by chance, last-minute intervention, or luck. It carves a specific class of incidents: unlike actual incidents, no harm occurred; unlike hazards, something already went wrong but was stopped before consequences materialized. The persistence mechanism is systematic reporting — near-miss reports feed into safety databases, learning loops, and predictive risk models where patterns of near misses reveal systemic weaknesses before they produce actual incidents. By tracking what almost happened, organizations build early-warning indicators. [formal: near-miss | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-reporting is a human-made organizational practice in which safety-relevant events, conditions, and observations are systematically documented and communicated through formal channels. It carves the practice of converting safety experience into actionable knowledge via incident reports, near-miss logs, safety observation records, and regulatory disclosures. Parameters: (1) the information must be safety-relevant, (2) it must be communicated through formal institutional channels (not informal conversation), (3) it persists in documented form accessible to others. The persistence mechanism is institutional record-keeping systems, regulatory compliance frameworks, and organizational learning processes. [formal: relatio periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.95]

Safety-metric is a human-made quantifiable measure designed to assess the state of safety conditions, track trends over time, and drive improvement actions within an organization. It carves the concept by specifying: (1) it must be quantifiable (numeric or ordinal), (2) it must relate to safety performance (leading indicators like training hours, lagging indicators like injury rates), (3) it must be used systematically within a safety management framework. The metric persists through data collection systems, reporting tools, and organizational memory. [formal: metricum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Hazard-mitigation is a human-made set of strategies and controls deliberately applied to reduce either the likelihood or the impact (or both) of identified hazards. It carves the concept by specifying three parameters: (1) the intervention type — engineering controls (physical changes to equipment/processes), administrative controls (procedures, training, scheduling), or personal protective equipment — each operating at a different point in the hazard chain; (2) the risk reduction target — likelihood, impact, or both — which determines whether the control is preventative or protective; and (3) the persistence mechanism through which hazard-mitigation endures: safety management systems (which institutionalize the controls), engineering standards (which fix physical interventions), and regulatory compliance frameworks (which mandate ongoing maintenance). Without these persistence mechanisms, hazard-mitigation would be ad hoc and transient. [formal: mitigatio periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-signage is a human-made system of visual indicators — signs, labels, color-coding, and symbols — designed to communicate safety information, warn of hazards, and direct safe behavior. It carves the concept by specifying three parameters: (1) the signaling modality — pictorial (ISO-style safety symbols), textual (instructional or warning text), chromatic (color-coded zones, e.g. red=fire, yellow=caution, green=safety equipment), or luminous (illuminated or photoluminescent markers) — each chosen for recognition speed and reliability under the relevant conditions; (2) the informational function — warning (hazard present), mandatory (action required), prohibited (action forbidden), or safe condition (exit, first aid) — which determines the symbol set and color palette; and (3) the persistence mechanism: regulatory standards (OSHA, ISO 7010, GHS) that standardize form, physical installation and maintenance cycles that keep signs visible and legible, and safety management systems that govern placement audits and replacements. Without these, signage degrades to decoration. [formal: indicium salutare | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A layer-of-protection is a single, independent safeguard designed to prevent a specific hazardous event or to mitigate its consequences when all upstream preventive measures fail. Each layer operates autonomously — its activation does not depend on the failure or operation of any other layer — and employs diverse mechanisms (physical devices, procedural controls, alarms, emergency systems) to interrupt a causal chain between a initiating event and an undesired outcome. Layers are arranged in a defense-in-depth sequence so that the overall system tolerates individual layer failures without loss of the safety function. The method persists through structured analysis (LOPA — Layer of Protection Analysis) applied during process hazard assessments and design reviews, maintained by engineering documentation and regulatory compliance frameworks.\n\n[formal: stratum protectionis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

Safety-management is the organisational framework that systematises hazard identification, risk assessment, and control implementation so that risk-management operates at a sustained, auditable level. It takes the ad hoc response to danger and converts it into a standing practice: hazards are catalogued, risks are ranked by likelihood and severity, controls are selected and deployed, and the whole cycle is monitored and reviewed on a fixed schedule. The mechanism of persistence is institutional — policies, procedures, training programmes, audit trails, and management review — rather than any single tool or document. It endures as long as an organisation chooses to govern risk by structure rather than by improvisation.

[formal: administratio periculorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-inspection is the systematic practice of visually examining workplaces, equipment, and processes against established safety standards and checklists to identify hazards, verify compliance, and produce records of findings and corrective actions. It persists through documented inspection protocols, scheduled review cycles, regulatory mandates, and the institutional repository of past inspection data that drives continuous improvement. [formal: inspectio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Behavioral-safety is a constructed methodology for improving workplace safety through the systematic observation, analysis, and modification of worker behaviors. It operates through a defined process: (1) defining target safe and unsafe behaviors through job analysis, (2) observing workers performing tasks using standardized observation protocols, (3) providing immediate, constructive feedback on observed behaviors, and (4) tracking behavioral trends over time to reinforce safe practices. The mechanism of persistence is institutional practice — it is sustained through organizational policies, trained safety observers, scheduled observation cycles, and data-driven feedback loops. Without these constructed mechanisms, the practice ceases to operate as behavioral-safety. [formal: behavioral-safety | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An incident-report is a structured document produced after an event — an accident, near-miss, or hazard discovery — to record what happened, how it happened, who or what was affected, and what corrective or preventive actions were taken. It operates as a feedback artifact in safety-management systems: by capturing empirical detail from real-world events, it feeds learning into risk-treatment decisions, audit trails, and regulatory compliance. The report carves its scope by requiring three elements: (1) a factual chronology of the event, (2) an analysis of contributing factors (not blame assignment), and (3) documented follow-up actions with responsible parties and deadlines. Without these elements, a narrative is merely a story; with them, it becomes an incident-report — a reproducible artifact that turns experience into institutional memory. [formal: incidentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Risk-treatment is the phase of risk management in which an organization selects and implements options to address identified risks. It follows risk assessment and encompasses four principal approaches: mitigation (reducing likelihood or impact), avoidance (eliminating the activity causing the risk), transfer (shifting the consequence to another party, as via insurance or contract), and acceptance (consciously retaining the risk with documented rationale). A risk-treatment is distinguished from risk-assessment by its orientation toward action: assessment carves and scores the risk landscape; treatment acts upon it. The definition requires that each treatment option specify (1) the risk it addresses, (2) the chosen approach from the four categories, (3) the responsible party, and (4) the resources or controls deployed. This transforms risk from a catalog entry into managed operational decisions. [formal: tractatio-risicus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A toolbox talk is a short, focused safety briefing delivered to workers or team members before starting a task or shift, designed to raise awareness of specific hazards and reinforce safe work practices. It is a structured verbal exchange — typically 5–15 minutes — led by a supervisor, safety officer, or peer, covering one or more topics such as equipment handling, environmental hazards, procedural updates, or lessons from recent incidents. Its persistence mechanism is organizational routine: scheduled at the start of shifts, documented in safety logs, and reinforced through repeat performance. The talk is not a formal training course but a recurring micro-intervention that keeps safety salient in the daily workflow.

[formal: oratio ad instrumentum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-governance is the system of accountability, oversight, and strategic direction by which an organization sets its safety policy, assigns responsibility, and ensures that safety-management operations are directed, monitored, and held accountable. Its parameters are: (1) a defined structure of roles and reporting lines that places safety oversight at the highest level of authority; (2) formal mechanisms for board- or executive-level review of safety performance; and (3) procedures that translate strategic safety direction into management action and verify compliance. The concept persists through organizational charters, regulatory frameworks, audit trails, and the institutional memory of accountability structures that outlast individual leaders. [formal: governance | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Emergency-response is the organized system of procedures, designated roles, and allocated resources activated when an incident threatens safety, continuity, or assets. It operates through predefined plans (emergency action plans, evacuation procedures, incident command systems), trained personnel, and practiced drills. The persistence mechanism is institutional documentation, regulatory requirements, and recurrent training exercises. [formal: responsio emergentiae | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.97]

A control measure is a deliberate intervention put in place to eliminate a hazard or reduce the likelihood or severity of harm in a workplace or operational context. It operates within a recognized hierarchy: elimination (removing the hazard entirely) takes priority over substitution (replacing the hazard with a less dangerous alternative), engineering controls (isolating people from the hazard), administrative controls (changing the way people work), and personal protective equipment (protecting the worker as a last line of defense). The persistence mechanism is a formal safety management system that documents, implements, monitors, and periodically reviews each control measure to ensure it remains effective and appropriate as conditions change. [formal: mensura repressiva | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.61]

Safety communication is the structured exchange of risk-related information, alerts, hazard warnings, and safety instructions among stakeholders in an organization or system. It encompasses both the channels used (briefings, signage, digital platforms, written procedures, incident reports) and the content transmitted (risk assessments, emergency procedures, lessons learned, regulatory changes). The persistence mechanism is an organized communication protocol embedded within the safety management system, ensuring that relevant safety information reaches the right people at the right time through designated formal and informal channels. [formal: communicatio salutaris | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.61]

Near-miss-reporting is the structured practice of recording, classifying, and submitting accounts of incidents that failed to cause harm only by chance — events where the causal chain was interrupted by luck rather than design. It operates through a defined reporting chain: discovery by an observer, documentation via a standardized report form (capturing conditions, sequence of events, contributing factors, and recommended controls), review by a safety officer or management representative, and integration into a hazard log for trend analysis. Persistence is maintained through digital safety management systems, regulatory record-keeping mandates, and organizational learning cycles that feed reported near-misses back into risk assessments and training. The practice converts luck-based non-events into systematic intelligence about system fragility.[formal: relatio reportandi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-climate is the organizational-level construct that measures collective attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions about the priority, value, and support for safety within a given organization. It is distinguished from individual safety attitudes by its aggregated, shared nature — it emerges from organizational communication, leadership behavior, policy consistency, and reward structures, and is measured through validated survey instruments that capture employees' shared perceptions. The parameters that define it are: (1) it must be shared/perceived collectively, not merely individual; (2) it concerns safety specifically, not general organizational culture; (3) it is measured through standardized instruments (e.g., Safety Climate Survey). It persists through repeated measurement cycles and organizational practices that reinforce or erode collective safety perceptions. [formal: clima securitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Management review is the formal, periodic practice by which an organization's top leadership evaluates the continuing suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of its management system. It operates through scheduled review cycles, documented outputs (minutes, action items, decisions), and input data from internal and external sources including audit results, performance metrics, stakeholder feedback, and corrective action status. The practice persists through institutionalized cadence — typically annual or biannual — and is codified in management system standards such as ISO 9001 (quality), ISO 14001 (environment), and ISO 45001 (occupational health and safety). It is not the management system itself nor its governance structures; it is the deliberate act of leadership looking back at system performance to direct future improvement. [formal: management review | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.90]

Technical debt is a human-made conceptual metaphor in software engineering that frames accumulated code quality degradation as a financial debt instrument. The metaphor maps development shortcuts — writing quick solutions instead of well-architected ones — to borrowed capital that accrues interest in the form of increased future development cost, reduced adaptability, and higher defect rates. It persists through developer awareness, documentation of known shortcuts, prioritization frameworks that weigh refactoring against feature work, and the recurring tension between delivery speed and code quality. The construct is not literal debt: no creditor exists, no principal is owed, and the interest rates are estimated, not contractual. Its power lies in making abstract quality trade-offs legible to both engineers and non-technical stakeholders. [formal: technical debt | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: no | epoch: 0.95]

A safety-exercise is a structured practice activity organized by human institutions to train personnel in safety procedures and evaluate organizational readiness. Its parameters are: (1) it is a simulated or tabletop scenario, not a real emergency; (2) it involves active participation by personnel who would respond in a real incident; (3) it produces after-action observations and improvements. It persists through institutional memory, documented exercises, and repeated practice cycles embedded in safety management programs. [formal: exercitium securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An emergency-procedure is a documented sequence of actions designed to manage an emergency situation and minimize harm to people, property, and operations. Its parameters are: (1) it is formally written, maintained, and accessible to relevant personnel, (2) it covers specific emergency scenarios with step-by-step instructions, (3) it assigns roles and responsibilities for each action, (4) it includes escalation protocols and communication channels. The persistence mechanism is institutional documentation, updated after exercises and actual incidents. [formal: proceduralitatem | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-observability is a systematic practice of making safety conditions visible through continuous data collection, monitoring, and reporting mechanisms. Its parameters are: (1) it involves defined sensors, indicators, and thresholds that mark acceptable vs. concerning safety states; (2) it produces dashboards, alerts, and reports that aggregate safety data for decision-makers; (3) it is maintained as an ongoing organizational capability, not a one-time assessment. It persists through institutionalized monitoring programs, automated data pipelines, and standardized reporting frameworks that outlive individual practitioners. [formal: observabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-investment is the institutional practice of committing financial and material resources to safety improvements, preventive measures, and risk-mitigation infrastructure. Its parameters are: (1) it involves a deliberate allocation decision made through budgeting or capital-planning processes, (2) the allocated resources are directed toward activities whose primary benefit is risk reduction rather than direct production, and (3) the investment is recorded in organizational accounts as a distinct line item or category. Its persistence mechanism is formal budgetary commitment tracked through organizational accounting, sustained by recurring allocation cycles. [formal: safety-investment | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-climate-survey is a human-made instrument consisting of a standardized set of items (statements or questions) administered to members of an organization on a Likert-type scale, scored across predefined dimensions (e.g., supervisory safety commitment, co-worker safety norms, organizational priority of safety vs. production, reporting climate, risk perception). Its parameters are: (1) domain dimensions drawn from established occupational health psychology frameworks, (2) a fixed item set calibrated through factor analysis, (3) a scoring key that maps raw responses to dimension scores, and (4) a normative or longitudinal reference frame for interpretation. It persists through structured administration protocols, score repositories, and the institutional memory of repeated cycles — not as a physical artifact but as a repeatable procedure encoded in survey platforms and organizational practice. [formal: survey-climaticus | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hazard-reporting system is a human-made process consisting of documented channels, standardized forms, and organizational protocols by which workers and observers record, transmit, and track identified hazards for assessment and corrective action. Its parameters include reporting channels (anonymous, named, digital, paper), hazard classification schemas, escalation pathways, and response-tracking mechanisms. It persists through organizational safety management systems, regulatory compliance frameworks, and standardized digital or paper-based reporting platforms. [formal: relatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-climate-survey is a human-made instrument consisting of standardized questions administered to organizational members to measure their perceptions, attitudes, and beliefs about safety policies, practices, and priorities. It operates by collecting anonymous or attributed responses that aggregate into quantitative scores tracking safety culture trends over time. The survey mechanism persists through regular administration cycles, validated question banks, and scoring methodologies that enable comparison across time periods and departments. [formal: survey | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A risk register is a structured record maintained by human practice that catalogues identified risks with their probability, impact assessment, assigned owners, and planned responses. Its persistence mechanism is the documented record kept current through organizational procedures and regular review cycles. [formal: registrum periculorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

A safety-indicator is a quantifiable measure maintained through systematic data collection that tracks safety performance across three categories: leading indicators (predictive measures such as training completion rates and safety observation frequency), lagging indicators (historical measures such as incident rates and lost-time days), and critical indicators (threshold-based alerts requiring immediate action). Its persistence mechanism is periodic measurement, aggregation, and reporting through organizational safety management systems. [formal: indicium safetyis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-review is a formal, systematic examination of an organization's safety management systems, operational processes, and compliance records. It is conducted by trained reviewers who evaluate documentation, observe practices, interview personnel, and inspect physical conditions against established safety standards and regulations. The review produces findings, observations, and corrective action recommendations that feed into the organization's continuous improvement cycle. Safety-reviews operate on scheduled cycles (annual, quarterly) or trigger-based events (after incidents, process changes, regulatory updates). They persist through written reports, corrective action tracking systems, and organizational memory embedded in safety management practices. [formal: revisio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A runbook is a structured, documented set of step-by-step procedures designed for executing routine operational tasks, performing troubleshooting, and responding to incidents in a consistent and repeatable manner. It is created by organizations to standardize practice, reduce errors during high-pressure situations, and preserve institutional knowledge so that operators without deep expertise can perform complex tasks correctly. The runbook persists as a maintained reference document or knowledge-base entry, updated as procedures evolve. [formal: liber manualis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety permit is a controlled authorization document that must be completed, reviewed, and approved before high-risk work begins. It functions as a final checkpoint: the permit identifies specific hazards associated with the task, prescribes required control measures (engineering, administrative, PPE), designates authorized personnel (issuer, receiver, work performer), specifies work boundaries and validity conditions, and requires verification that all controls are in place. The permit system operates as a procedural barrier — work may not commence until the permit is signed, hazards are communicated to all workers, and controls are verified. This mechanism ensures that high-risk activities undergo structured review at the point of execution, not merely during prior planning. [formal: auctio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety observation report is a structured document used to record findings from systematic workplace observations of work activities, behaviors, and conditions. It is filled out by trained observers who watch work being performed and note compliance with safe work practices, identified hazards, at-risk behaviors, and positive safety behaviors. The report captures specific, observable data rather than opinions or inferences. It serves as the primary mechanism for collecting behavioral and condition-based safety data, feeding into safety trend analysis, targeted coaching, and continuous improvement of safety performance. The observation report is distinct from incident reporting in that it records near-misses, unsafe conditions, and safe behaviors proactively rather than reactively after harm has occurred. [formal: observatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.17]

Safety protection is a systematic approach to shielding people, assets, and operations from harm through engineered barriers, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. It operates as a layered defense strategy: primary engineering controls eliminate or isolate hazards at their source, secondary administrative controls govern safe work practices, and tertiary personal protective equipment provides the last line of defense. The construct persists through safety standards, regulatory requirements, and organizational procedures that mandate protection measures. [formal: protectio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.95]

Incident investigation is a structured human process for examining workplace incidents to determine root causes and implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence. It operates through systematic evidence collection (interviews, documentation review, physical inspection), causal analysis using formal methods (5-whys, fault-tree analysis, fishbone diagrams), and documented findings that feed into organizational learning. Parameters: (1) triggered by a reportable event (injury, near-miss, property damage, environmental release), (2) requires trained investigators, (3) produces a written report with findings and recommendations, (4) feeds corrective actions back into the safety management system. [formal: investigatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety competition is a structured human practice in which teams, sites, or departments compete against shared safety metrics — such as lost-time injury rates, hazard-reporting frequency, or audit scores — to drive continuous improvement in organizational safety performance. The mechanism operates through published leaderboards, periodic recognition events, and reward structures that make safety excellence a matter of group prestige. Its persistence mechanism is the ongoing maintenance of safety metrics, leaderboard publication, and institutional memory of competitive cycles; without these maintained practices the construct collapses. Safety competition is the use of competitive benchmarking as a lever for safety improvement. This definition is Law 6 compliant: the parameters (shared metrics, recognition events, reward structures) are carved, and the persistence mechanism (metrics maintenance, leaderboard publication, institutional memory) is stated.

Safety leadership is the organized practice and role of leaders in setting direction, allocating resources, and modeling behavior for safety within organizations. It operates through formal mechanisms (policy setting, resource allocation, safety committee participation) and informal mechanisms (role modeling, safety conversations, visible presence). It persists through organizational roles, training programs, performance evaluation, and cultural transmission across generations of workers. [formal: dux | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety sampling is a structured human practice of drawing systematic samples from a work environment, process, or population to assess safety conditions, hazard exposure, or compliance levels. It operates through defined sampling frames, randomized or stratified selection procedures, standardized observation checklists, and recorded results that feed into safety assessments and improvement programs. The method persists through documented protocols, sampling schedules, and archived records that enable trend analysis across time. [formal: inspectio抽样 | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A failover is a reliability engineering construct in which a system monitors a primary component (server, link, data center, process) for failure signals — health-check timeouts, error thresholds, loss of heartbeat — and upon detection triggers an automated handoff of its workload to a standby or degraded component that is pre-configured to assume the role. The transfer may be hot (state shared, sub-millisecond switchover), warm (state rebuilt on failover, seconds-to-minutes), or cold (manual or scripted reconstitution, minutes-to-hours). Persistence is maintained through configuration files, orchestration scripts, or dedicated failover controllers that encode the mapping of roles to backup resources. The construct is sustained by operational procedures, monitoring tooling, and periodic failover drills that keep the backup path verified and operators trained.\n\n[formal: transumptio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety incentive is a structured behavioral intervention that uses planned rewards (positive) or penalties (negative) to shape safety-related conduct among individuals or groups. Its parameters are: (1) the target behavior (e.g., reporting near-misses, complying with PPE requirements), (2) the reinforcement schedule (frequency and predictability of rewards/penalties), (3) the administering authority (who controls the rewards), and (4) the measured outcomes (behavioral compliance rates, incident reduction). The persistence mechanism is institutional policy — codified in written programs, embedded in performance evaluation systems, and sustained through repeated application. The design space includes reward-based programs (bonuses, recognition), penalty-based programs (disciplinary actions), and hybrid models. Effectiveness depends on alignment with actual risk exposure: incentive programs that reward only lagging indicators (zero-injury days) can produce underreporting, while those tied to leading indicators (safety observations completed, hazards reported) reinforce genuine safety engagement. [formal: incentivum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A stakeholder-analysis is a structured method for identifying, classifying, and mapping the individuals, groups, or organizations that are affected by or can affect a decision, project, or system. Its parameters are: (1) a defined scope or boundary for what is being analyzed, (2) a set of criteria for categorizing stakeholders (e.g., influence, interest, legitimacy, urgency), and (3) an output that documents stakeholder relationships and their relevance to the subject. It persists through documented outputs — reports, matrices, registers — and through the shared mental models these artifacts create in the teams that produce them, enabling repeatable application across projects and disciplines. [formal: stakeholder-analysis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety isolation is a hazard mitigation technique that physically or procedurally separates a hazard source from personnel, equipment, or other processes to prevent unintended energy release or exposure. It operates through three mechanisms: engineered barriers (guardrails, physical partitions, containment structures), administrative controls (procedures, permits, lockout-tagout protocols), and spatial separation (distance, zoning, exclusion areas). It persists through the continued maintenance of physical safeguards, the enforcement of procedural controls, and the institutionalization of separation requirements in design standards and operational manuals. [formal: isolatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety baseline is a measured reference point established through human practice — for hazard exposure, control effectiveness, or safety performance — against which subsequent conditions are compared to detect degradation, verify improvement, or satisfy regulatory requirements. It is maintained through documented standards, calibrated instrumentation, and periodic re-measurement cycles that ensure the reference remains valid over time. [formal: basalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Continuous integration is a software development practice in which developers merge their code changes into a shared repository multiple times per day. Each merge triggers an automated build and an automated test suite, enabling the team to detect integration errors quickly — usually within minutes of the change. The practice relies on a central repository, automated build infrastructure, and a comprehensive suite of regression tests. It persists through CI server configurations, build scripts, and team discipline. [formal: integratio continua | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-exit is a designated emergency egress route — a clearly marked, unobstructed path for occupant evacuation from a building during emergencies. Its parameters include: minimum width per occupancy load, maximum travel distance to reach, illuminated signage, fire-rated construction, and continuous clearance from hazards. It persists through building codes, architectural design standards, regulatory inspection regimes, and ongoing facility maintenance practices. [formal: exitus | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-committee is a formally constituted organizational body — a group of individuals designated by charter, regulation, or governance structure to oversee, advise on, and promote safety practices within a defined scope (department, site, or enterprise). Its parameters include: membership composition (representatives from management, workers, and safety specialists), meeting frequency, mandate scope, and reporting authority. It persists through institutional record (charters, bylaws, regulatory filings) and human practice (regular meetings, minutes, recommendations). [formal: comitatus securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-baseline-metric is a quantified safety threshold — a numeric value or range established through risk assessment, regulatory requirement, or industry best practice, against which organizational safety performance is measured and verified. Its parameters include: the hazard domain it addresses, the measurement methodology, the acceptance criteria, and the review cycle. It persists through documented safety baselines in compliance manuals, automated monitoring dashboards, and periodic audit reports that maintain the metric as an active governance instrument. [formal: mensura | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety education is the systematic, curriculum-based transmission of safety knowledge, procedural competence, and hazard-awareness through institutional teaching methods. It operates via structured programs (classroom instruction, hands-on practice, e-learning modules, awareness campaigns) designed by organizations or professional bodies to build and sustain workforce capability. Its persistence mechanism is institutional reproduction: repeated delivery through trainers, training materials, and assessment systems embedded within organizations, regulatory frameworks, and professional certification regimes. [formal: instructio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

Code review is a structured practice in which one or more developers systematically examine another developer's source code changes before those changes are integrated into the main codebase. The practice operates through three mechanisms: (1) a diff or patch is presented to reviewers who inspect it for correctness, security issues, adherence to style guidelines, and architectural coherence; (2) reviewers leave inline comments and overall approvals or requests for changes; (3) the change is only merged after receiving the required approvals. The persistence mechanism is tooling-enforced social practice: review platforms (e.g., GitHub Pull Requests, Gerrit) institutionalize the gate, CI pipelines block unreviewed merges, and organizational norms sustain the behavior across team membership changes. The practice extends human cognitive capacity — no single developer can hold the entire codebase in mind — by distributing inspection across multiple perspectives. [formal: revisio codicis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-learning is the structured organizational practice of capturing, analyzing, and institutionalizing knowledge derived from safety events, near-misses, audit findings, incident investigations, and operational data. It operates through formalized processes — including incident debriefs, after-action reviews, lessons-learned databases, and corrective-preventive action tracking — that convert discrete safety observations into persistent organizational knowledge. The practice persists through documented procedures, training curricula derived from past events, and knowledge-management systems that ensure safety-relevant insights survive personnel turnover. Its mechanism of persistence is organizational documentation and recurrent training cycles that embed learned corrections into standard operating procedures. [formal: cognitio-salutaris | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Emergency plan is a documented set of procedures designed to guide human action during unexpected crises — natural disasters, security threats, system failures, or other disruptive events — specifying roles, communication channels, evacuation routes, and resource allocation to minimize harm and enable rapid recovery. Persistence mechanism: written documentation maintained by organizations, regularly updated and practiced through drills. [formal: plan_emergentiae | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-data is the structured collection and management of information relating to safety performance, hazards, incidents, inspections, and risk assessments. It is created through systematic recording, categorized for retrieval, and maintained to support ongoing safety analysis, regulatory reporting, and continuous improvement. Safety-data transforms discrete observations into institutional knowledge that guides preventive action and demonstrates compliance over time. [formal: securitas data | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-automation is a class of engineered control systems that automatically execute safety-enforcing actions when predefined conditions are detected. It comprises sensor-triggered devices (interlocks, safety instrumented systems, emergency shutdown actuators, automatic alarms) whose function is to prevent, mitigate, or contain unsafe conditions without requiring human intervention. The persistence mechanism is engineered design embedded in physical systems, validated through safety integrity level (SIL) certification and periodic functional testing. [formal: automatio automatizatio | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
